talks.title: From Vision to Reality: Building the Future of Cybersecurity | Accelerate25
talks.teaser: Shows how a single endpoint agent combines secure remote access with EDR to improve threat detection.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with the need for secure connectivity between an organization's resources and its remote users, which the speaker describes as a core part of the vendor's wider secure access strategy. It then turns to a unified offering that brings access security and endpoint detection and response together, so both run inside one agent on the device rather than as separate products.

The speaker frames this combined approach as a way to improve threat detection as AI-driven threats rise, and to give security teams better visibility. The examples stay high level, with no technical walkthrough, configuration detail or case data, so the segment reads as a product positioning overview.

For a practitioner, the takeaway is the direction the vendor is taking: pairing remote access controls with EDR in one endpoint agent, aimed at stronger detection and clearer visibility. Because the talk is brief and product-oriented, it is best read as an overview of that strategy rather than a how-to.

talks.title: FortiPAM with ZTNA Tagging Features | Products and Solutions
talks.teaser: A product demo shows how FortiPAM enforces ZTNA tags so only chosen Windows 10 or 11 clients reach privileged assets.
talks.summary:
The session walks through a small lab where Windows endpoints talk to FortiClient EMS, which feeds posture tags into FortiPAM over the security fabric connector before users reach target assets. The presenter maps ZTNA tagging to operating system version, creating separate rules that label Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices.

Configuration starts in EMS security posture tagging, then validates FortiClient registration and FortiPAM login while no tag policies block either OS. With everything linked, the demo edits a network interface’s ZTNA tag options, first dropping Windows 10 from the allowed list to produce an expected access denial, then restoring it. The same steps block and later reopen Windows 11 access.

Viewers see how administrators can tie privileged access to device context without rebuilding the whole stack, and how quick policy toggles on tags immediately change who may open the FortiPAM portal from each client type.

talks.title: FortiSIEM Threat Intelligence Demo | SecOps
talks.teaser: Shows how a SIEM enriches incidents and traffic with threat feed data and malicious verdicts.
talks.summary:
This short vendor demo shows how FortiSIEM combines threat intelligence from several sources to assess IP addresses, URLs, and domains. The presenter starts in the resources area, browsing malware domain, malware IP, and malware URL lists that refresh with indicators of compromise from an IOC feed. The external integration settings are then shown, where feed instances for that IOC service and VirusTotal are already configured.

Next, the presenter opens a high-severity incident and shows that threat context appears directly on the incident screen, so analysts do not need separate searches. In the explorer view, a source IP taken from the malware IP list is checked. Its threat verdict identifies it as malware command-and-control, supported by IOC lookups with C2 kill-chain phases and confirmation from VirusTotal. A threat icon marks the source address, and the presenter notes that analysts can also search the malware IP list manually to verify an indicator.

The demo closes with traffic to malicious URLs, presented as a breakdown of related web activity. The presenter argues that this enriched intelligence reduces false positives, speeds up incident response, and helps teams find threats proactively.

talks.title: FortiSOAR: How to Implement Decision-Making Logic and Update Records | SecOps
talks.teaser: Shows how to branch a FortiSOAR playbook on VirusTotal malicious scores and update indicator reputation.
talks.summary:
This demo picks up from an earlier video in which IP addresses were extracted and enriched with the VirusTotal connector, and adds decision logic to the same FortiSOAR playbook. A decision point reads the malicious field from the VirusTotal analysis results and routes the playbook down one of two branches. The malicious branch is taken when that count is greater than 12, and the suspicious branch when the count is greater than 1 and at most 12. Both conditions use the advanced condition option with a dynamic value, so no manual expression writing is needed.

Each branch gets its own update record step aimed at the indicator model. The step maps the indicator ID from the record and sets its reputation to malicious or suspicious, and the decision point is then wired to execute the matching step. The playbook is saved and tested by ingesting a sample alert from the alerts page, after which the IP address appears as suspicious among the indicators.

To verify the run, the presenter checks the playbook executions log, the latest VirusTotal analysis showing a malicious verdict from 11 vendors, and the input fields of both conditions to confirm they were evaluated correctly. The takeaway is that dynamic values can be dropped straight into condition fields, letting analysts build and adjust SOC enrichment logic in FortiSOAR without writing code.

talks.title: FortiSOAR: How to Implement Nested Playbook Execution and User-Driven Decision Points | SecOps
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a FortiSOAR playbook that pauses for analyst approval before blocking a malicious IP.
talks.summary:
Automated playbooks sometimes need a person to sign off before a risky action runs. This demo shows how to build a FortiSOAR playbook that starts on an indicator update and pauses for human review. Conditions limit the trigger to IP address indicators whose reputation has just changed to malicious. A manual input decision step then displays a dynamic title with the malicious IP, a short explanation, and an approve or reject prompt. A response step sends approval to a manual task for an analyst at urgent priority, while rejection goes to a no-operation step.

The presenter enables debug mode to inspect execution logs, creates a test indicator, and approves the pending request from the notification area. The flow then waits at the manual task, which the analyst marks complete, and the log confirms every step finished. A firewall action is replaced by the task to keep the example simple.

The second part turns the same logic into a reference playbook with no trigger that runs only when a parent playbook calls it. The parent first sets the indicator reputation to malicious, then calls the reference playbook with the full environment passed through so variables carry over. After clearing old records and ingesting a new alert, the reviewer approves the indicator and the parent reports successful execution. Nested playbooks and approval gates can work together.

talks.title: FortiSOAR: How to Pass Custom Variables and Use Step Input Using Jinja Filter | SecOps
talks.teaser: Demonstrates passing playbook variables between steps and building conditions from VirusTotal results.
talks.summary:
This FortiSOAR demo walks through a playbook that starts when a new IP address indicator is created. The trigger filters on the indicator type being IP address, and a variable step stores the indicator's value field under a chosen name. A VirusTotal connector step then runs an IP reputation lookup using that variable rather than the raw indicator field, which keeps the playbook flexible and reusable.

The presenter switches the playbook to debug logging and creates a test indicator. The enrichment result flags the address as malicious, confirmed by 11 security vendors. The execution log is then reviewed step by step: the trigger's input record, the assigned variable, and the connector's input arguments, which show the raw variable name before processing and the resolved IP address after processing. The connector output, specifically the last analysis stats, supplies the malicious count that is used in a later decision step.

The decision step uses an advanced expression that the editor generates when a field is clicked in the step results panel, so the expression does not have to be typed by hand. To make the test condition match, the presenter adds a separate score variable set to 11 and references it in the condition. The takeaway is that custom variables and the step results panel let analysts build conditional logic inside the playbook editor, while the debug log shows what each step received and produced.

talks.title: FortiSOAR: How to Extract an IP Address and Querying VirusTotal | SecOps
talks.teaser: Shows how a FortiSOAR playbook enriches a malicious IP address with VirusTotal reputation data when an indicator is created.
talks.summary:
The demo walks through FortiSOAR and shows how an IP address indicator can be enriched with VirusTotal reputation data, and how a playbook can run automatically when that indicator is created. It starts in the alerts and indicators views, where indicators are classified as malicious, suspicious or benign, and where a manually added indicator triggers an enrichment request to VirusTotal.

The presenter then builds a new playbook for IP enrichment with VirusTotal, set to trigger on indicator creation. The trigger can be limited to IP addresses, file hashes or domains, and the speaker chooses IP address. A connector step uses the VirusTotal action to get IP reputation, and the IP input is filled dynamically from the indicator record instead of being typed by hand. The playbook is saved in debug mode for detailed execution output. The speaker notes that execution priority can be adjusted but keeps the default setting.

To test the workflow, an alert about command-and-control activity tied to a malicious public IP address is ingested into the incident response module. The indicator is generated automatically from that alert, and VirusTotal flags the address with 12 vendor detections. The playbook execution log confirms the run, and the output section and attribute view show the last analysis statistics. The takeaway is that automated enrichment on indicator creation gives analysts reputation context for an IP address without a separate manual lookup.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for In-Depth FortiDeceptor Deceptor-as-a-Service Demo | SecOps.

talks.summary: At MWC25 TIM and Fortinet pitch TIM Guardian, bundling DNS filtering through full SASE with Fortinet gear as Italian enterprises face NIS2 pressure and skill gaps. Executives argue ARPU is flat while traffic doubles, positioning managed security as monetizable carrier value beyond connectivity.

talks.title: FortiGate CNF Azure Blob Logging | Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Shows how to deploy a FortiGate CNF in Azure, enforce a port 80 block policy, and verify denied traffic in blob logs.
talks.summary:
The demo shows how to deploy a FortiGate CNF in Azure and send its logs to an Azure Blob storage account. The presenter explains that the firewall sits in front of compute resources behind a load balancer, and that inspection runs as a managed service, so customers do not maintain the underlying firewall infrastructure. Registration with the CNF portal and onboarding of the cloud account come first.

The test environment is a public Azure load balancer fronting an Ubuntu virtual machine that serves web pages. In the portal, the presenter deploys a new CNF instance with blob storage logging enabled, selects the storage account created during onboarding, and links the firewall to the existing load balancer's front-end IP. The initial policy allows all traffic. The presenter then switches the policy set to a rule that blocks HTTP on port 80, after which pages on port 80 stop loading while port 8080 keeps working.

To verify logging, the presenter opens the blob container, downloads a log file with Azure Storage Explorer, and searches for denied entries. The sample entry shows destination port 80, action denied, and the policy name block Port 80. The takeaway is that a policy applied at the firewall decides which traffic reaches workloads, and the blob logs record each decision for later review.

talks.title: FortiGate CNF Standalone Deployment in Azure | Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Demonstrates deploying a standalone FortiGate CNF in Azure and blocking port 80 with a policy set.
talks.summary:
This vendor demonstration shows how to deploy the FortiGate cloud native firewall (CNF) as a standalone instance in Azure, sitting in front of a load balancer that fronts customer compute resources. The test environment is an Ubuntu virtual machine running Apache and Nginx, reached through a standard Azure load balancer with a public frontend address. Traffic bound for those backends is routed through the firewall for inspection before it is allowed through.

The firewall is provisioned from the CNF portal, where the Azure account is already registered. The instance is given a name, placed in a region and attached to the load balancer, while optional FortiManager, logging and sandbox integrations are left off. Provisioning takes roughly 10 to 15 minutes. Before any policy change, the default policy set allows all traffic, and both port 80 and port 8080 respond. The presenter then applies a policy set that denies HTTP on port 80 while allowing the other ports.

After the change, requests to port 8080 still load, but requests to port 80 hang. The packet capture in the troubleshooting view shows repeated SYN packets on port 80 with no acknowledgement coming back, while the port 8080 exchange is acknowledged normally. The takeaway is that a deny rule on a service can be confirmed from packet captures at the firewall, and that the policy applies to traffic reaching the load balancer.

talks.title: FortiGate CNF Azure Cloud Onboarding | Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for FortiGate CNF Azure Cloud Onboarding | Cloud Security.

talks.title: FortiGate CNF Managed by FortiManager & Logging to FortiAnalyzer | Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Shows how to deploy a FortiGate cloud-native firewall in Azure, manage it with FortiManager, and log to FortiAnalyzer.
talks.summary:
The demo walks through deploying a Fortinet cloud-native firewall in Azure from the Marketplace. The presenter picks a name and region, then sends logs to FortiAnalyzer rather than blob storage or another destination. FortiManager handles management when several instances run, and optional sandbox and FSSO integrations are mentioned. The gateway load balancer endpoint is pointed at the customer's standard load balancer so traffic reaches the firewall for inspection.

Once provisioning completes, the presenter copies the primary FortiGate details that show FortiManager mode and the logging target, then adds the device to FortiManager with those admin credentials. A configuration import brings in policy packages and interfaces, including the virtual wire pair used toward the gateway load balancer. A test policy blocks HTTP on port 80 while allowing all other traffic, and the install wizard pushes it to the firewall.

To verify, a web server on a virtual machine loads on port 8080 but times out on port 80. Searching FortiAnalyzer for the client IP shows the port 80 requests logged as policy violations, while port 8080 traffic matches the final allow-all rule. The takeaway is that several cloud firewall instances can be provisioned, managed and logged from one place, with the policy checked by a simple before-and-after test.

talks.title: Streamline SOC Integration with FortiAnalyzer in Under 5 Minutes | SOC Analytics
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Streamline SOC Integration with FortiAnalyzer in Under 5 Minutes | SOC Analytics.

talks.title: Introduction to Fortinet FortiPAM | Privileged Access Management
talks.teaser: Demonstrates a privileged access management product's credential vault, proxy mode and session recording in a short guided walkthrough.
talks.summary:
This video gives a short overview and demo of FortiPAM, Fortinet's privileged access management product. It frames the problem as privileged accounts being a common route for both outside attackers and insiders. The presenter says the product addresses this with a credential vault, access policies and session monitoring. Users reach it through a web browser, FortiPAM proxies connections to critical targets, and it integrates with other Fortinet identity and reporting products.

The demo moves through the administration portal and the setup of targets and secrets. A target is an IT resource that can be promoted to a secret, which carries rules for who may access it, when, and how passwords change. The presenter explains proxy mode, where traffic passes through FortiPAM first so the client device never receives the sensitive login details, and where an administrator can end connections that look inappropriate. A Windows server is opened over Microsoft Remote Desktop, and a verification step confirms that the stored credentials work. Antivirus and DLP profiles are also enabled, with file types such as batch and executable files selected.

The demo then opens a FortiDDoS management session through a web player, with the credentials pre-filled. Sessions to the targets are logged and monitored, and recording can be switched on or off per secret. The final section shows recorded sessions and their logs, which list source address, destination, time and the profiles used. The practical takeaway is that privileged sessions can be controlled, recorded and reviewed from one place.

talks.title: Universal ZTNA Demo | Zero Trust
talks.teaser: Shows zero trust access to private applications gated by device posture tags, from managed and unmanaged endpoints.
talks.summary:
The talk is a walkthrough of a Fortinet universal zero trust network access setup for private applications, with access granted only to authorized users on acceptable devices. A FortiGate acts as an application gateway, mapping virtual IPs to real servers in a data center. It pulls real-time endpoint posture from the EMS server and authenticates users through an authenticator and an Active Directory server. The presenter shows how EMS can auto-discover ZTNA applications from release 7.4.1 onward and how each application is then assigned to an endpoint profile group.

Posture tags drive the policy. An endpoint compliance tag requires conditions such as domain membership, antivirus status and no high or critical vulnerabilities, while a vulnerable tag marks endpoints with critical findings. A deny policy blocks tagged-vulnerable endpoints from every ZTNA application. For a third-party contractor portal, an agentless policy uses SAML single sign-on without device certificate checks, while managed devices must pass device and user authentication, tag checks, and antivirus and IPS profiles.

Live tests cover browser access to a web console through a SAML redirect, SSH to a manager server, and RDP to an Active Directory server, where the client tunnels traffic to mapped virtual IPs after authentication. An unmanaged device reaches the contractor portal after user login only, and a vulnerable device is blocked. Traffic logs show the matched rule, the server and the endpoint tags at connection time, which gives practitioners a way to verify posture-based access decisions.

talks.title: Fortifying the Future: How Mainline and Fortinet Revolutionize Network Security | FortiSASE
talks.teaser: Presents a managed SASE platform that secures internet, private and application access for users working from anywhere.
talks.summary:
David Sanmo, networking security leader at Mainline Information Systems, opens by framing network security as a top priority, since attacks are moving faster and relying more on automation and AI. Staff now work from many locations and sensitive data sits in many places, so the perimeter no longer ends at the office walls. He argues that practitioners need visibility into the posture of every asset and must keep securing it continuously, using the same context wherever a user or resource is located.

The middle of the talk introduces FortiSASE as a managed service that Fortinet runs, so the customer simply consumes it. According to the speaker, it addresses risk across internet access, private access and application access within one platform, instead of requiring an organization to maintain three separate solutions. He contrasts this with older remote access models that involved occasional patching, and says organizations now have to manage threats and posture on an ongoing basis.

To close, the talk presents Mainline as an expert-level Fortinet partner, a relationship described as continuous collaboration to bring strong technical solutions to customers. The speaker says Mainline supports Fortinet products across design, architecture, deployment and service, and presents Fortinet as suited to both current and future threats. The talk is brief and works as a vendor-positioning overview rather than a technical demonstration.

talks.title: Understanding Cybersecurity Regulations: Why You Shouldn't Fear Regulators | Brass Tacks
talks.teaser: Explains why financial regulation aims to contain cyber incidents and how CISOs and vendors share responsibility for security.
talks.summary:
Joe Robertson hosts Brass Tacks, a show aimed at business leaders, and his guest is George Fernandez, CISO and data protection officer at CMVM, the Portuguese capital markets supervisor. Fernandez speaks in a personal capacity. He traces his path from system administrator to security specialist, including roles at a European securities regulator and a development bank, before returning to CMVM.

On the CISO role, he argues the job is managerial and enabling. A CISO should remove obstacles for their team, understand how each department works, and look for ways to say yes securely, since blanket refusals push staff toward shadow IT. He also favours reporting to a board member such as the CFO or CEO rather than sitting inside IT, which avoids a conflict between running operations and managing security. On regulation, he frames it as protecting investors, keeping competition fair, and requiring firms to manage risk so that one organisation's incident does not spread across a sector. Under DORA, proportionality lets smaller firms use simpler risk management processes.

He then discusses the US CISA Secure by Design pledge, which matters to European firms because they buy American software and hardware. He welcomes shifting more of the burden onto vendors: no default passwords, multifactor authentication, prompt fixes for vulnerabilities, and longer support lifecycles. These matter for hospital devices and industrial control systems that cannot be upgraded easily. The practical takeaway for buyers is to expect secure defaults and continued security updates from the products they purchase.

talks.title: FortiSIEM Advanced Structured Analytics: DayOFWeek | Security Information and Event Management
talks.teaser: Demonstrates filtering FortiSIEM logs by weekday to spot RDP logins from a network range over weekends.
talks.summary:
This demo shows how to use the day-of-week function in the advanced structured analytics section of FortiSIEM. The function numbers the days of the week, with 1 for Monday through 7 for Sunday, so results can be narrowed to particular days. The goal is to find users who connect over RDP on weekends, which can point to unauthorized access.

The presenter builds a query over Windows terminal events and adds a regular expression filter on the reporting IP so it matches a 10.9 network range. That avoids needing to know individual addresses. The received-time attribute is then filtered with the day-of-week function set to 6 and 7, covering Saturday and Sunday. Results are grouped by day of week with a count of matching events, giving a per-day view of weekend activity. Adding the user field to the group-by display narrows the output to the specific accounts that logged in on those days.

The presenter notes that the same query can be saved as a rule to alert on this behavior and added to a dashboard for ongoing monitoring. The practical takeaway is that simple time-based filters, combined with network range matching, can surface logins that fall outside normal working days.

talks.teaser: Demonstrates a cloud-based scanner that checks applications in CI/CD pipelines and reports findings in a web portal.
talks.summary:
FortiDevSec is presented as a cloud-based application security tool that scans applications for vulnerabilities and fits into DevOps and CI/CD pipelines such as GitHub, GitLab and Jenkins. The deployment uses a thin Docker container with the scanners, placed in the customer environment, which communicates with the cloud service so results can be viewed in a web portal. The scanners cover static analysis, software composition analysis, secrets detection, container scanning and infrastructure as code. Supported languages and integrations with the Fortinet Fabric, FortiDAST, Jira and Visual Studio are also listed.

The middle of the talk is a live walkthrough of the portal. The main page lists scanned applications by risk rating, along with outbreak alerts, supply chain threat links and counts of scans in progress and completed that week. An infrastructure as code finding points to the exact file and line, while the details view gives the branch, commit ID and other information needed to fix it. Container results are presented in a similar way. A sample application shows static analysis and secrets findings, plus a software bill of materials that lists open-source packages and marks those with known vulnerabilities. The FortiDAST view then summarizes CVSS scores, vulnerability categories and top risks, and lists findings by URI and by the scanner that found them.

The takeaway for practitioners is that application scanning can be built into the development pipeline so developers can see where each issue lives and what change resolves it. The five-minute talk is a brief product overview and demo rather than a technical deep dive.

talks.teaser: A global sports tour outlines cloud SASE for roaming staff, Entra ID group alignment, and worldwide PoP selection for secure access.
talks.summary:
The presentation centers on how the DP World Tour secures a workforce that moves between events around the world. Organizers describe network security as a core challenge for agile, global tournament operations, and frame FortiSASE as the way to protect users regardless of location.

Implementation priorities emphasized frictionless rollout for end users and tighter integration with tools already in place. The team aligned Microsoft Entra ID security groups with the SASE platform to cut manual steps and reduce errors. They describe access checks that combine edge protection, identity management, segmentation, and cloud brokerage, with ongoing validation of user and device posture before resources are reachable. Existing Fortinet deployments were extended to improve connectivity reliability rather than replace everything at once.

On operations, they report no meaningful performance penalty and improved experience by routing through selected points of presence from Fortinet’s roughly 150 global locations. Professional services supported planning and timing. The rollout is positioned as ongoing architecture for delivering tournament technology anywhere, not a one-off project.

talks.title: SD-WAN Overlay-as-a-Service: Part 2 | Secure SD-WAN
talks.teaser: Shows how a single intent-based policy in Fortinet's overlay-as-a-service creates site-to-site access rules across SD-WAN FortiGates.
talks.summary:
This demo continues a series on Fortinet's overlay-as-a-service for Secure SD-WAN. The presenter's setup has four sites, three branches and one data center, and the goal is to let every site reach every other site without writing rules on each device by hand. The speaker builds one address group that covers all the local area networks in the overlay, then creates a single policy that allows traffic between them and pushes it out with an apply step.

To check the result, the presenter logs into the data center FortiGate and a New York branch FortiGate. The single intent-based policy has turned into several device-level policies on each unit, with six appearing on the New York branch. The second use case lets the branch sites reach a web server in the data center. The speaker creates a dedicated address object for that server and adds antivirus and IPS protection profiles, since the server may accept file uploads. After the policy is applied, the FortiGates again show multiple generated policies.

The practical takeaway is that the overlay service converts one policy written at the intent level into many per-device rules. The time and complexity saved grow with the number of sites, and security inspection can be attached to the same intent-based policy.

talks.title: FortiSandbox 5.0: FortiSandbox 5.0: Quicker, Faster and Scalable | Security Operations
talks.teaser: Walks through FortiSandbox 5.0's new AI engine, universal VM licensing, and SOC assist features for analysts.
talks.summary:
### Overview
FortiSandbox version 5.0 introduces major updates designed to enhance speed, detection, and scalability in combating unknown malware and phishing. FortiSandbox inspects files, websites, and network traffic for suspicious activity, having operated for over a decade. Version 5.0 introduces three primary enhancements: Advanced AI, Universal VM, and SOC Assist, along with a new connectivity and services widget and more than 50 additional features detailed in the release notes.

### Key Topics
- **Advanced AI and Purpose-Built Machine Learning**: An updated AI engine with regular model updates designed to detect more file-based threats and zero-day malware.
- **Universal VM**: Simplified virtualization licensing allowing mixed deployments across multiple operating systems.
- **SOC Assist**: A multi-part feature set built to streamline on-demand analysis, job review, and incident triage for security operations centers.
- **System Monitoring**: Centralized monitoring of appliance connectivity and operational status.

### Technical Details
- **Advanced AI Engine**: Detects emerging file-based threats, such as PDFs containing ransomware notes (for instance, ransom demands directed via Discord). This functionality is offered via the Advanced Sandbox bundled subscription, which includes real-time anti-phishing and IOC enrichment.
- **Universal VM Licensing & Deployment**: Users can access multiple virtual machines using a single license type. From the VM setting page, administrators can download available VMs from FortiGuard and configure clones locally or in the cloud across various operating systems, including Windows, Linux, and Android.
- **SOC Assist Features**:
  - *On-Demand Submission*: Provides enhanced ease of use and advanced analysis capabilities, such as skipping antivirus scanning, recording video of execution, and performing direct VM interaction.
  - *Job Detail Page*: Displays an AI-provided summary of context findings at the top, standard submission metadata, and analysis over time. Includes a Behavior tab with clickable, drill-down indicators and a Threat Intelligence tab featuring threat enrichment, an IOC listing table, and an attack matrix.
  - *Incident Assist Page*: Designed for daily operations to evaluate detected threats, answering operational questions such as who is targeted, how the threat was delivered, and the threat's nature, while enabling status tracking for ongoing investigations.
- **Connectivity and Services Widget**: Provides a consolidated system health dashboard to monitor whether the unit is fully operational.

### Takeaways
FortiSandbox 5.0 significantly refines security operations by integrating machine learning threat detection with modular virtual analysis environments. SOC teams gain deeper investigative controls through interactive VM sessions, video recording, AI context summaries, and dedicated incident evaluation workflows.

talks.title: Board Communication Essentials for CISOs: Meeting Exec Expectations | Brass Tacks
talks.teaser: Explains how CISOs can present cyber risk, asset ownership and metrics to executives and boards in plain terms.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with how cyber security has shifted from a technical concern to a business requirement. The guest, a global CISO at a coatings manufacturer operating in about 150 countries, points to customer contracts and laws such as the EU's NIS2 directive and DORA for finance as reasons companies can no longer leave security to one department. With attack surfaces spanning staff, factories and connected devices, he argues for a structured management system built on people, processes and technology.

The middle focuses on accountability. He describes asset owners, such as a marketing department owning its marketing plans, as holding the risk for their assets, while the security team identifies threats, recommends controls and monitors results. He outlines the three lines of defense, with operations first, risk and the CISO second, and internal audit third. For boards, he recommends covering the exposure surface, quantifying risk on a numeric scale and tracking indicators that show what security spending achieves. In one example, a 10% failure rate in phishing tests is easy for non-experts to grasp, and he notes that a 90% pass rate still leaves an opening for attackers.

On reporting lines, he argues the CISO needs authority and independence to assess risk wherever the role sits. Less mature organizations may keep the security team close to operations to build foundations, while mature ones may place it independently to avoid conflicts of interest. Practitioners should take away early agreement on risk ownership, numbers executives can follow, and metrics that show whether controls actually reduce exposure.

talks.title: Secure SD-WAN Customer Panel
talks.teaser: Three enterprise customers explain why they chose Fortinet Secure SD-WAN and what results they measured.
talks.summary:
Three enterprise customers described why they adopted Fortinet Secure SD-WAN. The hospitality group IHG, with about 6,200 hotels in roughly 100 countries, said its older infrastructure made rollouts hard to scale, offered little visibility and slowed guest check-in. Grupo Bimbo, a baking company in 34 countries, was pursuing a SaaS and multicloud transformation that needed secure connectivity and lower cost without losing performance. The Latin American bank, with over 3,000 branches, cited regulatory duties, customer data protection and the cost of carrier links.

IHG said an in-house build failed and that an RFP led it to a platform where most of the features it needed ran on the firewall it already used, at the best value. Grupo Bimbo valued adding SD-WAN within the same fabric, which avoided fragmented tools and suited its regional partners. The bank ran a proof of concept, lab tests and production tests, citing an analyst leader ranking, and keeps management in-house with only carrier links from providers.

IHG cut round-trip times by over 30% on day one and about 50% later. The bank saw roughly 14% lower response times for cloud applications like Teams, since branch traffic could go straight to the internet with security applied, and it resolved issues about 20% faster through a central console. Grupo Bimbo reported savings it reinvested in performance, plus redundancy the old setup lacked. The panel closed by stressing that reliability at the scale of thousands of sites matters most.

talks.title: FortiGate-as-a-Service Secure Wireless LAN | FGaaS
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiGate-as-a-Service centrally manages wireless access points, secures IoT devices and rates network security posture.
talks.summary:
The talk is a product walkthrough of FortiGate-as-a-Service, a cloud-managed setup for securing wireless networks across branch offices and campuses. It starts with deploying a FortiGate through the FortiGate-as-a-Service portal and using zero-touch provisioning to push access points to an external controller, identified by the FortiGate's management IP. The access points then appear on the FortiGate's Wi-Fi controller page waiting for authorization, since they connect over CAPWAP.

Next, the presenter configures an SSID in tunnel mode so that all wireless client traffic passes through the FortiGate for central monitoring and inspection. A firewall policy then lets IoT devices on that SSID reach the internet with security services applied. IoT detection identifies connected devices using FortiGuard intelligence, and the assets and identities view lists them, with each device matched against vulnerability data to show which ones are at risk.

The demo then covers responses. Administrators can use FortiGate policies for micro-segmentation, limit device communication, and quarantine vulnerable IoT devices until patches are available, which keeps them away from critical network segments. The security rating feature scores the device and its network by analyzing configuration, flagging weaknesses, and comparing results against industry best practices. The takeaway is that one cloud-managed controller can give distributed sites consistent wireless policy, IoT visibility and risk-based isolation.

talks.title: Web Proxy and Security Inspection with FGaaS | FortiGate-as-a-Service
talks.teaser: Shows a cloud-hosted FortiGate acting as a web proxy that filters URLs, content, applications and malware for a Windows client.
talks.summary:
FortiGate as a Service is a cloud-hosted FortiGate firewall that can run as a secure web proxy, so an organisation can filter web traffic without buying or maintaining hardware. The walkthrough starts by deploying an instance and enabling the explicit proxy on a listening interface. A proxy policy is then built on a profile that combines antivirus, web filtering, application control, IPS and SSL deep inspection. On the client side, a Windows machine is pointed at the proxy using either a PAC file or manual settings, and the FortiGate deep inspection certificate is added to the browser's trusted authorities so encrypted traffic can be inspected.

The tests show each control working in turn. Searches for gambling and weapons terms are stopped by content filtering, and a dating site is blocked by a URL filter rule. Application control blocks the Roblox gaming app, and antivirus scanning stops downloads of a test file and a malware sample. The security events view then breaks these out by category, with the web filter, application control and antivirus entries each showing the matched policy and, for antivirus, the FortiGuard signature reference.

The takeaway is that a single cloud proxy can enforce web access policy, guard against web-borne malware, and support bandwidth and compliance goals for both small and large organisations. The presenter stresses that the service scales with the business, so capacity grows without new hardware.

talks.title: Connect Code Flaws to Cloud Risk | Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Walks through Lacework Code Security, which flags vulnerable dependencies in repositories, pull requests and CLI scans.
talks.summary:
This video is a short feature overview of Lacework Code Security, a release meant to give teams full risk visibility across their application development pipeline. It argues that development work slows down when vulnerabilities are handled one at a time at different stages of the life cycle, and that the fix is to bring that data together with context. The scanning covers vulnerable packages and third-party libraries, software license compliance, and generation of a software bill of materials (SBOM) for audits.

The walkthrough starts in the code security dashboard in the console, which lists repositories connected through GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, CI/CD pipelines or a CLI scan. Each repository shows a count of vulnerabilities, their average CVSS score and a severity breakdown. Drilling into a branch lists the CVEs from the latest scan with the CVE ID, current version, fixed version and affected dependencies. A VS Code extension gives developers local feedback on code before it is committed.

Source control integration scans incoming pull requests and shows the findings inside the PR, where the team can decide whether to release the change or apply the suggested fix. When vulnerable dependencies are found, the tool opens PRs on its own, with details about the vulnerability and any automated fix. The CLI reports vulnerabilities, license compliance, SBOM and discovered secrets. The main takeaway is that developers and security or compliance teams can work from the same findings.

talks.title: Reduce Cloud Identity Risk | Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Follows a compromised EC2 instance to show how entitlement data exposes over-privileged roles and unused admin access.
talks.summary:
The demo walks through a fictional incident at Interlace Labs, where a newly onboarded contractor launched an example app on an EC2 instance carrying the standard instance profile and left it running. The first alert, a critical reverse shell connection on that host, showed four critical vulnerabilities, including a Java Log4j flaw, and one discovered secret. Responders traced the attached IAM role, whose policies granted broad SSM, KMS and RDS access, though no use of those permissions had been seen yet.

A second anomaly alert linked the same role and instance to RDS and KMS calls, create DB snapshot and create grant, a common early step for attackers seeking to pull database data from a cloud account. The entitlements view rated the profile high risk for resource exposure and sensitive API access, with only 44% of entitled resources and 63% of entitled services used. Comparing the June 3 and June 4 snapshots showed RDS and IAM newly marked as used, and the profile could read SSM parameters holding database connection details. The contractor user also held full admin access and hardcoded AWS API credentials.

The recommended fix was to strip administrative access from the contractor, since those rights had gone unused for 180 days, and to trim the instance profile in the same way. The team disabled the host, cut excess permissions, and started a wider initiative to rightsize access by sorting high-risk identities with low usage.

talks.title: Reduce the Risk of Cloud Misconfiguration | Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Demonstrates scanning infrastructure-as-code and container images in a CI pipeline to block vulnerable builds.
talks.summary:
This short demonstration shows how the Lacework platform can be wired into a software build to catch cloud misconfigurations and vulnerable container images before they ship. The first part connects a GitHub organization to infrastructure-as-code scanning, which checks template files against compliance policies. Each finding lists the policy name, its severity and the offending line. Where an automated fix is available, the tool can open a pull request containing the suggested change.

The second part covers container image checks. An inline scanner is created in the console with its own token, plus settings for scan limits, an identifier tag and a CI/CD policy. In the example GitHub Actions workflow, the image is built and then scanned by the inline scanner running as a Docker container. The scan step is set to fail on exit and to send results to the console, tagged with the build ID. A policy that blocks on critical, fixable CVEs stops the pipeline, so deployments to dev, staging and production do not run.

The speaker then traces the failed run back to the console by filtering container vulnerabilities on that build ID, showing end-to-end traceability. The talk closes by noting that a Kubernetes admission controller acts as a final check before an image reaches the production cluster. The practical takeaway is to enforce image scanning as a pipeline gate and to link each build to its scan results.

talks.title: Introducing Lacework FortiCNAPP
talks.teaser: A walkthrough shows FortiCNAPP composite alerts, compliance gaps, vulnerabilities, and attack paths for faster cloud incident response.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the idea that organizations differ yet share the same goals: limiting breach impact and acting quickly when incidents occur. Lacework positions its cloud security platform as combining prevention with response by analyzing large data volumes to supply context for faster decisions.

The demo centers on a cloud-native ransomware scenario surfaced through composite alerts, which bundle indicators of compromise to answer what happened and what it means. The walkthrough shows compromised cloud identity with full admin rights, then pivots to prevention: compliance auditing of access keys, host vulnerability lists with CVE and fix versions, and active package detection to prioritize running vulnerable software. Identity exploration highlights high-severity risks, and the explorer relates resources so exposure and privileged identity together raise priority.

Attack path analysis closes the loop, tracing a route from the public internet through gateway and security group misconfigurations to a host, and showing how broad identity privileges amplify risk. The takeaway for practitioners is to use consolidated alerting, hygiene checks, and graph-style path analysis to neutralize active threats and harden configuration before compromise.

talks.title: FortiSIEM Agents On and Off Network | Security Information and Event Management
talks.teaser: Shows how a FortiSIEM agent keeps forwarding logs through an internal collector and an internet-facing collector.
talks.summary:
This demo explains how a FortiSIEM agent on an endpoint behaves when it sits on the corporate network and when it moves onto the internet. The deployment shown uses one supervisor and two collectors: one inside the internal network and one facing the internet, with both reachable under the same DNS name. The presenter outlines the agent's benefits, including high-performance log collection, file integrity monitoring, user and entity behavior analytics, and event filtering to reduce log volume.

On the internal network, the workstation is shown in the CMDB with its agent running under a demo policy. An agent template links the endpoint to a virtual collector name, and a ping to the DNS name returns the internal collector's address, confirming connectivity. Collector health in the admin tab lists the collectors connected to the supervisor, and an analytics search grouped by collector name and reporting device displays the raw logs arriving from that host.

For the off-network scenario, the DNS name resolves to the internet-facing collector's address, so the agent sends its logs there instead. After the endpoint leaves the office, its CMDB IP address updates to the new public address, and the same analytics query shows its logs arriving through the external collector. The takeaway is that the agent keeps reporting consistent visibility wherever the user works, whether in an office, at home or in a public place with internet access.

talks.title: FortiProxy as ICAP Server Integration with FortiGate | Secure Web Gateway
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiProxy acts as an ICAP server for FortiGate, offloading antivirus, DLP and web filtering with live block tests.
talks.summary:
Organizations want web access that is both secure and fast, and this session looks at pairing FortiProxy with FortiGate so the firewall can hand web traffic off for deeper inspection. The speaker explains the ICAP flow: FortiGate intercepts an HTTPS request, sends the content to FortiProxy, and receives back the processed result. Along the way the proxy applies web filtering, antivirus scanning and data loss prevention before content reaches the user.

The configuration walkthrough covers creating a local ICAP server service on FortiProxy with antivirus, web filter and DLP profiles, then setting up the FortiGate side with an ICAP server entry, an ICAP profile pointing to that service, and a firewall policy in proxy-based inspection mode with deep SSL inspection. The demo then shows a malicious site blocked by the web filter, an infected file caught by the antivirus engine, and files containing credit card data stopped by DLP rules.

The speaker closes by checking the FortiProxy security logs, where each block appears under the antivirus, web filter and DLP views with the service, profile and response-modification method shown. The takeaway is that FortiGate can concentrate on firewalling and routing while FortiProxy handles the specialized content inspection.

talks.title: FortiNDR Cloud: OT Demo | Network Detection and Response
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how an NDR cloud service detects and investigates Modbus and SCADA attacks in operational technology networks.
talks.summary:
The demo opens with the problem of converging IT and OT networks, which leaves industrial environments exposed and calls for tools that reduce risk without disrupting operations. The presenter introduces the expanded OT coverage of FortiNDR Cloud, which offers detection, investigation, threat hunting and custom rules. The product portal's guide lists the supported event types and fields, including DNP3, DNP3 control, DNP3 object and Modbus events, which can feed investigations and rule creation.

The presenter then moves to the detections tab, where a SCADA Modbus-related attack has been flagged. The alert includes a description, the technique involved, recommended mitigation steps, the affected device IP address and signature details such as the rule ID, name, payload and category. An events view lets analysts search for activity before and after the alert to see what may have triggered it. Next, an investigation is created with a name, search criteria and a time frame. It runs in the background and reports when complete, and its results show source and destination IPs, protocol and connection duration.

To go deeper, the presenter adds a Modbus query that returns logs of function codes such as diagnostics, read coils and write single coil. A final SCADA query matches signature names and shows their categories, IDs, payloads and protocols. The takeaway is that analysts can use event-specific queries like these to investigate and hunt for threats within OT environments.

talks.title: Building Cyber Resilience: Aligning People, Processes, Tech, & Compliance | Brass Tacks Podcast
talks.teaser: A Fortinet CISO explains how cyber risk ties to business strategy, resilience, and executive responsibility.
talks.summary:
Host Joe Robertson talks with Danielle Manini, a Fortinet CISO for Europe who previously held CISO roles at several global companies. The episode is aimed at non-technical executives and board members. Manini says security discussions should start from business strategy, and she names three drivers: the growing volume of data from connected machines and AI, the speed at which external events force reactions, and the interconnection of partners, regulators and suppliers.

She frames these conversations around people, processes and technology, and their effect on finance, customer perception, internal performance and the organization's capacity to learn. Security can be a competitive edge when customers see their data protected. As executives face personal liability under rules such as GDPR and NIS2, she centres the discussion on resilience: continuity and disaster recovery plans, and the ability to recover and adapt after an attack. She also covers cloud outsourcing, where data control must be kept even when a provider runs the infrastructure, and operational technology, where availability often outranks confidentiality and integrity in production plants.

Her closing advice is to build security into projects from the start, which she says is cheaper and more effective than adding it later, and to keep educating staff on the threats they face. She sees mutual value between vendors and CISOs: vendors can learn how innovation affects business strategy, while CISOs can learn how vendors move quickly on innovation, and both aim to keep attackers out.

talks.title: Quantifying Cyber Risk: A Board-Level Cybersecurity Priority | Brass Tacks
talks.teaser: Explains how boards can weigh cyber risk in business terms, covering operational, reputational, compliance and strategic exposure.
talks.summary:
IDC analyst Mark Child explains why cyber security now belongs in board discussions. The EU's NIS2 directive makes senior management responsible for overseeing cyber risk measures and liable for infringements, and similar rules exist elsewhere. Because boards find the technical side hard to grasp, he suggests framing risk in four business terms. Operational risk is illustrated by a Scandinavian aluminium producer offline for almost a week. Reputational risk is shown by a UK telecom whose brand suffered after a large customer data leak. Compliance risk is shown by a hotel group that inherited compromised systems in an acquisition. Strategic risk is shown by a network equipment maker that lost its technical papers and R&D reports over years, and no longer exists.

Since the pandemic pushed firms online, CISOs have moved closer to the top, with one in five reporting to the CEO in IDC's survey. Traditional risk assessment is manual, subjective and slow, so demand is growing for quantification dashboards that prioritise vulnerabilities across on-premises, cloud, OT and IoT assets, often using AI or machine learning.

Mark recommends first identifying critical assets and presenting risks, after which the board sets risk appetite while the CISO manages the risk. Metrics such as mean time to detect, respond and recover should be chosen to suit each audience, and industry benchmarking helps reduce many numbers to a simple comparison with peers.

talks.summary:
The session introduces Fortinet’s FortiGate-as-a-Service model for delivering next-generation firewall capacity without customers owning and racking hardware upfront. FortiPoints act as the currency for the service and are purchased through the FortiCloud Marketplace; the demo assumes an account already holds enough points to order appliances.

The walkthrough follows the FortiCloud ordering UI from login through placement of a new FortiGate. Viewers see how to name a deployment, pick a site, choose among hardware SKUs such as the 91G, 901G, and 3501F lines, and attach UTP or Enterprise protection plus optional add-on subscriptions. Software release selection, optional high-availability pairs versus a single unit, and per-device IP addressing limits are explained, along with declaring Internet bandwidth between 100 megabits per second and 10 gigabits. After order confirmation, provisioning status is tracked until the unit becomes active within minutes, with billing dates visible for planning.

Operators retrieve the initial management password, sign in through the assigned management IP, and can confirm HA state from the system menus. The closing message positions FGaaS for MSPs and enterprises that want on-demand FortiOS bundles—including SD-WAN, secure SD-WAN-style hosting, and wireless-controller use cases—under a pay-as-you-go model that reduces data-center capital spend.

talks.title: FortiGate Managed Service Onboarding | Cybersecurity Services
talks.teaser: Shows how to onboard to the managed FortiGate service, from selecting devices and users to enabling FortiManager Cloud.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this walkthrough, Paolo Grassi, Senior Director of Product Management overseeing the Managed FortiGate Service, demonstrates the onboarding process for new customers using the FortiCloud dashboard. The service leverages FortiManager Cloud for cloud-based centralized device management. The onboarding walkthrough covers reviewing device entitlements, stepping through the onboarding wizard, configuring role-based user access, submitting the initial request, and performing local device authorization to finalize managed service operations.

### Key Topics
- **Service Navigation & Device Overview**: Navigating to 'Managed FortiGate' via FortiCloud Services and understanding device registration, entitlement states, and timeline tracking.
- **Preparation & Customer Classification**: Specifying whether an account operates as a Regular Customer (managing internal FortiGates) or an MSSP (managing client FortiGates).
- **Deployment & Device Selection**: Selecting the deployment region for the FortiManager Cloud instance and importing entitled FortiGate devices.
- **User Management & Role Assignment**: Assigning granular roles (Administrator, Initiator, Approver) to support corporate separation of duties or combined privileges.
- **Submission & Service Timelines**: Finalizing requests, uploading supporting documentation or notes, and tracking progress against an expected three-business-day turnaround.
- **Central Management Authorization**: Configuring Fabric Connectors on individual FortiGate firewalls to authorize management access via FortiManager Cloud.

### Technical Details
- **Dashboard Location**: Accessed under `Services > Cloud Services > Managed FortiGate` on FortiCloud.
- **Customer Types**: Users choose between 'Regular Customer' (own FortiGates) and 'MSSP' (client devices under the FortiCloud account), which customizes subsequent wizard fields.
- **FortiManager Cloud Provisioning**: Customers select a hosting region from a dropdown list to deploy the cloud instance used by the Managed FortiGate service team.
- **Device Import**: Populates serial numbers, descriptions, and location metadata automatically from FortiCloud for devices holding active, non-onboarded service entitlements.
- **Access Roles**: Requires at least one of each role:
  - *Administrator*: Manages portal settings and accesses the user management section.
  - *Initiator*: Creates service or change requests.
  - *Approver*: Reviews and approves change requests created by other users.
- **Local Device Configuration**: After the backend instance is provisioned, authorization is finalized in the FortiGate GUI under `Security Fabric > Fabric Connectors > Central Management`. The status must be set to `Enabled` with type set to `FortiManager Cloud` (leaving default parameters intact), generating an authorization request processed by the service team.

### Takeaways
The onboarding workflow integrates directly with FortiCloud to automate device discovery, user imports, and instance provisioning. Successful deployment requires active service entitlements, proper setup of required administrative and operational roles, and a specific local device authorization step inside FortiOS Central Management settings before the Managed FortiGate service team can actively monitor and manage customer firewalls.

talks.title: Network Access Control Made Simpler | FortiNAC
talks.teaser: Shows how SNMP-led FortiNAC visibility enables phased access control and fabric tagging without disruptive inline deployment.
talks.summary:
Network access control still carries a reputation for complexity because many deployments begin with 802.1X, certificates, and RADIUS. The discussion argues that organizations can start simpler by using SNMP community strings and APIs many networks already expose, placing FortiNAC at the center of the environment to ingest data from switches, wireless, IoT, and other gear without necessarily sitting inline.

The speakers walk through a phased path: visibility first in a non-intrusive mode, then access control informed by what endpoints are actually on the wire, and finally automated response such as isolating a malicious client. They contrast decentralized inline NAC with out-of-band visibility, highlight broad multi-vendor support, and show how fabric connectors send dynamic tags to FortiGate policies so PLCs, printers, and similar devices get tighter rules than VLAN placement alone. Built-in FortiOS NAC features can segment outdated iPads or headless IoT without an extra license, with FortiNAC added when centralized identity checks or scale demand it.

Parting guidance stresses asking whether teams truly know every connected device, leveraging existing SNMP where possible, and deferring enforcement until confidence grows. Zero trust is framed as revalidation after disconnect, returning endpoints to a default or isolated VLAN until policy checks pass again. Hot customer topics include hybrid cloud identity, very large endpoint counts, and extending visibility as infrastructure moves.

talks.title: Deliver Digital Experience Monitoring for Coffee Shop Networking with FortiMonitor | DEM Platform
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiMonitor measures application performance for remote workers on unstable networks, from cafes to home offices.
talks.summary:
This is a short product walkthrough of FortiMonitor, a digital experience monitoring platform aimed at employees who work from anywhere, including cafes, hotels and home offices. It argues that secure remote access does not guarantee good performance for enterprise applications, especially over unstable connections, and that this gap is what the platform is meant to close.

The demo covers where measurements come from. Public sensors in data centers around the world sit alongside SD-WAN devices and agents inside the corporate environment, and endpoint agents run directly on user devices. Synthetic transactions run before any real work starts and report latency, packet loss, jitter and average opinion score. In the example, a laptop in a home office is compared with sensors at headquarters. For a G Suite complaint from the past six hours, the same period can be checked on the affected device and on other devices, both on the corporate network and over the public internet.

The speaker also shows threshold-based alerts that open a report when a metric goes out of range and capture device memory, processor, storage and network usage during the incident. A path view traces routes from many locations to the Google data center hosting the application, so teams can compare sites and look back at how paths changed over time. The takeaway is a move from reactive support to proactive support, with problems located before users report them.

It also highlights deployment flexibility across on-premises, cloud, and hybrid setups, secure web access for bring-your-own-device and contractor scenarios, stronger software-defined WAN visibility, and optional third-party integrations tuned to each account.

The close emphasizes AI-assisted operations, near-real-time SD-WAN support, self-healing, and automated zero-trust configuration as ways partners can offer higher-value services. talks.teaser: Presents Fortinet's unified SASE platform and its newest features, including remote browser isolation and sovereign deployments.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that hybrid workplaces and multicloud environments produce fragmented, complex infrastructure, and that point solutions create silos that slow down management and fixes. It presents a unified approach to secure access, positioning Fortinet's SASE offering as a single-vendor platform built on one operating system, with one data lake, one agent and one management platform. Administrators can oversee the whole security ecosystem from one place.

The middle section covers the breadth and flexibility of the offering. It lists more than 15 SASE capabilities, with remote browser isolation newly added, and says deployment can be quick. Zero trust and security enforcement can run on premises or in the cloud, whether staff work in an office, remotely, or in a hybrid model. A newly introduced Sovereign SASE option lets large enterprises, governments and service providers install a complete stack on their own premises to keep data private and under their control.

The closing part highlights AI-driven operations, including generative AI assisted operations, real-time SD-WAN self-healing and automated ZTNA configuration. The speaker ties the design to common concerns such as rising complexity, increased risk and skills shortages, and says consolidation is meant to improve security efficacy and visibility. Viewers are invited to a virtual summit on October 10 to learn more.

talks.teaser: A FortiSASE walkthrough covers web filtering, zero trust private access, endpoint posture checks and SaaS data protection.
talks.summary:
The speaker walks through FortiSASE, Fortinet's cloud-delivered secure access service edge, and explains how a remote user connects to the nearest point of presence. Security enforcement happens there, before traffic reaches the internet, a SaaS application, or a private resource in a data centre or public cloud. The demo covers the management console, the endpoint tags that drive access decisions, and SSL inspection options that come with the native license, including exemptions for regulated sectors.

Internet access is shown first. A social networking category is blocked for a test user, an exception allows one specific site, and the logs show both the block reason and the pass-through entry. The speaker then shows the endpoint from the admin side, including installed software, hardware trends and five detected vulnerabilities. Posture checks run about once a minute: when Windows Firewall is turned off, the endpoint loses its compliance tag and access to a private AWS-hosted web server is cut off.

SaaS controls come last. Personal Microsoft Office sign-ins are blocked while corporate sign-ins work, SharePoint uploads are allowed while downloads are denied, and pasting a file containing card data and personal details into ChatGPT is stopped by inline DLP. The takeaway is that internet access, private access, endpoint posture and SaaS inspection can be set from one console.

talks.title: FortiADC Adaptive Learning WAF Demo | Application Security
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for FortiADC Adaptive Learning WAF Demo | Application Security.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this demonstration, Gerard Garcia, Technical Marketing Engineer at Fortinet, introduces the Adaptive Learning Web Application Firewall (ALWAF) feature on FortiADC. The Adaptive Learning engine analyzes datasets generated from live incoming client and server traffic to continuously learn, evaluate statistics, and provide tailored WAF policy recommendations. These recommendations can be accepted, ignored, or deleted by an administrator. ALWAF complements FortiADC's core capabilities in load balancing, traffic optimization, and acceleration by automating and streamlining application security policy creation.

### Key Topics
- **Licensing Requirements**: ALWAF can be evaluated using a 30-day free trial on new FortiADC 7.6.0 deployments, or unlocked in production via a WAF signature license or a bundle license.
- **Virtual Server & Decompression Configuration**: Traffic inspection for payload types such as XML and JSON requires HTTP decompression to be configured and bound to the virtual server.
- **Adaptive Learning Profiles**: Profiles define parameters including name, sampling rate, false positive threshold, learning duration (set to one minute for testing), actions (deny, alert, block, silent deny, or CTA), and protected URL lists.
- **Policy Recommendation Lifecycle**: Reviewing generated analysis data and deciding whether to accept, ignore, or delete recommended policy additions.

### Technical Details
Garcia demonstrates configuring a virtual server named `VS_HTTP` bound to a decompression profile named `decompress01` with configured URI and content-type settings, ensuring JSON and XML data streams can be parsed. A WAF profile named `test_al` is bound to the virtual server to monitor incoming traffic.

Using an adaptive learning profile named `adaptive learning fastest` configured with a 1-minute learning window, Garcia executes several demonstrations using curl scripts from the desktop:
1. **XML Detection**: A curl script sends traffic containing `bot_test.html` to `VS_HTTP`. After the 1-minute learning cycle, the analysis engine generates a recommendation to enable XML protection, which is accepted.
2. **JSON Detection**: A subsequent curl request generates traffic statistics and, after one minute, triggers a recommendation to enable JSON protection limits. This recommendation is accepted and reflected under the `test_al` profile.
3. **Bot Detection**: Prior analytics data is cleared using the delete option. Garcia executes a curl script repeatedly in rapid succession. The high request frequency (reaching 4 requests per second) triggers a recommendation to enable bot protection.
4. **Web Attack Signature & Combined Detection**: A curl script simulating an attack is run multiple times. The engine produces dual recommendations: web attack protection and bot detection. Accepting these updates automatically binds attack signature protection, JSON validation, XML validation, and bot protection into the active profile.

### Takeaways
FortiADC's Adaptive Learning WAF reduces manual tuning overhead by learning from traffic patterns in real time and providing discrete, actionable security recommendations. Administrators maintain oversight by choosing to accept, ignore, or delete suggested protections for web attacks, bot traffic, XML, and JSON payloads.

talks.title: Exploring Software Supply Chain Security: Debunking GenAI and LLMs Hype | Brass Tacks Podcast
talks.teaser: Explains software supply chain attacks and the real risks of generative AI, aimed at executives and non-technical leaders.
talks.summary:
Guest Ricardo Ferrera, a European field CISO, explains why software supply chain attacks matter to business leaders. He cites SolarWinds in 2021 as a major example of malicious code entering network management software. He then describes a recent open-source case that unfolded over years: an attacker built trust with a sole maintainer who was dealing with health problems, then hid code that surfaced during the build process and could affect SSH, which he said 80 to 90 percent of devices use.

On generative AI, he argues the hype outpaces proven returns, though organizations should start building skills now. He sorts AI risks into availability, integrity and privacy. Availability can suffer from data poisoning that yields wrong answers or from inputs that drain resources and inflate costs. Privacy risk arises when protected data can be pulled out of a model, which he said has already happened.

His practical advice is to build security into AI pilots from the start and treat them like any other software project. He recommends data lineage to track how data changes across systems, red teaming to attack your own environment before adversaries do, and software bills of materials to inventory how software was built. He closes by urging buyers to vet purchased software and apply emerging security methods to emerging technology.

talks.title: How a Leading Manufacturer Leveraged ZTNA | Customer Stories
talks.teaser: Shows how a global manufacturer moved from VPN-only access to managed ZTNA with device posture checks and off-net web filtering.
talks.summary:
A global manufacturer with more than 100 locations and about 150 firewalls, and a long-time Fortinet customer, set out to build the foundation for a zero trust strategy. Its earlier unmanaged FortiClient only provided VPN. The team replaced it with EMS-managed FortiClient on all endpoints within three months, keeping users connected over VPN throughout, so ZTNA could be layered on afterward.

The first applications moved to ZTNA were file servers and ERP systems, chosen because they are the main reasons staff connect over VPN. With managed clients, configuration changes reach endpoints on the fly as long as they can reach EMS, so devices no longer need to be brought into a facility to be reconfigured. ZTNA posture tags let the team check whether a device is encrypted with BitLocker, has its patch management software installed, and is patched, so readiness can be confirmed before a user reports a connection problem. The managed client also enabled web filtering for devices off the corporate network, which the unmanaged client could not do and which leadership had requested.

The speaker stressed that patching and data backups are table stakes, and that the firewall security services, such as FortiGuard, were enabled from the start through zero-touch deployment. The takeaway is that a phased move, starting with endpoint management and then posture-aware access to the most-used applications, can add zero trust controls without disrupting users, and that consistent baseline controls give the organization confidence in its security posture.

talks.title: How Cyber Risk Has Evolved Into Business Risk | Brass Tacks Podcast
talks.teaser: Explains how cyber threats become executive-level business concerns and what boards and security leaders should do about them.
talks.summary:
Host Joe Robertson talks with Alan Sanchez, EMEA chief information security officer at Fortinet, about why cyber risk now means business risk. Sanchez argues that any threat to a computerized process can threaten the whole company, so leaders should first map the assets that matter most in their value chain, then keep up with tightening compliance rules. He cites the EU Digital Operations Resilience Act, aimed at banks and financial firms, as an example where regulators define resilience as how a business recovers from disruption rather than only restoring servers.

The CISO, in his view, translates business goals into security requirements for sales, finance and legal leaders, and must cover operational technology that was once isolated but now connects to networks. He compares security to a Formula 1 braking system: it lets a company go faster with confidence and lets product teams respond more closely to market demand. He also wants staff across departments to act as an extra line of defense, and wants the CISO to report directly to the board rather than several layers down.

For boards, he recommends framing risk as scenarios with costs and benefits, in plain language backed by documented evidence of potential losses. He uses the Titanic to warn against dismissing security warnings for financial reasons, and notes that many incidents trace back to known gaps, such as factory default passwords left on newly deployed devices. Boards that do not put security on their regular agenda, he concludes, are flying blind.

talks.title: Onboarding the Board with Cybersecurity | Brass Tacks Podcast
talks.teaser: Explains how executives and boards can grasp cyber risk, meet regulations like NIS 2, and build the teams to handle it.
talks.summary:
Host Joe Robertson opens the Brass Tacks podcast, which covers cyber security from a business angle for executives and board members. His guest, Wulf Gang Bitomsky, is CIO at FCC Environment, a waste management company operating at more than 160 sites across seven Central and Eastern European countries. They begin with legal duties: GDPR is already in place, while the EU's NIS 2 directive newly extends obligations to waste management.

Cyber security, he argues, reaches well beyond IT. HR runs yearly training, legal teams track regulation, and procurement holds suppliers to security terms. When briefing non-technical boards, he suggests framing issues as risk and opportunity and accepting graded decisions rather than a simple yes or no. Organizations should also pick tools that fit their needs instead of chasing every new product, and build career paths to attract scarce talent, including people retraining from other departments.

He stresses that checklists are only a starting point and that rehearsal matters as much, comparing it to firefighters who train constantly. Exercises should include communications staff, legal staff and the board so leaders stay calm in a crisis. Security should also join new products and projects early rather than act as a late obstacle. He closes by saying cyber security belongs on everyone's agenda, since incidents can hit anyone.

talks.summary:
This short partner-focused session makes the case for SASE as a response to hybrid work security. It opens with a scenario of a company whose staff are spread across regions, connecting from many devices to reach sensitive data, websites and applications. Traditional security models often struggle with that spread, leaving gaps and adding complexity. An example IT manager is introduced who juggles many separate security tools, worries about compliance and has little visibility into what remote employees are doing.

The core idea is that SASE converges networking and security into a single cloud-native service. According to the talk, it brings together firewall as a service, a secure web gateway, a cloud access security broker and zero trust network access, with AI-powered security functions, all managed from one platform. The speaker argues this simplifies infrastructure and gives consistent, secure access to applications and the web regardless of where a user is located.

For partners, the talk frames the opportunity as helping customers move to a more integrated, scalable network, with claimed benefits of lower overheads, reduced risk and a better user experience. The suggested approach is to identify a customer's pain points in hybrid work security, demonstrate how the platform addresses them, share success stories and offer a pilot so the concrete benefits can be shown.

talks.title: Enhance User Experience with Application Monitoring | FortiMonitor Demo
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiMonitor tracks application availability, network quality and path changes from multiple vantage points.
talks.summary:
This demo walks through application monitoring in FortiMonitor. The presenter starts from the applications list, where each monitored application is measured from several vantage points: endpoints, on-site collectors, public probes and SD-WAN devices. A Microsoft Teams check shows performance over the last day, week and month, with a map that displays how each location is doing. Network quality checks record packet loss, jitter and latency from each vantage point. Path monitoring runs a traceroute and ping every ten minutes, showing each hop along the route and the loss and latency between hops. An HTTPS GET check is shown with an alert configured, so an error or a slow response triggers a notification.

The presenter then moves to the location views. On a Wi-Fi machine, Wi-Fi signal strength is charted over a week and hourly speed test download results are shown. On a wired laptop used as a synthetic test location, CPU, memory, disk and network utilization are collected every minute, alongside network quality over time and the availability of several URLs tested from that machine. Charts can be viewed over an hour, a week, a month or a year, and the presenter notes that data is kept for a year by default and two years with extended retention.

The closing point is that application monitoring is one of several use cases in the product. The presenter says DNS checks, certificate expiration checks and scripted transactions are covered in separate videos. For administrators, the practical takeaway is that a single view can connect what end users experience with the network path and endpoint conditions behind it.
