talks.teaser: Explains how Fortinet's unified SASE bundles networking and security services into one cloud platform with shared policy.
talks.summary:
In this Packet Pushers Heavy Networking episode, Fortinet's Nirav Shah explains what the vendor means by unified SASE. He presents it as a cloud-delivered offering that brings about 15 security and networking functions under one policy and console, built on the company's long-running operating software. He also separates the machine learning used by its threat intelligence labs from a newer AI assistant for operations.

Shah ties zero trust to verifying identity, device posture and context before granting access, with the connection proxied and rechecked roughly every 30 to 60 seconds. The architecture spans more than 140 points of presence, some in owned data centers and some hosted with a public cloud. Users can connect through a unified agent, an agentless web gateway, wireless access points, or SD-WAN, and digital experience monitoring runs synthetic checks against SaaS apps such as Office 365.

On consolidation, Shah cites a customer that replaced a third-party VPN and reported savings of 40% plus, and a mining company that cut costs by 68% after consolidating routers, SD-WAN and remote access. Licensing is per user, starting at 50 users, with a claimed 3x to 5x per-user cost advantage. The host called these claims bold. Practitioners should weigh the single policy across internet, private and SaaS access against latency and vendor-reported savings they would need to verify themselves.

talks.title: LIVE: Interview with the Ultimate Fabric Challenge Champions | Accelerate 2024
talks.teaser: Global competition winners discuss preparation habits, certification study, home labs, and lessons for entering cybersecurity careers.
talks.summary:
A host speaks with the first-, second-, and third-place finishers in the year’s global Ultimate Fabric Challenge about how they reached the podium and what they do day to day. Jesse describes a long path from network infrastructure into security as a senior project engineer at a Minneapolis managed service provider. Alan works remotely for an Australian MSP after drifting into security through a short vendor training course years earlier. Ben is a solutions architect and certified trainer at a distributor who treats varied partner work as ongoing competition practice.

Each winner explains preparation differently yet points to the same backbone: structured vendor training, admin and lab guides, hands-on home labs, and certifications pursued along the way, including advanced exams completed just before the event. They contrast timed competition pressure with perfectionist habits, stress breaking problems into fundamentals, reading configuration with intent, and valuing relationships built with engineers worldwide across repeat events.

Closing guidance targets people entering the field: follow genuine interest among the industry’s many roles, build labs or other hands-on paths, learn processes not only outcomes, accept failures as growth, and keep studying as technology shifts. They also note mentoring students, revisiting fundamentals before advanced topics, and encouragement for diverse participation in competitive settings.

talks.title: FortiGate VM on AWS Secures Your Cloud Infrastructure | Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Outlines how FortiGate VM on AWS adds firewall, intrusion prevention, and zero trust access controls to cloud workloads.
talks.summary:
This vendor video presents FortiGate VM on AWS as an enterprise next generation firewall for protecting cloud workloads. It lists features including IPS, web filtering, malware protection, application control, scalable zero trust remote access, and SD-WAN connectivity, with threat updates from FortiGuard Labs. It also notes VPN and ZTNA support backed by SSL inspection, compatibility with newer Graviton instance types, and integration with AWS Gateway Load Balancer for automatic scaling.

Within the cloud, the firewall inspects traffic moving in, out, and between workloads so granular rules can be applied where they are needed. The video describes automation scripts that push malicious IP or DNS addresses flagged by AWS GuardDuty into dynamic FortiGate policies, shortening the time to protection. For hybrid and multi-cloud setups, FortiOS is positioned as a single management layer across deployments, filling gaps left by native provider firewalls and providing consistent SD-WAN across clouds and on-premises sites. Integration with AWS Transit Gateway or AWS Cloud WAN is mentioned as a way to streamline routing.

The closing segment points viewers to a 30-day free trial in the AWS Marketplace and to a contact option for learning how FortiGate can strengthen an AWS environment. The main takeaway is a product overview rather than a technical walkthrough, since the video covers the feature set and deployment options without any demonstration.

talks.title: FortiADC Scripting Content Routing Demo | Application Security
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiADC Lua scripting routes web traffic to specific server pools based on host, user agent and source IP.
talks.summary:
This demo video shows how to use scripting for content routing on a FortiADC virtual server. Content routing lets a single service IP and port send traffic to several server pools, which can hold different servers or hardware for different parts of an application or different sites. Some matching conditions cannot be built in the standard GUI rules, such as inspecting the user agent header. For those cases the demo uses a Lua script that runs on traffic events and calls a function, available from version 7.4.3, that chooses the real server directly.

The demo sets up two content routing pools: one containing all three real servers and another containing only two of them. The script first checks whether the host header matches a given pattern, and if so, selects the two-server pool. Within that pool, requests from the administrator's IP address using a Safari browser are pinned to the third real server. All other traffic falls through to the all-server pool and is load balanced across the three servers. Debug lines in the script help confirm which branch was taken.

The presenter tests the configuration from the command line with wget, varying the host name, user agent and source address. The results show the selected real server switching between two and three when the user agent is Mozilla instead of Safari, and the pinning applies only when every condition matches. Requests that do not match the host pattern are balanced across all three servers. The takeaway is that a short script can cover routing logic that the GUI cannot express, while simpler conditions remain easier to handle with standard rules.

talks.title: FortiFone FON-380B Phone Tutorial | FortiVoice
talks.teaser: Guidance covers FortiFone FON-380B transfers, parking, conferencing, voicemail, and programmable key LEDs within FortiVoice.
talks.summary:
The session introduces the FortiFone FON-380B as an IP desk phone tied into FortiVoice, with conference calling, voicemail, peer dialing, call history, and other features only briefly sampled in the short format. Outgoing calls can start from the handset, dial pad, or call history via soft keys; speaker and headset buttons support hands-free and Bluetooth use.

For inbound traffic, the display shows caller details before the user answers with the handset, speaker, headset, answer soft key, or ignores and declines according to FortiVoice call-handling rules. Hold and resume manage busy periods; star-40 or administrator-programmed auto park places calls in park slots, with retrieval by dialing the slot or a park appearance key whose LED flashes yellow when a call waits in that slot. Attended and blind transfers, plus three-way conferencing, round out call control. Programmable keys use green, red, and yellow LED states for idle, ringing, active calls, hold, and do-not-disturb. Voicemail access via PIN covers folders, playback, deletion, and callback from a message.

Practitioners deploying FortiVoice and this handset gain a concise map of everyday controls—history redial, park and transfer flows, LED meanings, and voicemail menus—without touching provisioning or security policy.

talks.title: FortiFone FON-580B Phone Tutorial | FortiVoice
talks.teaser: The demo walks through placing and receiving calls, parking, transfers, conferencing, LED line status, and voicemail on the FortiFone 580B.
talks.summary:
The session introduces the FortiFone 580B as an IP desk phone tied to FortiVoice, aimed at everyday calling rather than exhaustive feature coverage. Outgoing calls can use the handset and dial pad, call history with soft keys, speakerphone, or a Bluetooth or wired headset. Incoming calls show caller details; users may answer via handset, speaker, headset, answer soft key, ignore (stop ringing but stay answerable), or decline (follow FortiVoice call-handling rules).

Active calls support hold and resume, with hold state visible on screen; held calls can be parked for pickup at another extension. Parking works by dialing star-40 during a call or using an administrator-assigned auto-park programmable key, with prompts for the slot number; retrieval uses the park slot dial string or a park-appearance key whose LED flashes when slot 301 (for example) is in use. Transfers include attended (consult then complete) and blind (direct handoff). Three-way conferencing adds a third party from an active call. Programmable keys show extension or line status through green, red, and yellow LED patterns, including do-not-disturb.

Voicemail uses the message-waiting indicator and on-screen counts; the voicemail button, PIN entry, folder tabs, and play or delete soft keys manage messages, with optional callback from the more menu. Viewers should leave knowing routine calling, parking, transfer, conference, status LEDs, and voicemail workflows on this model.

talks.title: FortiFone FON-480B Phone Tutorial | FortiVoice
talks.teaser: Walks through the FortiFone FON-480B's calling, parking, transfer, LED and voicemail features for everyday use.
talks.summary:
This short demo video is a user guide for the FortiFone FON-480B IP phone, which works with a FortiVoice system. It starts with placing outgoing calls, either by dialing from the handset or by choosing an entry from call history, and then switching between the handset, speakerphone and a paired Bluetooth headset. Incoming calls come next, covering how to answer with the handset, speaker, headset or the answer key, how to silence a ring with ignore, how to decline so the call follows the system's handling rules, and how to place a caller on hold and resume.

The middle section covers call parking and transfers. A call can be parked by dialing a code during the call or by using an auto park key set up by an administrator, and it is retrieved by dialing the park slot or pressing a park appearance key, whose LED flashes yellow when a call is waiting. Transfers are split into attended transfers, where the user speaks with the destination first, and blind transfers, which send the caller straight through. The video then explains three-way conference calling and the LED colors on programmable keys: solid green for idle, flashing green for an incoming call, solid red for a call in progress, flashing yellow for a held call, and solid yellow for do not disturb.

The video closes with voicemail. A message waiting indicator and an on-screen count show new messages, which are opened by entering the voicemail PIN and then moved between folders, played, deleted or returned by dialing the sender. The takeaway is a practical reference for day-to-day use of the phone's core features rather than a discussion of security issues.

talks.title: FortiSwitch Rugged Expands With New High Performance Switch Offering | OT Security
talks.teaser: Walks through the FortiSwitch Rugged 424F-PoE's port layout, PoE budget, redundancy and pairing with rugged FortiGate firewalls.
talks.summary:
This short product video introduces the FortiSwitch Rugged 424F-PoE, a switch aimed at industrial and critical infrastructure settings such as the power grid, where dependable communication networks support time-sensitive operations. It comes in a 1RU rack-mount form factor with a management port and a USB 2.0 port. Its ports are 12 RJ45 ports at 2.5 GB per second, 12 2.5 gig SFP+ ports, 4 10 gig SFP+ ports and two 40 gig QSFP+ ports. The PoE budget is 420 watts, with up to 60 watts per port, and the presenter says this is the largest PoE budget of any rugged FortiSwitch so far.

The video then covers performance and build. Latency is stated as less than 1 microsecond, and Precision Time Protocol is available on every interface. Two redundant DC power inputs are included, and the fanless rugged casing is described as suitable for harsh climates, shocks, vibration and protection against small debris. Paired with a FortiGate, the switch is presented as guarding access to a facility's SCADA infrastructure against intrusion and its management systems against ransomware. Several switches, locally or across sites, can be managed together through Fortinet's flagship products.

The closing section explains availability features, including high availability, seamless redundancy and Parallel Redundancy Protocol. It contrasts HSR, a ring topology that sends data in both directions, with PRP, where each node connects to two separate networks. The presenter notes that both protocols give seamless failover when a single network component fails. The practical takeaway for OT network teams is that one converged Ethernet design can combine switching capacity, power redundancy and firewall-based protection in harsh environments.

talks.title: Managed FortiGate Service Overview | NOC
talks.teaser: Outlines Fortinet's managed FortiGate service for network operations, covering its use cases, core areas and three-step onboarding.
talks.summary:
The session introduces Fortinet's Managed FortiGate Service, a cloud-based network operations offering meant to complement a customer's existing NOC capabilities. The presenter starts with the pressures facing network operations teams: difficulty hiring and keeping skilled engineers, larger attack surfaces, and growing infrastructure that makes consistent change management hard. The service is pitched as a partner-oriented answer to those gaps, delivered around the clock and built on Fortinet security best practices and established methodologies.

Coverage spans next-generation firewalls and other use cases such as remote access. The offering is organised into three areas. Device provisioning covers deploying units and preparing them to protect a network under security standards. Change management covers evaluating, implementing and verifying configuration changes and firmware upgrades so performance and uptime are preserved. System hardening covers incident containment and remediation, plus identifying configuration weaknesses and applying measures to strengthen the security posture.

The benefits section says customers get round-the-clock augmented operations with people, processes and tools, access to Fortinet's NOC experts, and less complexity, which frees internal teams for strategic work. Onboarding takes three steps: buy the service entitlement, register the contract registration code in a Fortinet cloud account, then complete onboarding through the managed service portal.

talks.title: AI Threat Analytics | FortiADC
talks.teaser: Demos Fortinet's AI Threat Analytics for FortiADC, covering prerequisites, incident grouping, severity scoring and attack logs.
talks.summary:
A Fortinet technical marketing engineer presents AI Threat Analytics for FortiADC as a feature overview followed by a live portal demo. The feature groups attack activity seen across an application's attack surface into incidents, then scores severity so analysts can focus on the dangerous items and set aside low-value notices and misfires.

The talk starts with three prerequisites. The ADC must run release 7.4.2 or later, a Threat Analytics license is needed either as an add-on or within an AI security bundle, and the feature must be enabled from the Security Fabric fabric connectors page of the ADC dashboard. The presenter then confirms that the device serial number matches between the ADC and the cloud-side Threat Analytics instance, so the deployed unit and its license line up.

In the portal, the presenter reviews dashboard widgets covering total threats, top attack types, incidents by country, top attack resources, incidents by severity, and top attacks by CVE ID. After filtering to the provisioned ADC, the view shows blocked threat totals and a breakdown of known attack categories. The attack logs view sorts events by critical, substantial and moderate levels and shows client, server and threat details for each entry. The closing takeaway is practical: confirm version, licensing and connector setup before expecting incidents, then use grouping and severity to triage. The talk is a short product tour rather than a technical analysis, so it gives little detail on how the models work.

talks.title: FortiNDR Cloud: Detection Triage | SecOps
talks.teaser: Walks through triaging a TrickBot staging download alert, from enriching affected hosts to deciding on incident response.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through triage of a detection in FortiNDR Cloud. An alert reported that two internal workstations had matched a rule for a TrickBot staging download. The rule keyed on a specific user agent and a server response declaring a Windows executable, and the presenter confirmed that both hosts had made successful HTTP requests over port 80 to the same external IP address. The requested URI looked like a PNG image, but the response type showed a Windows binary.

Next, the presenter enriched the hosts and the remote address. Historical entity data supplied DHCP names, MAC addresses, Kerberos user accounts and observed software. One host carried a name suggesting it was posing as a domain controller, which looked suspicious for an accounting workstation. The remote IP had no passive DNS history, which suggested direct connections without a domain name, and it belonged to a hosting provider the presenter did not recognize. Both downloaded files carried PE headers, and VirusTotal flagged them across many engines, with one labeled as Emotet.

An investigation was then opened, with queries for outbound SSL traffic on ports 447 and 449 from the two hosts. These returned substantial activity. A search for earlier executable downloads from the same source found requests starting about two hours before the alert. Based on these findings, the presenter judged the activity malicious and passed the hosts to the incident response team for remediation.

talks.title: FortiNDR Cloud: Entity Panel Overview | SecOps
talks.teaser: Shows how the FortiNDR Cloud entity panel surfaces passively collected history for IP addresses, domains and file hashes.
talks.summary:
Scott Hall walks through the entity panel in Fortinet's FortiNDR Cloud, a network detection product. The panel holds historical data gathered passively by observing network traffic, covering IP addresses, domain names and file hashes. Any of these can be opened with a click from elsewhere in the product, and the panel starts with a summary before breaking out the individual data sets.

For an internal host, the panel shows passive DNS records that link domains to the addresses that answered them, and detections where that address was the impacted host. DHCP data supplies the MAC address and host name when a sensor can see DHCP traffic. Kerberos and NTLM observations reveal the associated domain, workstation and user. Software is inferred from user agent strings and server banners, which can hint at the operating system even without an endpoint agent installed. For an external IP address, the WHOIS record identifies the netblock owner and contacts, and VirusTotal data lists related URLs, malicious activity and samples that others have submitted.

For a file hash, the panel combines static analysis of Windows executables downloaded by a sensor, PE file details, and file names seen in network traffic, along with any VirusTotal verdicts. The presenter's takeaway is that an analyst can gather historical context on hosts, addresses, domains and files during an investigation without first deploying an agent or running manual lookups.

talks.title: Configuring a FortiAP for use with FortiSASE | FortiSASE
talks.teaser: Demonstrates zero-touch provisioning of a FortiAP 431F into FortiSASE and basic wireless and security policy setup.
talks.summary:
The demo opens with zero-touch provisioning of a FortiAP 431F access point. In the FortiCloud account, the unprovisioned device is found under the cloud services section, selected, and assigned to the FortiSASE target location. Once provisioning starts and the device shows as provisioned, it appears in the FortiSASE portal's list of managed access points, where it can be authorized.

With the access point authorized, the presenter builds the wireless side of the setup. An SSID object is created with a network name, a chosen security mode and credentials. The default AP profile is then opened so the radio mode, channels and other technical settings can be adjusted before saving.

The final section covers security configuration. The default security profile is opened from the configuration menu, and the web filter is customized by setting website categories to allow, monitor, block, warn or disable. DNS filtering is shown as well, where specific domains or domain categories can be allowed, monitored or redirected. The takeaway is a simple way to deploy a managed access point with filtering applied through the SASE service.

talks.title: FortiABP Advanced Bot Protection Quick Deployment Guide | Application Security
talks.teaser: Shows how to deploy a cloud bot-protection service behind an ADC and a web application firewall.
talks.summary:
This video is a quick demo of FortiABP, a cloud-based advanced bot protection service. Client traffic passing through an ADC or web application firewall policy is redirected to the service, which uses a machine learning model to spot malicious automation such as data harvesting, credential stuffing, account takeover and DDoS attacks, then suggests a response.

The presenter walks through deployment in three parts. First come the prerequisites: the advanced bot domain setting that ships enabled on the ADC must be disabled through the CLI, both devices need a valid license, and the operator needs credentials for the cloud portal. Second, an application is created in the portal by entering a domain name and choosing a region. Pre-provisioning then starts, and a professional engagement team analyzes the application, identifies the URLs to protect and inserts the required JavaScript. The presenter said this takes two to three days, and a demo site in the portal shows approval comments and the pre-provisioning entries.

Last, the devices are configured. On the ADC, the connector is checked, a new bot protection entry is created, the application ID copied from the portal is pasted and verified, and the profile is attached to the virtual server policy. The web application firewall follows the same pattern from its bot mitigation section, after confirming the feature is enabled on the dashboard. The video closes by reviewing the connector listing to confirm both devices are connected.

talks.title: Akira Ransomware | FortiGuard Labs Outbreak Alert
talks.teaser: Outlines how the Akira ransomware group gets into networks through old Cisco VPN flaws and weak remote access logins.
talks.summary:
Jonas Walker of FortiGuard Labs presents an outbreak alert on Akira, a ransomware group that has hit many organizations worldwide and reportedly brought in over 42 million dollars. He explains that this kind of revenue lets ransomware groups reinvest in research and recruit more operators, which tends to expand their capabilities over time.

The group gets into networks in a few ways. It exploits Cisco VPN vulnerabilities from 2020 and 2023, one scored above 9 and another at 7.5. It also finds internet-facing remote desktop systems and logs in with credentials that were either brute-forced or taken from earlier data breaches, often on accounts without multi-factor authentication. The talk notes a recent shift in the group's tooling from C++ to Rust, likely to evade detection after older tools were flagged. Although Akira was first observed in early 2023, telemetry now shows its indicators active again, including malware hashes and IP addresses used for command and control and data exfiltration.

The speaker recommends subscribing to outbreak alerts for early awareness and points to deeper analysis from FortiGuard research and outside sources such as CISA. He maps protective measures to a framework built around identify, protect, detect, respond and recover. For defenders, the practical next step is to hunt for Akira activity in their own environment and check whether they were already affected.

talks.title: On Course for the Vendée Globe 2024 with Romain Attanasio | Episode
talks.teaser: A French offshore sailor describes his path to the Vendée Globe and his preparation for a foiling boat campaign.
talks.summary:
The sailor traces his route from early sailing trips with his great uncle in Brittany to his goal of racing the Vendée Globe, the solo non-stop round-the-world race he calls the Everest of the seas. He describes the race as mostly pain with a smaller share of intense happiness, and explains that he returned to the event on a foiling boat. He arranged the project before finishing his previous race, and new sponsors backed it after a few weeks of discussion.

The middle of the talk covers the preparation for the double-handed Transat Jacques Vabre from Le Havre to Martinique, which he sailed with his co-skipper Sebastian over eight months. He explains how the foiling boat lifts clear of the water in calm conditions, how little time remained before the start, and how his team had to make sure every detail of the boat was ready. The crew finished seventh, and the arrival in Martinique was followed by time with his son, which he treats as an important way to recharge after long periods alone on board.

The talk ends with the boat in refit and his own physical training ahead of the solo race. He will be without his co-skipper this time, and he expects the single-handed campaign to be much harder.

talks.title: On Course for the Vendée Globe 2024 with Romain Attanasio | Episode
talks.teaser: Ocean racing prep pairs with student lessons on nutrition, movement, and rest during a Play International visit aboard the boat.
talks.summary:
The episode frames the weeks before the double-handed Transit Jacques Vabre, a transatlantic run to Martinique via the Equator, as a stretch of media demands, organizer briefings, weather planning, training, and time with the shore team while the boat is readied.

Play International brings students aboard to meet the skipper and ask about eating well, moving well, and sleeping well—themes the NGO ties to its Sports Games work. The segment stresses partnership value beyond visibility, then shifts to how elite sailing balances risk, speed, and boat preservation. Racers wear helmets, endure punishing motion, and rely on route choice plus onboard tech such as adjustments, computers, autopilots, and sensors on fast foiling hulls.

The speaker reflects on learning from a double-handed campaign ahead of returning to solo racing. The next goal is another solo event meant to earn qualification miles toward the Vendée Globe after this double-handed leg.

talks.title: On Course for the Vendée Globe 2024 with Romain Attanasio | Episode
talks.teaser: Sailors train for solo ocean racing, ready ultralight boats, and earn Vendée Globe slots via three years of qualifying miles.
talks.summary:
The piece opens at a French solo ocean-racing training center described as the only worldwide reference facility of its kind. Coaches work to spot high-potential skippers and run sessions that mimic solitary racing: safety technicians stay aboard without joining maneuvers, fleets start together on the same wind angle to chase maximum boat speed, and crews blend skipper intuition with instrument data. Offshore legs add full maneuver practice, weather sequencing, strategic tracking, and return briefings.

With the race start two days away, preparation shifts to making the boat as light and reliable as possible—line trims, electronics, engine checks, mast hardware, sails dried and unfurled—while stowing spares for emergencies. The narrator describes rising pre-start anxiety and the qualification rules that sum race miles over three years so only the most active campaigns secure a Vendée Globe berth. At sea, life aboard becomes cramped and loud as foils and hull impacts resonate through carbon fiber.

The closing arc contrasts the urge to quit with the satisfaction of finishing a competitive solo leg. Faster sailing feels more stable after a year of adaptation; landfall brings exhaustion and disorientation, then relief. The story ends on the paradox that although skippers sail alone, family, a longtime supporter at each start, sponsors, and unseen followers make the endeavor a shared effort.

talks.title: On Course for the Vendée Globe 2024 with Romain Attanasio | Episode
talks.teaser: Interviews trace family support, adviser roles, and sponsor partnerships behind a skipper's multi-year push toward the 2024 Vendée Globe.
talks.summary:
The piece opens with a family perspective on growing up with a father who races offshore, including his father's own mini-transatlantic setback and unwavering commitment once he chooses a course. An close adviser describes helping the skipper weigh options without dictating decisions, and building the professional network that eventually attracted backing when the boat initially had no sponsor.

Sponsor voices explain why they joined the project, emphasizing passion, performance, and communication expectations for a brand ambassador on a visible sporting venture. The skipper recounts meeting musician Francis Cabrel through a mutual contact, gaining an additional sponsor, christening the boat, and sailing together.

The closing stresses that reaching the Vendée Globe after four years of preparation depends on a wide circle of supporters, reinforcing that the solo race is never truly a solitary effort. For viewers, the through-line is how relationships—not only funding—shape readiness for an extreme endurance event.

talks.title: Training Institute Academic Partner Awards | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Partnerships, certifications, and labs reveal paths into cybersecurity while confronting a shortage of roughly four million roles.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with Fortinet’s academic partner initiative, which embeds vendor technical training and certifications into university cybersecurity programs at more than seven hundred institutions worldwide. Hosted as an award-related conversation, it frames a persistent global shortage—cited as roughly four million unfilled roles—and the need to recruit beyond existing professionals.

An instructor based in Sweden describes teaching both students and customers, recruiting through the academy, and balancing certifications as a hiring baseline against engineers who excel outside exam formats. A former CNC machinist who entered the field in 2021 explains shifting from manual industrial work, valuing diplomas plus industry credentials for job visibility, and preferring integrated hands-on labs—including exam tasks that walk through full processes—while noting limits of purely remote practice versus physical gear.

Practitioners hear that passion and diverse backgrounds can feed the pipeline, that stable lab portals reduce educator overhead, and that the field rewards lifelong learning, open knowledge sharing, and collaboration even among competing vendors because adversaries remain the common threat.

talks.title: Security Awareness Curriculum | Education Technology
talks.teaser: Presents Fortinet's free security awareness curriculum for primary and secondary schools, covering digital safety and technical skills.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the Fortinet Security Awareness Curriculum, a free cybersecurity program offered to primary and secondary schools in countries around the world. The presenter argues that security awareness should begin in childhood and that lessons must match the way students are used to learning. The curriculum was built from the ground up for students rather than adapted from material written for adults.

The program is organized into age-based levels and seven cyber strands. Topics include building a positive online presence, safeguarding privacy, making ethical choices when using technology, understanding how new technologies affect daily life and future careers, recognizing cyber threat tactics, and judging whether online information is reliable. Each lesson stands on its own, so teachers can teach them in any order in classrooms, homerooms or advisory periods. Suggestions are included for linking lessons to other subjects, extending them, and turning them into multi-day projects.

Teachers receive guides with background information, definitions of key terms, simplified technical explanations and classroom activities that encourage teamwork. Pre-built slides, handouts and multimedia assets are also provided. Fortinet's wider security awareness service adds online training for staff and faculty to help them recognize and report threats in email, online or in person. The talk ends by directing viewers to scan a QR code to obtain the curriculum from the platform.

talks.title: The Latest SASE Innovations from Fortinet | Unified SASE
talks.teaser: Covers Fortinet's unified SASE platform and new FortiOS 7.6 features for digital experience, browser isolation and DLP.
talks.summary:
Fortinet's John Maddison explains unified SASE, which combines cloud security, SD-WAN-based security and security for cloud-hosted applications into one service that gives users consistent secure access from any location. The foundation is FortiOS, which runs in appliances, in Fortinet's cloud and in data centers under the same operations and policy. He argues that the client matters as much as the cloud and on-premises pieces: the FortiClient agent should provide SASE, ZTNA and digital experience monitoring, with EDR planned. Where no agent can run, such as access points, 5G extenders or switches, a hardware agent connects to SASE and is managed from the same console.

On zero trust, he says many implementations check a connection once and stop, while the client can assess device posture on every connection and feed that into the policy engine. Among the FortiOS 7.6 SASE additions, end-to-end digital experience monitoring is built into FortiSASE and correlates device metrics such as CPU, memory and Wi-Fi strength with application experience to locate problems. Remote browser isolation is now a FortiSASE feature for agentless and BYOD users browsing the web. Advanced DLP uses AI and machine learning from FortiGuard services, including generative AI-based detection of data sent to large language models. Third-party SD-WAN can also connect to the platform.

The talk closes with SOC-as-a-service integrated into SASE, bringing CISO and CIO teams closer together, and a market forecast that secure networking will outgrow networking by 2030. The takeaway for practitioners is that converging networking and security across cloud, network, client and data center is the route to business outcomes.

talks.title: 's Industry-Leading Innovations | FortiOS
talks.teaser: Outlines FortiOS 7.6 updates covering GenAI tooling, data protection, a unified agent with EDR, and new managed services.
talks.summary:
John Maddison, Fortinet's chief marketing officer, outlines new capabilities in FortiOS 7.6, the company's network security operating system that runs in real time. He describes FortiOS as the base of the Security Fabric, developed over more than twenty years so that Fortinet's products can work together.

He highlights four enhancements. Generative AI features are being added to operations tooling to help with analysis and decision-making. Data protection is being strengthened so sensitive information stays secure wherever it sits in a hybrid network. EDR functionality is being added to the FortiClient unified agent, which already covers ZTNA, EPP, SASE, digital experience monitoring, PAM and NAC, with the aim of reducing the number of separate agents. Additional managed services are also being introduced to take routine work off operations teams.

Maddison then explains how FortiOS runs across FortiGate models with custom ASICs, applying common policies across on-premises, remote and cloud environments and extending to wired, wireless, IoT and OT networks. He frames the updates as a way to reduce risk and complexity and to lessen the impact of the cybersecurity skills gap. Further details are available on the Fortinet website.

talks.summary:
The conversation centers on how Women in Cybersecurity (WiCyS) helps people—especially veterans, active-duty members, and military spouses—find footing in the field. The guest describes joining WiCyS as a mentor for a veteran apprenticeship pilot, then co-founding the WiCyS Military Affiliate with Kristen Cotton to give veterans and spouses dedicated community and balanced leadership representation.

Fortinet’s training outreach and WiCyS partnership frame much of the middle: joint education efforts, member networking, job pathways, and a well-attended networking fundamentals boot camp that underscored basic networking as an on-ramp. A personal military deployment story illustrates how one crew member bypassed controls and posted movement details online, triggering a bomb threat, a canceled port call, and more than 60 consecutive days at sea—used to stress that people can be assets or risks and that security needs breadth beyond pure tooling.

The close offers career rationale for women: wide role choice (hands-on, policy, risk, and more), global importance as adversaries adopt AI, and rewarding impact. The global skills gap is cited at just under 4 million jobs. Advice to newcomers is to build and use networks, research specialties from vulnerability management to GRC or IAM, and pursue passion areas; the guest’s current work runs executive cyber-crisis simulations for leadership decisions including ransomware response.

talks.title: and Qualcomm: How Customers Can Get the Most out of Wi-Fi 7 | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Explains Wi-Fi 7 features such as multi-link operation and interference puncturing, and why enterprises are adopting them.
talks.summary:
Fortinet and Qualcomm discuss Wi-Fi 7, the latest wireless standard, and why organisations are weighing it now. The guest links demand for newer Wi-Fi to interactive video, cloud gaming, AR and VR, and dense fleets of IoT sensors and cameras. In sectors such as healthcare, finance and manufacturing, inconsistent wireless performance can cause delays or safety risks, so predictable behaviour matters as much as raw speed.

The conversation then walks through three feature groups. Faster connections come from 4K QAM modulation and 320 MHz channels. Multi-link operation lets a client use several bands at once, either alternating between links to avoid congestion and reduce latency, or sending on both to raise throughput. Adaptive interference puncturing lets the radio drop only the damaged slice of a wide channel and keep using the rest, which makes wide channels more dependable.

The discussion closes with deployment advice. Faster wireless needs matching wired capacity, so edge Ethernet ports and higher PoE budgets should be planned in advance. Newer client devices are also needed to take full advantage of the newer security features. Fortinet's Wi-Fi 7 access point, built on Qualcomm's networking platform, serves as the example, and Qualcomm noted its service-defined Wi-Fi and AFC support for 6 GHz standard power.

The guest explains that smaller businesses moving to the cloud want someone else to run their environment, so the carrier aims to offer simple, pre-configured packages with default policies sized for each customer segment.

The discussion then turns to the vendor relationship. Fortinet supplies a broad portfolio rather than a single product, and the guest argues that one large platform sold for a small use case drives up cost without fitting the need. Deutsche Telekom therefore works with Fortinet to find the right-sized products, testing them in its labs and adapting existing offerings to suit each segment. The carrier contributes its networking expertise, while Fortinet contributes security knowledge, and the two combine to build offers they believe are compelling for the market.

The interview closes with both sides expressing satisfaction at the partnership. For a practitioner, the main point is that managed, simplified security bundles for smaller organisations depend on matching product scope and cost to real requirements, which a service provider can tune by combining network and security skills.

talks.summary:
Derek Mankey speaks in a studio at Mobile World Congress about the threats facing telecom and service providers. He describes telecommunications as the most targeted sector at present, ahead of enterprise networks, operational technology in manufacturing and mining, and public defense. Familiar threats such as ransomware and wipers remain, and the rollout of 5G cores, private 5G networks and new sites adds a fresh attack surface that includes infrastructure attacks and API exposure.

The discussion then turns to collaboration. Fortinet points to its long involvement in industry sharing, including the Cyber Threat Alliance it founded in 2014, which has 37 members and includes telecom operators. Further work covers threat research with the World Economic Forum, mapping criminal ecosystems through Cyber Crime Atlas, and working with Interpol and law enforcement to disrupt the actors behind attacks.

The closing point is that attackers spend much of their effort on initial access and on selling entry to compromised networks. The speaker frames the response as layered: security technology to raise the bar for criminals, plus industry-wide cooperation and secure-by-design practices.

talks.summary:

The host notes that the vendor works with thousands of managed security customers and hundreds of telco customers, so supporting them and helping them innovate is a priority.

The executive names three focus areas. The first is AI, which the company says it has used for more than a decade and now applies to automate security operations offerings, helping with both threat handling and a shortage of skilled staff. The second is a unified SASE approach, which the speaker says has been well received by technology partners after strong growth in that segment over the past several years. The third is a newer effort to help service providers monetize security by protecting business and consumer end users through digital wellness offerings.

The executive closes by stressing that service providers have been a core market for more than 20 years and that continued investment in innovation is meant to help them monetize and evolve. For practitioners, the takeaway is that automation is positioned as a response to talent gaps, while security is framed as a revenue source for providers rather than only a cost.

Davis explains that Fortinet's converged platform announcement shifted the approach from pushing individual products to asking customers which business outcomes they want. Taking customers on a journey that covers secure networking, a universal access component and secure operations depends on partners who can design, deliver, monitor and manage the solution, while Fortinet supplies the technology. Partners also bring artificial intelligence capabilities and easier consumption models, including flexible and managed service provider options.

The discussion closes on the idea that cybersecurity sits inside a wider business context, so system integrators offer a holistic view that goes beyond security alone. The takeaway is that the aim is to become part of a customer's blueprint, rather than simply transacting product through partners.

The session is framed as guidance for showing prospective customers how Fortinet’s FortiSASE MSSP portal works. It positions the portal as centralized management for managed security service providers who must deploy and operate SASE across many end clients, and it suggests opening questions about juggling multiple subscribers and matching technical staff to permission needs.

The walkthrough starts at partner login, where technical staff can see tenant-wide data such as user counts, license expiry, and how security points of presence are spread per license. Selecting a managed FortiSASE instance is shown two ways: from the active licenses view or via the organization context switch in the account menu. Setup flows through FortiCloud registration as an MSSP partner, defining organization hierarchy, global role-based access with read-write, read-only, or no access per service area, optional user groups tied to job duties, and separate IAM users for portal access. Administrators create suborganizations for end customers, monitor account growth on the organization dashboard, issue invitation tokens, provision FortiSASE SKUs, and approve inbound customer requests so a tenant joins the partner hierarchy.

Practitioners should treat the demo as an operational map: one cloud console for multi-tenant visibility and access control, with RBAC and grouping to keep large technical teams efficient while customers are onboarded through invitations rather than ad hoc account sprawl.

talks.summary:
FortiGuard SOCaaS is a cloud-delivered managed security service offering 24/7 monitoring, backed by Fortinet threat intelligence and a SOC platform, with dedicated analysts handling investigations and triage. The speaker outlines three onboarding steps: buy an entitlement for each device, register the devices in a Fortinet cloud account, and submit an onboarding request through the service portal. Logs arrive from an on-premises FortiAnalyzer or FortiAnalyzer Cloud, and partners can subscribe per device to serve their own clients.

The demonstration covers onboarding a new client under an MSSP account. The presenter sets the log collection method to FortiAnalyzer Cloud, selects one of three entitled devices, and optionally edits names or limits monitored subnets, where omitting them means all subnets are watched. Escalation contacts come next, then the request is submitted and tracked until it reads fulfilled. The device then appears under My Assets with its entitlement and license expiry.

A root dashboard summarizes all clients and devices, and the operator switches between client accounts where alerts correlate to each onboarded device. An opened alert shows attack details, playbook-based analysis and recommendations, plus related events, indicators and affected endpoints. Reports for configuration tuning, health and threat protection are available, and a sample health report is shown. The takeaway is running managed monitoring for many customers from one portal.

talks.title: See How FortiEDR Detects and Defuses Lateral Movement | Endpoint Security
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiEDR's default policy catches LockBit ransomware spreading across a domain and blocks lateral movement over RPC.
talks.summary:
The video introduces FortiEDR, an endpoint protection product, and its default exfiltration prevention policy, which uses built-in rules to separate malicious connection requests from legitimate ones. Policies run in prevention mode, which blocks violating activity, or in simulation mode, which only raises alerts. The demo uses simulation mode so the attack can run in full and its techniques can be studied.

The example is LockBit 2.0, a ransomware-as-a-service variant with enhanced propagation. Run on a domain controller, it encrypts files, drops a ransom note and replaces the wallpaper with payment instructions. Logs show several rules firing: the machine learning engine flagged the file as malicious, and a suspicious application attempted connections. The malware also pushed a group policy to domain machines that disabled Windows Defender real-time protection, then copied itself to every host it found. Telemetry exposed the PowerShell command behind the policy push, and the investigation view revealed traffic over port 135, an RPC port attackers abuse for lateral movement.

The presenter notes that in prevention mode FortiEDR would have stopped LockBit before execution and blocked the later steps, marking them with protection icons. When suspicious process flows appear, the product cuts outbound communication and file system access for those processes. These responses aim to prevent data exfiltration, command and control, file tampering and ransomware encryption.

talks.title: FortiGate VM Deployment from Google Market Place | Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Shows how to deploy a FortiGate firewall VM from Google Cloud Marketplace and set up its first firewall policy.
talks.summary:
The video walks through launching a FortiGate virtual firewall from the Google Cloud Marketplace, covering both the bring-your-own-license and pay-as-you-go options and selecting the pay-as-you-go path for the demo. It goes through the launch settings, including adding an external network interface and confirming the network and subnetwork, then deploying the instance.

Next it shows how to reach the new appliance's web admin panel, accepting the expected browser warning about the default self-signed certificate, retrieving the generated password, logging in as admin and changing that password. With access in place, the firewall policy is introduced as the element that governs traffic passing through the device, since every flow needs a matching policy. The parameters covered are the incoming and outgoing interfaces, source and destination addresses, which can be wide open or tightly restricted and may use a virtual IP for internal resources, and services defined by TCP and UDP port numbers. Services are contrasted with application control, which inspects packet content to identify the protocol.

When traffic can start from either side, a separate policy is needed for each direction, and the remaining options add further inspection and protection. Policies are evaluated top-down, and a newly created firewall has an implicit deny that blocks anything not matched by a permitted policy. The takeaway for a practitioner is that a cloud firewall deployment only does useful work once its policies are ordered and scoped to the intended traffic.

talks.title: Meeting Networking and Security Needs with Fortinet | Customer Stories
talks.teaser: Explains how a small dealership group's IT team uses Fortinet endpoint and XDR tools after a ransomware attack.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who leads enterprise networking and security at McCombs Enterprises in San Antonio, Texas, describes a group that runs automotive dealerships alongside real estate, oil and gas, and venture investments. About 1,300 staff at roughly 11 locations, with three to four thousand devices, are supported by a small eight-person IT team. The company moved away from an almost entirely Cisco network toward Fortinet so that security and networking could be managed from a single view. It now uses FortiGate, FortiSwitch, FortiAP, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiAuthenticator, FortiSandbox, FortiClient and FortiEDR.

The endpoint story centres on a ransomware attack. The team had begun replacing a competitor's endpoint product with FortiEDR when an attack hit in October. The only machines spared were those already running FortiEDR, so the rollout was accelerated. Because dealership endpoints sit on showroom floors and in open service bays where members of the public can reach them, the speaker says endpoint protection was essential. XDR then let the staff correlate endpoint events with network activity instead of reviewing isolated alerts, which mattered for a team with little spare time.

Early XDR visibility was unsettling because it revealed what devices and users were actually doing. After tuning reduced noise and alert fatigue, and the managed service cut the time staff spent threat hunting, the picture became more manageable. The speaker now ranks Fortinet as the most important vendor, ahead of Microsoft and VMware. Planned next steps include further tuning, broader fabric visibility, FortiSOAR automation and possibly FortiSIEM.

talks.title: Osquery Forensic Investigation & Response | FortiSIEM
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiSIEM's osquery integration runs live and scheduled endpoint queries, then contains a host during an incident.
talks.summary:
The demo shows how FortiSIEM 7.1 uses osquery to give SOC analysts live forensic visibility on Windows endpoints. The presenter creates a Windows agent template, adds built-in queries for running processes, Windows services and startup programs, and associates that template with a workstation through a host-to-template association applied by policy. A custom query listing active users is written, tested and saved, and a live run of the process query shows results directly in the console. Templates can also run queries on a schedule, with results generating reports or incidents.

The incident portion starts with a high-severity alert on an endpoint, tied to persistence and privilege escalation through a modified Windows service. Using the investigate action, the analyst reviews the running processes and services on the host and drills into the affected service to support root cause analysis. Findings can be exported as a PDF to share with other teams.

To contain the threat, a remediation script blocks the impacted host on the firewall. The action history confirms the host was quarantined. The main takeaway is that templates, scheduled queries and live queries can support both detection and response from a single console.

talks.title: SD-WAN Overlay Orchestration in FortiManager | SD-WAN
talks.teaser: Shows how a FortiManager wizard builds a full-mesh SD-WAN overlay across dual-hub data centers and branch sites.
talks.summary:
The video introduces the overlay orchestrator in FortiManager 7.2 and later, a guided wizard for deploying SD-WAN networks at no additional licensing cost. The example scenario is a corporate network where branch offices need access to data center resources and must also reach each other directly on demand. Two hub sites sit in geo-redundant data centers, one designated primary and the other secondary, and every site has dual ISP links that feed a full-mesh overlay.

Before running the wizard, the branch devices are placed in a single device group and given basic interface addressing. The four-step process covers the topology, which is dual hub in an active-passive arrangement with autodiscovery VPN enabled for on-demand branch-to-branch tunnels. It then asks which FortiGate acts as primary hub, which WAN underlay ports each hub uses, and which hub port advertises to the rest of the network. The final step associates the region with an existing SD-WAN template and hub and branch policies. The wizard then generates BGP and IPsec templates and groups them into template groups.

The demo stresses installing new interface configuration before any policy that references those interfaces. Hub device settings are pushed first, followed by hub policies, then branch device settings and policy packages. Each install completes in seconds. Back in the monitor view, the overlay shows as up, and a FortiGate can be selected to inspect details such as its routing table. The practical takeaway is that a full SD-WAN overlay with redundant hubs can be stood up in minutes through a guided workflow rather than hand-written configuration.

talks.title: The SEC’s New Incident Disclosure Ruling | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in The SEC’s New Incident Disclosure Ruling | FortiGuardLIVE.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this episode of FortiGuardLIVE, Anthony Giandomenico ("Tony G") and Jim Richburg discuss the implementation of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) ruling on cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and incident disclosure. The ruling requires publicly traded companies to disclose material cybersecurity incidents on Form 8-K within four business days (96 hours) of determining materiality. In addition, organizations must outline their cybersecurity governance and risk oversight processes in annual 10-K filings. The discussion examines how companies can prepare, navigate cross-functional decision-making, manage overlapping regulatory requirements, and address unintended consequences.

### Key Topics
- **Incident Disclosure Mandates (Form 8-K):** When a publicly traded company experiences a cyber incident deemed material, it must file an 8-K disclosure with the SEC within four business days (96 hours) after making that determination.
- **Annual Governance Filings (Form 10-K):** Annual disclosures require companies to describe board-level and executive oversight of cybersecurity risk, risk management processes, whether a CISO is present, and how committees oversee prevention, monitoring, detection, and mitigation.
- **Determining Materiality as a Team Sport:** Materiality decisions cannot rest solely on the CISO. Evaluating impact requires technical investigators, the CFO (for financial implications), business line owners, and General Counsel scrutiny.
- **Adversary Weaponization and Insurance Unintended Effects:** The discussion touches on threat actors testing the rule, such as the BlackCat ransomware group filing an SEC complaint against a compromised victim that had not reported the incident. Richburg also notes how public budgets showing cyber insurance coverage can lead adversaries to target specific organizations knowing insurers have the capacity to settle.
- **Regulatory Harmonization:** Overlapping mandates—such as the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) requiring 72-hour reporting—create compliance friction. The speakers emphasize efforts aligned with the National Cyber Strategy to harmonize reporting so victimized companies are not overwhelmed during incident response.

### Technical & Operational Details
- **Rulemaking Adjustments:** Following industry feedback on early drafts that raised concerns about revealing operational details that could assist attackers, the SEC backed off requests for granular policies and procedures. Instead, the final rule requires companies to disclose whether they have risk management processes rather than detailing the internal mechanics.
- **Exemptions and Delays:** Delays beyond the four-day disclosure window are permitted for national security or active law enforcement investigations, allowing agencies like the FBI to request SEC disclosure delays when premature public notification would compromise an ongoing criminal investigation.
- **Regulatory Deconfliction Strategy:** For companies subject to both SEC rules and CIRCIA's 72-hour requirement, the recommended operational approach is to default to the shorter reporting window, leverage established SEC materiality case law to define significance, and work with agencies such as CISA.

### Takeaways
- Determining whether an incident is material is an organizational "team sport" involving security, finance, legal, and operational leadership.
- Incident response plans and playbooks must be treated as living documents and updated to account for strict federal reporting timelines and cross-functional escalation pathways.
- CISOs and leadership should establish proactive relationships with local law enforcement (such as the FBI) prior to an incident to facilitate disclosure delay requests if public reporting would compromise an investigation.

talks.title: Introducing Fortinet's FortiGate 4800F | NGFW
talks.teaser: Shows Fortinet's FortiGate 4800F blocking 800 Gbps of DDoS flood traffic while still carrying over 2 Tbps of legitimate traffic.
talks.summary:
The video introduces Fortinet's FortiGate 4800F, presented as the vendor's most powerful next-generation firewall, and uses distributed denial-of-service attacks as the case to examine. The presenter notes that launching such an attack can be cheap for the attacker, and the lab test was run with Keysight's APS-M8400 traffic generator on eight 400 gigabit Ethernet ports to push firewall throughput toward 3 terabits per second.

The test combined 2.2 terabits per second of legitimate HTTP traffic, built from 1 megabyte file transfers, with 800 gigabits per second of UDP flood traffic that began one minute after the baseline load had ramped up. Two DDoS policies were enabled on two 400 gigabit interfaces, and a deliberately low threshold for UDP floods was set so the NP7 network processing chip's drop rate would be visible. Sessions stayed offloaded to the security processing unit, and CPU usage stayed negligible apart from a small cost for writing anomaly logs.

Once the flood started, the firewall dropped the attack traffic without measurable effect on legitimate throughput or CPU load, and the anomaly event logs recorded the flood counts. The presenter's takeaway is that the NP7 hardware acceleration lets DDoS protection run without a performance penalty, which matters for service providers using CGNAT or security gateway deployments. These are vendor claims demonstrated in a controlled lab setup.

talks.title: Threat Predictions for 2024 | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Predicts 2024 threat trends, from AI-written phishing and deepfake scams to blurring lines between state and criminal attackers.
talks.summary:
Douglas Santos and Aamir Lakhani, speaking for FortiGuard Labs, present their 2024 threat predictions. They expect vulnerability counts to keep rising as more researchers and vendor zero-day programs surface flaws. Automation and AI let attackers move faster, and nation-state groups and cybercriminals increasingly share the same modified open-source tools rather than custom code.

AI has also removed the grammar errors that once flagged phishing emails, so awareness training should not rely on them. The speakers describe a proof of concept that combined open-source tools to find office documents, hide them inside image files and transfer them unnoticed. They also cite a deepfake video of a cryptocurrency executive promoting a fake double-your-money scheme, and say the line between advanced persistent threat groups and cybercrime actors is blurring as talent and tools move between them.

Their data showed about 30% of categorized advanced persistent threat and cybercrime groups active in the first half of 2023, and roughly two-thirds of the more than 500 known techniques in use. The takeaway is to focus on techniques rather than group names. Defenders should map the techniques relevant to their industry and region, prioritize detection engineering, purple teaming and threat hunting over hash and indicator lists, and test incident response plans against them.

talks.title: Advisor: GenAI Assistant for FortiSOAR | Demo
talks.teaser: Shows an AI assistant helping a SOC analyst triage a malware alert, pivot to threat research, and draft a response playbook.
talks.summary:
The demo shows Fortinet Advisor, a generative AI assistant inside FortiSOAR, supporting a security analyst through a malware alert. The alert came from FortiSIEM and was described as a Dragonfly-related template attack. Reputation data from FortiGuard and VirusTotal had already been attached to the file hash, and the severity was raised to critical during automated enrichment. The recommendation engine linked it to a related alert about suspicious SMB server traffic, and the assistant explained how the two events could connect, from an initial weakness to the later deposit of malware.

The walkthrough then changes persona. The analyst escalates the case to the incident team and raises a priority intelligence request for the threat intel team. In the threat management module, a researcher opens a workspace built around that alert and asks the assistant about the actor group, its targets, tactics and objectives, and the MITRE techniques it uses. The answers come back as a curated list that can be linked to the investigation, added to notes and used to generate a summary report. Last, a playbook designer asks for a response playbook. The assistant first returns an outline that the user can review, edit or remove items from before it generates the full playbook.

The main takeaway is that AI-generated context can carry one alert through triage, research and playbook design, with a person reviewing intermediate output before acting on it. The session is a short vendor demonstration of a preview feature, so it shows workflows rather than independent testing of accuracy.

talks.title: Achieving Better Visibility with the Fortinet Security Fabric | Customer Stories
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Achieving Better Visibility with the Fortinet Security Fabric | Customer Stories.
talks.summary:
This customer story features Kevin Morrison, VP and Chief Information Security Officer at Driven Brands, discussing the organization's deployment of Fortinet security solutions to address challenges posed by its large, geographically dispersed footprint.

**Organization Overview**
Driven Brands operates approximately 4,400 shops and locations worldwide as the largest aftermarket auto services company, owning brands including Midas, Take Five Oil, Take Five Car Wash, Auto Training Institute, and 1800 Radiator parts distributor. The company manages security for corporate-owned locations while franchise locations operate as independent, autonomous networks.

**Primary Security Concerns**
Morrison identifies operational ransomware as the top cyber risk, consistent with threats facing most organizations. Third-party risk from supply chain dependencies ranks as a secondary concern—ransomware affecting manufacturers from whom Driven Brands sources parts could create downstream operational disruptions, affecting the company's ability to serve customers.

**Fortinet Adoption Strategy**
Morrison considers Fortinet best-of-class, having encountered the technology early in his career as a network security engineer. Upon joining Driven Brands just over a year ago, he found the organization had already begun evaluating Fortinet, which he endorsed as a strategic long-term partnership. The primary motivation was consolidating and standardizing security controls across the company's geographically dispersed entities.

**Implementation Benefits**
Fortinet's firewall serves as a key layer in a defense-in-depth strategy, positioned where risks primarily reside. Consolidation has provided significantly improved visibility around incoming threats, while standardization across locations enables consistent security controls. Morrison emphasizes that this unified approach allows the organization to maintain best-of-class security practices.

**Organizational Structure**
Morrison's security team operates within IT, enabling close collaboration between security, infrastructure, applications, and corporate systems teams. This convergence between security and infrastructure ensures alignment on roadmaps and strategic direction, making the organization safer through coordinated decision-making.

**Future Direction**
The company plans to leverage Fortinet's consolidated portfolio to reduce the total number of controls while maintaining security effectiveness, aiming to simplify operational burden for the security team without compromising protection.

talks.title: Secure Connectivity and the New FortiSwitch | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Covers Fortinet's new campus switches, their Security Fabric integration, and FortiLink NAC for onboarding IoT devices.
talks.summary:
Two Fortinet presenters introduce the company's new campus switches and place them within its secure connectivity platform. The switching line has been developed for over a decade to integrate with the Security Fabric, spanning access, campus aggregation, core and data center tiers. The newest additions are the 600 series, a high-density multi-gigabit switch with 25 gigabit uplinks and power over Ethernet for access points, servers and workstations, and the 2048F, which aggregates switches across multi-building campuses and can also serve 25G servers.

The discussion then turns to FortiLink, which connects switches to a FortiGate so they appear in the central dashboard once powered on and connected, with some basic configuration already in place. Administrators can manage VLANs, redundant links and access policies from one console, and no extra license is needed to join the fabric. The speakers also describe FortiLink NAC, which can be enabled on edge ports in a few clicks. Its policies work from layer 2 through layer 7 to identify and act on IoT and OT devices, while some granular OT capabilities require add-on licenses.

To close, the presenters cover the AI-driven operations product, which combines switch, security and WAN data to troubleshoot issues and predict configuration problems. They also mention upcoming switches for micro-branches that combine local networking with SASE services. The main takeaway is that one management view can span core to perimeter, and that access for connected devices can be controlled without heavy manual setup.

talks.title: NSE Certification Program Updates | Cybersecurity Certification
talks.teaser: Outlines the revised NSE certification levels, from fundamentals to expert, and the career paths they open.
talks.summary:
Mike Pas presents recent updates to the NSE certification program, which the training team describes as more scalable, flexible and modular. The program now has five proficiency levels and 11 certifications, so learners can focus on what is relevant to them and earn badges that show specific skills. He also addresses whether existing certifications stay valid after October 1.

The walkthrough starts with the fundamentals level, which covers the threat landscape and the techniques attackers use to reach systems and data. Learners then choose one or two electives: Getting Started in Cyber Security for non-technical roles, or Technical Introduction to Cyber Security for technical roles. The associate level is a new course from October 1 that covers operating FortiGate firewalls and how common features work, aimed at security operators and admins of small and medium networks. The professional level has three certifications, and learners pick a path such as network security, security operations, or public cloud with AWS or Azure exams.

The solution specialist level offers five certifications covering network security, public cloud, security operations, zero trust access and OT security. The expert-level FCX validates deep knowledge of designing, configuring and troubleshooting complex networks and requires both a written and a practical exam. The overall message is that the program builds a foundation from fundamentals up to expert level.

talks.title: Supporting Veterans Through Cyber Career Initiatives | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Explores how veterans can move into cybersecurity careers, from translating military skills to finding mentors and training.
talks.summary:
Rob Rashotte, Fortinet's vice president of the Fortinet Training Institute, hosts a short Veterans Day conversation with Tom Marsland, chairman of the board at VetSec, a volunteer-run nonprofit that helps veterans find cybersecurity jobs. Marsland describes his own path: a 22-year Navy career that began in nuclear power work on submarines, with collateral IT and governance duties along the way. While still serving, he researched civilian cyber roles and built a transition timeline. He says his hardest steps were turning military experience into a resume, learning to interview, and networking professionally on LinkedIn, all while handling administrative tasks such as VA claims and separation processing.

The discussion then turns to why cybersecurity suits veterans. Marsland points to situational awareness, attention to detail, cross-functional teamwork, and the ability to pick up new skills quickly after frequent moves. Both agree the field demands lifelong learning because it changes fast. Marsland says VetSec's main resource is its community of roughly 6,600 members, who mentor one another on resumes, interviews, technical topics and benefits, and who usually answer questions within minutes. The group also helps members sort low-cost, quality training from boot camps that overpromise.

Rashotte closes by describing the Training Institute's Veterans Program, which serves service members, veterans and military spouses, and Marsland's seat on its advisory council. Rashotte also notes Fortinet's goal of training one million people in cybersecurity by 2026. The two suggest that many people in the industry have military backgrounds, so newcomers often find colleagues who made the same move, and viewers were directed to the Training Institute page on fortinet.com.

talks.title: Exploring Threat Informed Defense with MITRE Engenuity CTID | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Examines threat-informed defense, ATT&CK-driven reporting, Workbench collaboration, and robustness scoring for detection analytics.
talks.summary:
Defenders often collect large volumes of threat data yet struggle to translate it into prioritized, testable controls. A program manager from MITRE Engenuity’s Center for Threat Informed Defense outlines the organization’s threat-informed defense triad: cyber threat intelligence, defensive measures, and test and evaluation in a loop where evaluation results refresh intelligence and priorities.

The dialogue connects that model to FortiGuard’s operational use of MITRE ATT&CK, including a global threat landscape report that maps observed activity to tactics and techniques and uses heat maps to show commonly detected techniques within each tactic. ATT&CK is described as a shared language for adversary behaviors that outlasts specific malware or infrastructure, though the matrix keeps growing and each technique can be carried out many ways. ATT&CK Workbench is highlighted as a containerized way to blend proprietary notes with the public knowledge base, support roles and collaboration, and keep pace with twice-yearly ATT&CK updates instead of fragile spreadsheets.

The session also covers Summiting the Pyramid, which scores detection analytics by robustness—the effort required to evade them—based on observables left on systems and the sensors that capture them. Contrasting brittle hash matching with stronger signals such as embedded original file names illustrates how teams can improve coverage before an analytic silently fails. Fortinet describes using Workbench to align researchers and product teams around technique-level detection gaps.

talks.title: Social Engineering and Phishing Tactics | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Explores how social engineering differs between advanced groups and cybercriminals, plus training and deception-based defenses.
talks.summary:
A podcast-style conversation between two hosts traces social engineering beyond phishing emails and draws parallels with magic's misdirection and trust-building. It contrasts advanced persistent threat groups with cybercriminals: both may use similar lures, but criminals usually chase fast payment, while the more sophisticated groups aim to stay under the radar and keep long-term access, sometimes even through job placements.

The discussion walks through real-world style examples. One guest describes a penetration test in which a tablet gifted to an employee led them to enter Salesforce, VPN and directory credentials into preloaded apps, and the employee had not reported it for fear of losing the device. Other cases include a fake conference organiser asking for a speaker's home address, a fake firefighter pretext used to reach a data center, and a business email compromise reinforced by a follow-up deepfake voice call. The guests also explain how researchers use sock puppet accounts to observe underground forums without exposing themselves.

The conversation then turns to awareness training, with the advice that phishing simulations should not punish staff or become competitions, and that ongoing programs work better. On defense, the hosts stress planning for initial access failure through layered segmentation and permissions. They describe a customer who placed honeypots in an isolated segment, where alerts on scanning and SSH login attempts exposed an insider pivoting from a compromised system.
