talks.title: State of Ransomware Settlements | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for State of Ransomware Settlements | FortiGuardLIVE.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this episode of FortiGuardLIVE, Derek Manky (VP of Global Threat Intelligence at Fortinet's FortiGuard Labs) and Aomar Marrakchi discuss the evolving landscape of ransomware settlements, criminal business models, and defensive strategies. Reflecting on over a decade of tracking ransomware since 2010, the speakers explore how attackers have transitioned from broad opportunism to highly organized, selective enterprise models targeting massive multi-million-dollar payouts.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Extortion and Wipers**: Ransomware playbooks have advanced beyond double and triple extortion into incorporating wipers. Previously confined primarily to Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) operations, wipers are increasingly leveraged by ransomware gangs to hinder post-incident forensic investigation by destroying evidence, as well as serving as intimidation to compel victims into paying.
- **Cryptocurrency Preferences**: Threat actors have largely shifted away from privacy-focused coins like Monero in favor of Bitcoin. While Monero offers built-in privacy, liquidating millions of dollars is difficult. Bitcoin provides broader liquidity, easier settlement access for victims paying seven-to-eight-figure ransoms, and simpler conversion and money laundering pipelines into real-world currency.
- **Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) Business Model**: The operational model has evolved from a pay-per-install (PPI) approach with thousands of unvetted actors to a pay-per-purchase (PPP) commission model. RaaS core operators now curate exclusive networks of vetted, skilled affiliates who receive the majority share of ransoms. These affiliates focus on high-value targets demanding seven- to eight-figure ransoms, leaving lower six-figure demands behind.
- **Diversified Distribution Vectors**: Ransomware deployment is increasingly distributed through an array of initial access vectors, including botnets, website and CMS plugins (such as WordPress plugins), ad networks, phishing campaigns, and macro-enabled office documents.

### Technical Details
Defending against contemporary ransomware requires mapping and disrupting complex attacker infrastructure rather than solely focusing on malware binaries. Infrastructure encompasses initial delivery mechanisms, vetted affiliate portals, command-and-control (C2) servers, money mule systems, and laundering networks. Proactive defenses highlight multi-layered prevention—incorporating endpoint security, web filtering, DNS filtering, and integrating threat intelligence into AI/ML-driven detection models to stop intrusions before encryption or data wiping begins.

### Takeaways
- **Incident Response as an Ongoing Practice**: Organizations should maintain active, tested incident response plans that adapt continuously to modern ransomware trends, including wiper recovery and antiforensic tactics, rather than treating incident response as a reactive measure activated only during a crisis.
- **Proactive 'Shift Left' Defense**: Given that ransomware settlements now reach tens of millions of dollars, the return on investment (ROI) heavily favors proactive defense and automation (AI-powered SecOps) to intercept threats early.
- **Technology Combined with People**: Robust security posture relies on modern orchestration, automation, AI integration, and continuous training, recognizing that human defenders alone are too slow to keep pace with dynamic cybercriminal syndicates.

talks.teaser: Explains why cloud provider firewalls fall short for enterprises and how a managed cloud-native firewall service addresses those gaps.
talks.summary:
An analyst from Enterprise Strategy Group interviews Fortinet's Vinod Sundaraj about network firewalls for public cloud infrastructure. Survey findings cited in the discussion show that many teams pick cloud service provider firewalls for ease of management, ease of use and scalability. The speaker argues that these native tools are first-generation offerings: they give basic protection up to layer 4 using access control lists, lack deep application visibility and advanced threat prevention, and leave signature updates to the customer.

Fortinet's answer is the FortiGate cloud-native firewall on AWS, a managed service. Its security functions closely match the company's virtual next-generation firewalls; the real difference is who runs the infrastructure. Customers who want to offload that work get a low-friction, automated, consumption-based service and only need to define and deploy policy. Dynamic object-based policies use metadata tags instead of tying rules to network addresses. The conversation also covers hybrid estates, where FortiManager applies consistent policy across cloud and on-premises, and integration with AWS Firewall Manager lets operations teams manage security from the AWS console.

The practical takeaway is that native cloud firewalls may be simpler to run but often lack the inspection depth enterprises need. Teams weighing a managed option should check which protections are included, who maintains signatures, and whether policy can stay consistent across their environments.

talks.title: Universal ZTNA | Product Demo
talks.teaser: Shows zero trust network access built from endpoint posture tags, ZTNA proxy rules, and cloud web filtering in a vendor demo.
talks.summary:
The demo walks through zero trust network access built from the FortiClient endpoint agent, the FortiClient EMS management server, and the FortiGate Universal ZTNA proxy, with SAML single sign-on through a FortiAuthenticator. Four managed endpoints in two user groups show how the same internal resources behave differently depending on who is connecting and from where. EMS endpoint profiles set malware protection, web filtering, application firewall rules and vulnerability scanning, and zero trust tags are built from checks such as Active Directory group membership, domain logon, antivirus status and BitLocker state. A device with too many critical or high vulnerabilities receives a vulnerable tag, which can be used to deny access.

On the FortiGate, those tags feed ZTNA rules that match the source user, the published server or URL, and the required tags, with security inspection applied per resource. Access was tested for a remote engineer, an on-premises IT user, and an on-premises machine running an outdated Windows install with vulnerable applications, which was denied every resource. Client certificates issued by EMS verify each connection, and SAML lets a supported application log the user in without a second password prompt. The FortiGate logs record each allowed and denied attempt.

The second half covers FortiSASE, the cloud-delivered version that reuses the same tagging model for remote users and thin-edge sites. Web filtering blocks categories such as proxy avoidance and pornography for both. Enabling TLS inspection exposed malware hidden inside encrypted HTTPS sessions that had been invisible before. The practical takeaway is that access decisions can rely on device posture, not just identity, and that ZTNA and SASE can be combined.

talks.title: The State of Cybersecurity for OT Environments | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Explains why OT security lags behind IT and how inventory, segmentation and least privilege help protect industrial networks.
talks.summary:
Willie Nelson, a field information security officer for operational technology, joins Jim Richberg to discuss the state of OT security. He cites a 2022 operational technology report that found organizations still move slowly toward full protection, and a survey figure of 93% of participants reporting at least one successful breach. The pair argue that safety and reliability usually outrank security in OT, so an attack can quickly become a physical problem for a production line.

The conversation then turns to ransomware and connectivity. Nelson argues that air gaps around industrial sites are often a myth, since engineers and contractors bring laptops onto the network and then reach the internet from them. He says operators now deliberately connect devices for remote control, so exposure is a conscious choice. Both speakers agree that OT and IT are converging, and they describe legacy systems running for decades with outdated interfaces that are hard to update.

Their advice starts with knowing your assets through a good inventory, then segmenting the network. They urge a principle of distrust, meaning least privilege and constant identity checks, much like the need-to-know model used in government. Virtual patching and data loss prevention can serve as compensating controls, which requires working closely with automation engineers. Existing frameworks such as the CISA Maturity Model and NIST guidance offer roadmaps, and the closing point is that automation and machine learning can help close the skills gap.

talks.title: Career Pathways in Cyber | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Explores different routes into cybersecurity careers, from networking backgrounds to threat intelligence, with advice on persistence.
talks.summary:
This short webinar-style conversation between two security strategists looks at how people move into cybersecurity careers. The guest recounts starting in telecommunications and networking, then being pointed toward security by an early employer who said that solid networking skills and an understanding of process would make the switch manageable. The hosts stress that the field has many entry points, from compliance and auditing to secure coding and research, and that the right path depends on a person's skills, motivation and interests.

The guest then describes the current role, which combines data science with security research to study attacker behavior in Latin America and the Caribbean. Telemetry from the vendor is used to understand what attackers do in each region and industry, and those findings feed into defensive strategy and portfolio planning. The guest also mentions pursuing a doctorate in artificial intelligence to apply data to prediction and decision-making, and recalls an early period at the vendor, including an internal training week, that shaped the direction of the career.

For newcomers, the pair point to discipline, patience and passion as the core foundations. Surrounding yourself with people who are stronger than you is presented as a driver of growth, and early frustration with offensive techniques is described as normal. Intensive study in the early twenties is framed as something that compounds over a career, and people from other industries are encouraged to bring transferable skills into security. The main takeaway is to find a genuine curiosity before chasing a particular role.

She then welcomes Rob to outline Fortinet's security awareness and training offering.

Rob explains that the service is delivered as software as a service, so organizations of any size can deploy it without heavy setup. The content was built by Fortinet's training experts on NIST guidelines and is aligned with research from FortiGuard Labs so lessons track current threats. Beyond courses, the package includes posters, tip sheets and other resources, because he frames awareness as building a culture rather than a single training event. Fortinet staff complete the training every year. An education edition is being offered free to US school districts after a White House summit commitment, and industry-specific versions are planned for other sectors.

Rob closes by pointing viewers to free, self-paced training on Fortinet's training site, along with the Network Security Expert certification program, which he says has issued over 1 million certifications across more than 230 countries and territories. The main takeaway is that phishing defence depends on repeated, organization-wide habits rather than occasional courses.

talks.title: Tech Bytes: Fortinet’s ZTNA Differentiation Starts With The OS | Packet Pushers
talks.teaser: Explains how Fortinet builds zero trust network access from one OS, endpoint client and policy server, and how to move off VPN.
talks.summary:
This sponsored Packet Pushers discussion explains zero trust network architecture (ZTNA) as a set of cooperating components rather than a single product: a client-side element, a policy and authentication element, and an enforcement point. The guest contrasts this with a plain firewall rule, which enforces access without tying it to a client or identity. Firewalling remains in a zero trust design, but the enforcement point may sit on an appliance, at an SD-WAN edge or in the cloud.

Using Fortinet's products as the example, the guest walks through a session. The client authenticates on every connection and presents a device certificate, and a TLS 1.3 tunnel carries traffic to the enforcement point. Policy checks cover identity, application identification and endpoint admission, such as running processes and antivirus status. The guest argues that one operating system across on-premises, cloud and service deployments avoids the gaps of stitching separate products together, and that this keeps licensing simple. Latency is discussed through faster TLS 1.3 setup and local inspection on the client.

On migration, the guest says a VPN client can run alongside ZTNA, so applications can move over gradually instead of in one cutover. The main preparation is auditing existing VPN access, especially broad any-to-any rules, and classifying users. A practical approach is to pilot with a technically capable group, learn from it, and then widen the rollout.

talks.title: What's new in FortiAnalyzer 7.2
talks.teaser: FortiAnalyzer 7.2 brings SOC automation, shadow IT and recon detection, FortiGate IOC checks, and IoT edge visibility for faster response.
talks.summary:
Fortinet presents the headline capabilities in FortiAnalyzer 7.2 for security teams that rely on centralized logging, SOC workflows, and FortiGate telemetry. The session opens on automation: ServiceNow moves from a one-way incident export into FortiSOC, where analysts can build low-code playbooks. Current actions push incident updates to ServiceNow; the narrative outlines near-term paths such as lightweight ITSM-style ticketing for smaller environments and bidirectional sync so ticket changes in ServiceNow appear in FortiAnalyzer and shorten response time.

The middle focuses on visibility and event handling inside FortiSOC. Out-of-the-box handlers target shadow IT on user endpoints, surfacing unsanctioned applications, unauthorized use, and file exfiltration where approved software alone is easy to inventory. A separate handler flags endpoint reconnaissance, motivated by long-dwell intrusions that still probe the network; it fires when an endpoint reaches on the order of a hundred distinct destination addresses within a very short window. Administrators also gain expanded IOC detection on FortiGate local traffic to catch misuse of misconfigured appliances from inside or against DMZ assets.

The close covers IoT and OT at the edge: FortiAnalyzer adds visibility and anomaly detection for attached devices, with inventory tracking and malware protection tied to FortiGate. The Raspberry Pi example illustrates an unknown rogue device phoning home to command-and-control. Practitioners should treat 7.2 as a bundle of ready-made handlers and integrations to wire into existing SOC and edge programs rather than a single feature switch.

talks.title: SSL/TLS Inspection Demo | FortiGate
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiGate SSL inspection decrypts traffic to block a malware download and a risky Facebook post.
talks.summary:
This short product demo argues that SSL inspection matters because most web traffic is now encrypted, and that a firewall which cannot read that traffic misses threats hidden inside it. It walks through the FortiGate SSL inspection security profile, which can decrypt outbound traffic to the internet and inbound traffic aimed at internal servers hosting applications, including several certificates for several applications. The profile sets how blocked and untrusted certificates are handled, whether server name mismatches are enforced, and whether protocol and cipher compliance applies. Administrators can exempt reputable sites, web categories, or address objects defined by FQDN, IP address, or geolocation from decryption.

The presenter then explains why deep inspection is also needed for application control, since many cloud file upload and download functions and most Facebook features can only be identified when traffic is decrypted. Decryption also helps prevent data exfiltration. The profile is attached to a security policy, and decrypted traffic can be mirrored to a server for archiving and analysis.

In the live demonstration, the profile first runs in certificate-based inspection mode. A malware download from an internal test server over HTTPS succeeds, and a Facebook wall post goes through even though the application control profile blocks it. After switching to custom deep inspection, the same malware download is decrypted, detected and blocked, and the Facebook post is blocked and logged. The antivirus logs show the blocked Grand Crab ransomware file, and filtering the application control logs by the Facebook post application shows the related entries. The takeaway for practitioners is that certificate-only inspection leaves encrypted threats and application policies unenforced.

talks.title: Manage Cloud Risk Through Actionable Insights | FortiCNP for AWS
talks.teaser: Presents how FortiCNP for AWS correlates and prioritizes cloud alerts to reduce manual triage work.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a problem many organizations face as they move critical workloads into the cloud. Adding more tools tends to fragment security operations and flood teams with alerts that lack context. Risks build up faster than they can be resolved, and analysts have to triage results by hand, which consumes time, lowers productivity and can cause critical risks to be missed.

The presenter introduces FortiCNP as a cloud-native protection solution that integrates natively with AWS security services and the Fortinet Security Fabric. It correlates and contextualizes alerts while ranking the highest-risk resources. Its resource risk insights technology weighs findings across all integrated cloud solutions. Because the integration is built in from the start, the product gives deep visibility across an organization's cloud footprint, aiming to speed up alert response and make better use of AWS security investments already made. Consistent workflows are meant to extend coverage across services without losing productivity.

For high-priority risks, FortiCNP connects to digital workflow solutions that automate and manage remediation. Fixes that belong in the CI/CD pipeline can be backed by stopgap remediations from Fortinet cloud security solutions, which protect against threats until permanent fixes are in place. The closing message is that the product removes integration friction, prioritizes critical risks and streamlines cloud security management for AWS workloads. A free trial is offered through AWS Marketplace.

talks.title: Deception Technology for IT/OT/IoT Environments | FortiDeceptor
talks.teaser: Shows how decoy systems lure attackers across IT, IoT and OT networks and feed alerts into Fortinet response automation.
talks.summary:
Moshe Ben Simon, product manager for FortiDeceptor, presents deception as a low-friction way to spot threats already inside a network. He frames the problem around operational technology: many OT devices run legacy systems or cannot be taken down for patches, and growing IP connectivity and remote access paths let attackers reach converged IT and OT environments from anywhere. Decoys are virtual fake assets that imitate IT devices and industrial control systems, drawing intruders away from real targets.

He describes the product as combining honeypot style decoys with threat analytics and mitigation in one appliance or VM form. Decoys cover Windows, Linux, ERP, point-of-sale, medical and SCADA systems, and a wizard deploys them in a few clicks, with custom OS images supported for those who need them. The console handles decoy deployment, passive asset discovery and incident analysis. In the demonstration, captured engagements showed an attack against Modbus traffic and another against the EIP protocol.

Because decoys only trip on unauthorized activity, their alerts can feed automated responses. Integration with FortiGate and FortiNAC, along with FortiSiem, FortiSoar and FortiAnalyzer, lets containment actions run across the Fortinet fabric. The takeaway for practitioners is to consider deception as a complement to existing detection, especially for devices that cannot report their own telemetry.

talks.title: Update on Trending Cyber Threats | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Reviews recent RCE outbreaks, Discord-delivered malware, and travel lures, with patching and awareness takeaways.
talks.summary:
Derek Menke and Marla Connie review the threats that have been trending recently. Their focus is remote code execution flaws, which they say attackers now prefer because they allow access without physical contact. They point to a Confluence vulnerability and a Microsoft MSDT exploit, both of which were widely deployed. Outbreak telemetry showed two attack waves within roughly two weeks: the first followed patch releases, and the second often reflected mutated variants of the same attack.

The middle of the discussion covers the campaigns that followed these exploits. One payload was spread through Discord, which the speakers describe as a trusted channel that attackers use for delivery. A targeted attack on a coffee shop in Ukraine used Google Loader with an NSIS installer, an older framework that malware still relies on. They also cover travel-themed lures about hotel bookings and flight changes, paired with remote access trojans. Wipers combined with ransomware were noted as raising the damage once an initial foothold exists.

The speakers close on social engineering, which they call one of the most effective tactics because it asks a user to grant access they already hold, even when multi-factor authentication is in place. Their practical takeaways are that disabling affected services as mitigations correlates with waves subsiding, that patch timelines matter, and that training and awareness remain central. Further details are on the FortiGuard outbreak alert page and the Fortinet threat research blog.

talks.title: FortiGate User Identification | NGFW
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding FortiGate User Identification | NGFW.
talks.summary:
## Overview
This video demonstrates FortiGate's user identification feature in next-generation firewalls (NGFW) and covers both agentless and agent-based deployment configurations. The feature enables the firewall to map network traffic to specific users by consolidating user and group information from multiple sources, with all data available in the FortiGate dashboard's User tab.

## Information Sources
User information and IP mappings are pulled from:
- Active Directory
- RADIUS
- Syslog
- Exchange
- eDirectory
- Citrix Terminal Server

## Configuration Methods
Two primary approaches are detailed:

**Agentless Configuration (FSSO Polling)**: Fortinet Single Sign-On periodically polls Active Directory at fixed intervals to retrieve user information. Administrators define an LDAP server as the source and select specific Active Directory groups from which to pull user information.

**Agent-Based Configuration**: A collector agent is deployed on a server within the domain controller's network. The transcript mentions using 4D Authenticator as an example collector agent. This approach provides enhanced functionality, enabling the collection of user mapping information from additional sources including syslog servers, Citrix Terminal Servers, and Exchange servers.

## Implementation & Usage
Once the fabric connectors for identity are configured, administrators use the User Authentication tab to define user groups. These groups can be incorporated into security policies to control user access. All traffic traversing the FortiGate is mapped to specific users and can be viewed in the logs.

## Practical Demonstration
The video includes a live demo showing:
- A test user (Ron Smith) logged into a desktop behind the FortiGate
- User web traffic to allowed sites (YouTube, Yahoo) appearing in the Forward Traffic Logs with username mapping
- Blocked traffic (poker.com) recorded in web filtering logs with the associated username

All user activity is accessible through the Log and Report section, where the Forward Traffic Logs display all traffic with associated usernames, enabling granular visibility into who accessed what resources through the firewall.

## Key Benefits
User identification enables security policies and access controls based on user identity rather than IP addresses alone, and provides detailed audit trails linking specific network activity to individual users.

talks.title: FortiGuard AI Powered Web Filtering Service | FortiGuard Security Services
talks.teaser: Shows a FortiGate web filter profile blocking malicious sites, phishing attempts and YouTube searches.
talks.summary:
The video introduces the web filtering service in FortiGate, a cloud-delivered feature that draws on FortiGuard threat intelligence to control web traffic. It highlights more than 90 web categories for granular control, three predefined filters that simplify setup, and custom filters tailored to an organization. Administrators can let specific user groups override blocked categories after they authenticate.

Next, the static URL filter can block unwanted addresses using simple matching, wildcards or regular expressions, with block, allow or monitor actions. Near real-time blocking of malicious URLs found by the sandbox is also available, and content filters can stop banned words in search engines, including YouTube, across several languages. Once the profile is built, it is attached to a security policy so that traffic is filtered.

The demonstration covers three cases. A user reaching a site that presents a certificate issued for another domain is stopped with a block notice, even after choosing to proceed. A phishing URL is blocked before the connection and the user sees a page explaining why. On YouTube, the video plays normally, but a search for a configured term is blocked. The FortiGate logs tie each event to a username, drawn from single sign-on, the authenticator or client telemetry, and show malicious, phishing and content-filter entries with detail views. The main takeaway is that layered profiles plus user-level logging make web-borne threats visible and enforceable.

talks.title: Configuring FortiVoice NFS Storage | FortiVoice
talks.teaser: Shows how to attach NFS-backed network storage to a FortiVoice phone system and share its call data from TrueNAS.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how FortiVoice can move stored voicemail, call recordings and fax files off its local disk and onto network attached storage, using the Network File System protocol. The example storage target is TrueNAS, a free NAS platform. The presenter walks through enabling the NFS service in TrueNAS, creating a storage pool from a selected disk, and adding an NFS share with its path, root user and group mapping, and optional limits on which hosts or IP addresses may connect.

On the FortiVoice side, the walkthrough goes to the system configuration storage tab, selects NAS with NFS, and enters the TrueNAS IP address, the default port 2049, and the NFS path noted earlier. Applying the settings starts the mount, which can take several minutes. Once the status shows OK, FortiVoice has created its folder structure on the NAS and is using it for storage.

The final section covers optional read access for users. The example enables SMB in TrueNAS and creates a Windows share on the voicemail folder with guest access and an open default ACL, then opens it from Windows Explorer by IP address. The presenter leaves user creation and access control lists to the TrueNAS documentation.

talks.title: Configuring FortiVoice iSCSI Storage | FortiVoice
talks.teaser: Walks through building an iSCSI target on TrueNAS and attaching it to FortiVoice for extra storage.
talks.summary:
FortiVoice can keep call recordings, voicemail and faxes on local storage, but it can also use network-attached storage to expand capacity. This video shows how to connect the phone system to an iSCSI target, using TrueNAS as the storage server. iSCSI is the protocol the phone system supports for this purpose.

On the TrueNAS side, the walkthrough starts by enabling the iSCSI service and setting it to start automatically. It then creates a storage pool from an available disk and adds a zvol sized to the space to be used. Next, a block share is built: a portal on a chosen IP address using the default port 3260, an initiators group that allows all initiators, and an authorized access group with a username and password. A target, an extent tied to the zvol with TPC enabled, and an associated target with a LUN ID complete the share.

On the FortiVoice side, the administrator opens the storage settings, selects NAS, and enters the iSCSI credentials along with the TrueNAS address and port. After applying, the device is tested and then formatted, and the presenter notes that the format process can take at least five minutes. Once the status is refreshed, it shows OK and the storage is ready. The result is a clear path for adding iSCSI capacity to the phone system.

talks.title: What's new in Fortinet Secure SD-WAN FOS 7.2? | SD-WAN
talks.teaser: Covers Fortinet Secure SD-WAN 7.2 additions: an overlay wizard, zero-touch provisioning, and category-based steering rules.
talks.summary:
This vendor video presents what is new in Fortinet Secure SD-WAN with the 7.2 operating system release. It opens by linking SD-WAN adoption to remote work and more sophisticated attacks such as ransomware, and positions the product as a market leader in that space.

The main additions are the SD-WAN overlay wizard, which helps build a scalable, redundant overlay. The user selects a topology, defines the role of each device, and enters network settings, then applies the configuration to devices in a region. The wizard's templates can be applied to new devices for zero-touch provisioning, so one configuration maps to many branch deployments and onboarding time is reduced. For smaller deployments without a central manager, the fabric self-orchestrator lets Security Fabric devices automatically build a secure overlay for inter-site traffic. VRF-based LAN segments are kept across locations and placed in their matching route tables, giving end-to-end segmentation.

The release also lets administrators use FortiGuard categories as destinations in SD-WAN rules. Whole business-critical categories can be steered over a preferred link and non-critical ones over a less preferred link, which shifts policy from individual rules or applications to business intent. The talk adds MOS scoring and monitoring for voice and video traffic, with MOS-based SLA thresholds that set minimum link requirements based on user experience. It closes by noting that this builds on earlier application performance monitoring for SaaS applications.

Short says his firm began in carrier service migrations and, after evaluating several SD-WAN vendors, chose to standardize on Fortinet because it covered SD-WAN as well as data center and wider attack surface protection through its Fabric approach.

He credits the partner program's training for efficiency. Engineers who complete the NSE courses troubleshoot, configure and roll out large enterprise deployments faster, which lets the firm scale. He describes the SD-WAN and ZTNA specializations as a broader philosophy rather than one product, spanning endpoint detection, email protection, firewalls, sandboxing and incident response through FortiGuard. Short adds that holding a vendor-recognized specialization, alongside customer references, makes buying decisions quicker for customers.

On zero trust, Short advises partners to start at the edge and work inward, addressing attack surfaces first because they are the easiest area to improve with limited effort. He notes that many customers still treat zero trust as a product rather than a framework, so much of the work is education. The session closes with a pointer to Fortinet's Engage program blogs and articles about the specializations.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Integrated, AI-Powered Network Detection and Response | FortiNDR.
talks.summary: Fortinet markets FortiNDR as an AI-driven network detection and response layer for ransomware-style advanced persistent cybercrime. The narrator cites MITRE CTID findings that fifteen techniques dominate observed activity by mimicking legitimate admin behavior. FortiNDR promises baseline anomaly detection, weak-cipher heuristics, a virtual analyst for scope tracing, and fabric integrations to quarantine hosts through firewalls, switches, or NAC plus third-party APIs. The segment is promotional, emphasizing faster validation and orchestrated response amid tool sprawl and staffing gaps.

talks.title: Securing Remote Workforces with FortiSASE | FortiSASE
talks.teaser: Shows FortiSASE protecting remote users with SSL inspection, web and app filtering, and zero trust access.
talks.summary:
The demo tours FortiSASE, a cloud service for securing remote workers, beginning with the portal. Dashboards show connected users, managed endpoints, license usage, application and website activity, and threat reports that can be filtered by threat type, action or alert level. Administrators set VPN policies for SSL traffic and policies for clientless users redirected by a PAC file, and group security profiles for use in those policies.

SSL inspection comes first. With deep inspection enabled in the security profile but not enforced in the VPN policy, a malicious encrypted file downloads. After enforcement, the content is decrypted and the download is blocked, which the presenter ties to more than 95 percent of web traffic being encrypted. Web filtering then blocks a malicious site and a gaming category, and filtered logs show the user's blocked activity.

Application control blocks gaming apps, certain collaboration apps, file uploads to a cloud storage app and access to a personal Google Drive account, and the threat view lists each violation. The final use case, secure private access, requires a compliant endpoint with tags such as AV, device authentication by certificate, then SAML single sign-on. The user reaches resources in their own department, while the ZTNA rules block another department's resource based on user group and tags.

talks.title: FortiSASE Overview | SASE
talks.teaser: Walks through FortiSASE's portal, SSL inspection, web filtering, app control and zero trust access in a product demo.
talks.summary:
FortiSASE is a cloud secure access platform built on the FortiOS operating system and backed by FortiGuard AI-powered security services. The walkthrough starts with the cloud portal dashboard, which shows connected users, how they connect, their location, managed endpoints and license usage. Tabs summarize applications, websites and threats, while configuration covers SSL VPN and secure web gateway policies for clientless users. Security profiles are grouped under one tab, start with recommended defaults, can be customized, and are applied to policies for layer 7 inspection.

The demos begin with SSL inspection: a malicious encrypted file downloads until deep inspection is enforced in the VPN policy, after which the download is blocked. Web filtering resets the connection to a malicious site and blocks the gaming category in the Play Store, with the certificate issued by the FortiSASE instance itself. Application control blocks gaming, collaboration apps such as WeChat, Discord and Google Chat, file uploads to Box and access to personal Google Drive accounts. All of these violations appear in the activity logs and web filtering logs.

The final section covers zero trust network access. Admins authorize the FortiGates acting as gateways at each data center, then apply endpoint profiles and zero trust tags based on telemetry such as antivirus status. A compliant IT device reaches IT resources after certificate-based device authentication and SAML sign-in, while attempts to reach another department's resources are blocked by user group and tag rules. The main takeaway is that encryption covers about 95 percent of web traffic, so SSL inspection is essential.

talks.title: Ultimate Fabric Challenge | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Three winners of Fortinet's Ultimate Fabric Challenge describe how they prepared, competed and what advice they would offer.
talks.summary:
Fortinet's Rob Rashotte interviews the top three finishers of the inaugural Ultimate Fabric Challenge global championship, held at Accelerate 2022. The challenge is a timed competition of about three hours in which contestants solve a series of objectives to build the most secure network they can with Fortinet products. Regional expert summits during the previous year sent qualifying teams to the global event, but at the championship the competitors worked individually, and everything was based on FortiOS 7.2.

The winners explain how they prepared. One read the public documentation for FortiGate and FortiManager and studied the new 7.2 features. Another took a holiday in the US to adjust to the time zone and reviewed likely challenge content with a colleague. The third relied on regular SD-WAN demo work and on the new 7.2 material in the pre-event package. The panel agreed that day-to-day familiarity with the management interface helped them locate settings quickly under pressure.

Asked for advice, the winners recommended knowing new features and products well, reading public documentation, and taking the free FastTrack workshops, which include lab time for hands-on practice. They noted that scores were close and positions shifted during the event, so competitors should keep going. They also discussed how NSE certifications build credibility with employers and customers, and what they planned to do with their prize money.

talks.title: Tech Bytes: Fortinet’s Switching and Wireless LAN portfolio | Packet Pushers Podcast
talks.teaser: Explains how Fortinet's switches and wireless access points are managed and secured through its firewalls.
talks.summary:
This Packet Pushers Tech Bytes episode introduces Fortinet's switching and wireless LAN portfolio, which the guests say has been developed for close to twenty years and is the company's second-largest product area by revenue after firewalls. They explain why these products get less attention than the firewalls, and why Fortinet argues that security should reach beyond the WAN into the LAN, down to individual switch ports and access points.

The core of the discussion is integration. Switches and access points are managed by the FortiGate firewall through a proprietary protocol that stacks them into one logical management unit, so security policy, wireless configuration and switch settings can be handled from one console. The guests say offload processors keep the firewall from becoming a bottleneck, and that network access control and identity-based microsegmentation are built into the same platform. They also state that Fortinet does not use feature licensing, so access points and switches do not need separate licenses.

For multi-site operations, FortiManager pushes policies and configurations across many FortiGates, and an optional AIOps appliance analyzes client metrics such as signal strength, latency and jitter. The guests stress that customers choose their own level of automation. They describe a school district that replaced a firewall, a wireless controller and a separate switch management system with a single box. The episode closes with product notes: Wi-Fi 6 is shipping, Wi-Fi 6E is coming soon, and a three-radio access point can reassign its radios to add capacity when user numbers spike. The main takeaway is that fewer devices and one policy source can simplify both operations and security.

talks.title: Cyber Readiness and the Threat Landscape | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Examines rising threat speed and sophistication, including ransomware and zero-days, and the people, process and technology defenders need.
talks.summary:
Host Derek Menke interviews Renee Torin, deputy CISO and vice president of information security, about the threat landscape findings from the FortiGuard Labs second half 2021 report. They describe threats growing in sophistication and speed, with attackers quickly exploiting fresh zero-day vulnerabilities, and cybercrime groups increasingly operating in an advanced persistent threat style. Ransomware, including more destructive wiper variants, features heavily in their discussion.

Torin argues that organizations should plan on being targeted and focus on readiness: detection and monitoring capabilities, a sound incident response plan and a recovery plan to get operations back quickly. Proactive measures discussed include sandboxing to detonate suspicious files before they run, deception technology that can slow attackers and reveal lateral movement or insider activity, and disciplined patch management, since many successful attacks still exploit unpatched systems. They note that dwell time has been rising while the attack window has been shrinking, which makes faster detection more important. Automation, orchestration and SOAR can free analysts from routine log work so they have time for training.

The pair conclude that there is no single fix, and that people, process and technology must work together. Free training resources were mentioned as one way to address the cybersecurity skills gap, and the low barrier to entry for attackers who buy kits and malware makes the threat landscape harder to manage.

talks.title: Secure SD-WAN 7.0 Demo | SD-WAN
talks.teaser: Shows centralized SD-WAN management in FortiManager, covering health checks, steering rules, security profiles and analytics.
talks.summary:
This demo presents Fortinet Secure SD-WAN 7.0 as managed from FortiManager, the centralized orchestration console, across a data center and nine branch sites. The presenter starts with provisioning templates, which in this release can be bundled with BGP templates and other template types into template groups for zero-touch deployment. Branch SD-WAN templates then define member interfaces grouped into underlay and overlay zones, along with performance SLA health checks. These probes can target internal or internet-bound destinations over IPv4 or IPv6 and use active, passive, or combined measurement, with thresholds for latency, jitter and packet loss.

Next, the demo covers steering rules, which can match on user identity as well as on addresses and applications drawn from the internet service and application control databases. Four steering strategies are compared: manual pinning, best quality, lowest cost gated by an SLA threshold, and load balancing across members that meet their SLA. Forward error correction and packet duplication are mentioned as remediation for voice and video. The presenter then adds security inspection to an internet access firewall policy by selecting security profiles, including certificate and deep SSL inspection, and notes that FortiManager also manages switches and access points.

The final section shows analytics. A global dashboard colour-codes sites by SLA status and link state, a table view drills into one site with bandwidth and preferred-path indicators, and per-SLA charts support troubleshooting. Monitor and summary views add rules utilization and top SLA issues, and a reports engine with editable templates closes the demo. The main takeaway is that one console covers policy, steering, security and visibility for a distributed SD-WAN network.

talks.title: OpenID Connect (OIDC) FortiAuthenticator | Fortinet Demo
talks.teaser: Shows how to configure OpenID Connect single sign-on on FortiAuthenticator, from relying party setup through sessions and access logs.
talks.summary:
The demo introduces OpenID Connect support, added to FortiAuthenticator in version 6.4.1. The presenter describes OpenID Connect as an identity layer that sits on top of OAuth 2 and presents it as a more flexible single sign-on option than SAML. The walkthrough follows the usual flow: a relying party sends the login request to FortiAuthenticator acting as the identity provider, the user signs in and grants access, the provider issues a token, and the relying party validates that token before it establishes the session.

On the administrator side, the presenter creates an authentication portal and a policy, then sets up the OpenID Connect service. A relying party is defined with an authorization code policy, two claims are added for username and email (with the email claim mapped to the email user attribute), and a redirect URL is entered to finish the configuration. The session view is then shown, where active sessions can be listed and revoked by the administrator.

The final part checks the access logs. The login events show a successful authentication, the provider returning a token, and the relying party verifying it. For administrators, the takeaway is that the setup is a short sequence of portal, policy and relying party settings, and that the session and log views give visibility into each OpenID Connect login.

talks.title: Threat Landscape Developments | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Reviews threat trends, including the Spring4Shell response, wiper malware, satellite modem attacks and teen cybercrime arrests.
talks.summary:
The episode opens with Spring4Shell, a flaw in the Spring Java framework that can expose object properties and sensitive data and, in the worst case, allow remote code execution. The hosts note that a patch was available quickly and that signatures from security vendors arrived within about 24 hours, so there was no mass exploitation comparable to Log4j. They attribute this partly to the exploit needing more skill and to a fast, coordinated response across the industry, which leaves attackers with less time to weaponize it.

The discussion then turns to wiper malware, which the hosts describe as a growing trend this year. They cite more than five threat signals on wipers in the first quarter, naming examples such as HermeticWiper, DoubleZero and CaddyWiper. Their concern is that destructive payloads are moving into criminal playbooks that combine ransom demands with data destruction, and that some activity may be state-linked. They also describe AcidRain, destructive malware that targeted satellite communications by attacking modems at remote sites and firmware. It was reported to have taken remote management offline for roughly five to six thousand wind turbines. The hosts see this as convergence between advanced threat actors and cybercrime groups, with operational technology in remote areas as a likely target.

The final segment covers law enforcement. UK authorities arrested teenagers, aged roughly 13 to 18, connected to a well-known extortion group, and some linked bitcoin wallets were reported to hold over 15 million dollars. The hosts stress that prosecution carries lasting consequences and that the industry should keep offering legitimate paths for young people with these skills.

talks.title: Security Fabric with Cybersecurity Mesh Architecture | Security Fabric
talks.teaser: Explains how a vendor's unified security fabric combines network, endpoint and cloud protection with shared data and automation.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with common customer goals: preventing ransomware and phishing, letting staff work from anywhere, and connecting multiple clouds. The speaker argues that these larger initiatives are better served by a platform-wide approach than by buying individual point products one at a time.

The central idea is a security fabric designed from the start to cover the whole attack surface, with domain expertise in network, endpoint and cloud. Networking and security are converged so that detection and real-time enforcement work everywhere. The speaker describes a large partner ecosystem spanning technology, threat intelligence, DevOps and process automation, along with a unified policy and management framework. Research teams supply machine-learning models that are pushed into products in near real time, and the products draw on the same data set used by the security operations center, giving one view of network performance and security posture.

The closing argument is that automation is now necessary, because automated, AI-driven attacks have to be met with automated defenses. The speaker presents this as a proactive posture that adjusts as risk changes inside an organization, and invites viewers to talk with an expert about secure, high-performance connectivity.

talks.title: Introducing FortiOS 7.2 | Fortinet
talks.teaser: Previews FortiOS 7.2 features for converged networking, inline threat prevention, and per-user licensing.
talks.summary:
The discussion is a host-led interview with John, who covers FortiOS 7.2 against three challenges raised by security leaders and SOC teams. On unseen threats, John argues that detection alone is not enough. Version 7.2 moves a sandbox capability into prevention, so suspicious files can be held at the network level until a verdict arrives. He links IPS signatures to device context and virtual patching, since ransomware often follows exploitation of a vulnerability, and says correlating in-house antivirus, IPS and application data helps narrow what counts as unknown.

The second challenge is the divide between security and networking teams, which John says creates performance and security gaps. He describes converging SD-WAN, firewalling, routing and switching with security, and measuring user experience from the endpoint through Wi-Fi and SD-WAN to the application. For OT environments, he flags ransomware risk from remote access and recommends segmentation, firewalling, visibility and network access control as part of an architectural plan.

On speed, John says humans cannot keep pace, citing Log4j spreading 50 times faster than earlier samples, and favors a few integrated platforms that automate responses. Purchasing comes last: hybrid environments are licensed by device, throughput or user, and Fortinet is moving to per-user pricing across endpoint, network and cloud. Practitioners should ask vendors how detection and prevention are handled and plan architecture across several years.

talks.title: What is Fortinet's SD-Branch Solution? | SD-Branch
talks.teaser: Demonstrates Fortinet SD-Branch by unifying FortiGate, switches, and APs with SD-WAN steering, segmentation, and automated quarantine.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with branch networking pressures from work-from-anywhere, IoT scale, and partial cloud adoption, and argues that dispersed users and devices widen both agility and security gaps. Fortinet’s Security Fabric—integrated gear sharing telemetry, threat intelligence, and automation—is positioned as SD-Branch’s foundation, with emphasis on lower total cost of ownership when switches and access points do not need separate licenses.

The core is a live-style walkthrough from one FortiGate console: physical topology, device identification, quarantine from the map, dashboards for LAN clients, FortiLink authorization for a managed switch and AP, VLANs including a remote server behind a captive portal for an employee group, and employee versus guest SSIDs with distinct firewall and web filtering. SD-WAN rules steer Microsoft, Dropbox, and inventory application traffic using performance SLAs that highlight when latency exceeds targets. Firewall policies segment guest Wi‑Fi, employee Wi‑Fi, and server egress; a virtual IP supports remote desktop to the branch server.

Automation ties a high compromised-host rating trigger to automatic quarantine until staff remediate. The close shows an employee logging in on the remote server before reaching a cloud inventory site. For operators, the takeaway is consolidated branch operations, path-aware application steering, and fabric-level response woven into one deployment story.

talks.title: FortiFone Softclient for Mobile Overview | FortiFone
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in FortiFone Softclient for Mobile Overview | FortiFone.
talks.summary:
This video provides a product demonstration and tutorial of the FortiFone mobile soft client, a unified communications application available for Android and iOS devices. The tutorial walks through the core features and user interface elements.

Outgoing Calls: Users can initiate calls using the dial pad. The application provides hands-free operation via the speaker function and allows selection of audio output methods (speaker or Bluetooth headset) through an audio menu. Calls can also be initiated from the device's call history or contact list by selecting an entry and tapping the call icon.

Incoming Call Handling: When the soft client is running, incoming calls appear with an answer icon. Calls can be answered even when the device screen is locked using the standard device method. Unwanted calls can be declined, and the caller follows the call handling settings configured for the extension on FortiVoice.

Call Transfers: Two transfer types are supported. Attended transfers allow the user to speak with the intended recipient before completing the transfer—initiated by tapping the transfer icon, selecting attended transfer, dialing the recipient, and then confirming transfer once the recipient agrees. Blind transfers send the call directly to the recipient without prior conversation. Both methods provide successful transfer notifications.

Conference Calling: Users can add a third party to an active call by tapping the add call icon, dialing the party, and then tapping merge calls to establish a three-way conference. The manage conference feature displays parties separately, allowing users to end individual calls while maintaining the conference with other participants.

Visual Voicemail: The application displays new voicemail notifications on the device lock screen. Users can access all voicemail messages for their extension, play messages with progress bar controls, and perform actions such as deleting messages or calling back the sender. These options are available both from a dedicated voicemail screen and directly from the main interface.

talks.title: Zero Trust Edge | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Explains how zero trust edge combines SD-WAN, firewalls and ZTNA across on-premise and cloud networks.
talks.summary:
Peter Newton and Nirav Shah open by describing the pressure boards place on IT leaders to pursue digital acceleration. They note that organisations invest in modern networking across LAN, WAN, cloud and OT edges, using technologies such as SD-WAN, 5G, Wi-Fi 6 and cloud-delivered networking. These tools often operate as separate point products that lack awareness of each other, and security is frequently bolted on afterwards, which is the gap the speakers set out to address.

The conversation then turns to work-from-anywhere, where staff split their time between office, home and travel and need one consistent policy throughout. The speakers explain that zero trust has shifted from authenticating a user once at network entry to verifying each access to an application, and they mention architectures from NIST and an analyst firm. ZTNA is presented as the enabling technology, with remote workers and on-site enforcement as its main use cases. Fortinet's ZTNA is firewall-based, so it can run on premises, as a virtual instance in the cloud or as a cloud-delivered service.

The closing section frames Zero Trust Edge as a step-by-step journey rather than a move to cloud on day one. Organisations first converge SD-WAN, next-generation firewalling and ZTNA on premises, then extend the same capabilities to remote users through the cloud under one policy. The speakers stress keeping on-prem firewalls and segmentation for internal threats. The takeaway is to combine networking and security decisions and favour a platform that consolidates them.

talks.title: Ransomware Settlements and Cyber Insurance | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Explores why ransomware keeps growing and whether cyber insurance and negotiated settlements can serve as a real defense.
talks.summary:
Derek Manke of Fortinet's FortiGuard Labs joins host Jim Richberg to describe the current ransomware landscape. He says activity jumped sharply in the first half of the previous year and has stayed high, and that payloads are becoming more targeted and destructive, with wiper features now combined with extortion. The pair link this growth to cryptocurrency, since criminals can move funds quickly across many coins and platforms. They also describe an ecosystem that has matured to the point of offering help desks that walk victims through buying crypto and making transfers.

The conversation then turns to cyber insurance, which organizations often see as a way to avoid dealing with criminals. Manke agrees it is a useful safeguard but argues it cannot be a silver bullet or a stopgap. Policies typically cover measurable costs such as fines and equipment replacement, but not business losses or reputational damage. Public sector bodies can be especially exposed, because their spending is published and attackers can estimate coverage limits. Paying a settlement also does not end the threat, since criminals often return for more and shift to other targets.

The speakers agree that ransomware needs a shared response involving governments, technology providers, insurers and organizations. Manke stresses that the basics come first, including strong security controls and offline backups, with insurance and negotiation considered only after other layers have been explored. The host notes that repeat victims may see insurers reduce payouts or withdraw coverage. The main takeaway is that insurance adds a layer of protection but does not replace prevention.

talks.title: Global Threat Landscape Report | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: FortiGuard analysts review H2 2021 report findings on persistent cybercrime, Log4j-scale speed, and automated API-driven attacks.
talks.summary:
Derek Menke and a FortiGuard colleague walk through themes from Fortinet’s second-half 2021 threat landscape report, framed as advanced persistent cybercrime: criminal groups increasingly mirror nation-state style reconnaissance, weaponization, and zero-day use, with malware authors moving beyond simple scripting into languages such as C++, Go, and Java while staying stealthy.

They stress that ransomware stayed at the highest levels observed through 2021 alongside more destructive activity such as wiper malware. Speed dominates the narrative: the attack window keeps shrinking, with Log4j driving unprecedented prevalence in just ten days and a reported exploit spread rate fifty times faster than a comparable window for ProxyLogon. Mass internet scanning after disclosure left defenders facing roughly twenty-four to forty-eight hours to prepare and respond. Telemetry tied to MITRE ATT&CK shows execution through API and scripting exceeding sixty percent of code execution techniques versus about twenty percent relying on user interaction, reflecting attacker automation built into kits and scan workflows.

Further report highlights include Linux ELF payload volume roughly quadrupling from the first to the fourth quarter of 2021 as criminals target IoT, OT, and consumer Linux devices, plus more than twenty thousand net new CVEs logged in 2021 while breaches still leverage flaws twelve to forty-eight months old. Practitioners should pair patching and asset awareness with SOC automation and integration to match adversary speed and scale.

talks.title: How to Manage False Positive Events with FortiEDR | Endpoint Security
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiEDR handles inconclusive alerts via cloud analysis, policy-driven triage, and granular exceptions for safe applications.
talks.summary:
The session walks through how FortiEDR deals with inconclusive endpoint alerts when new events need a decision. When Fortinet cloud services and the FCS security engine mark an activity as a false positive, the product reclassifies it as safe, creates a matching exception so the same pattern does not fire again, and archives the alert without manual rework. Analysts can read a digest of that analysis in the event handling comment or drill into the full investigative steps.

A TeamViewer example illustrates policy-led triage rather than purely automated verdicts. The XDR engine adds context: manual execution by a named user, valid publisher signature, clean sandbox behavior, and usage stats showing the app elsewhere in the estate with connections to a known-good address. After review, an operator can classify the item as safe, set an exception, and archive it. Exceptions can scope to collector groups, destinations, users, or the triggering rule, with wildcards on process name or path and optional parent-process limits; scripting tools can allow specific scripts per engine, and the exception manager centralizes review and edits.

The walkthrough also notes excluding a trusted process from monitoring so benign binaries stop generating noise entirely. Together, the flow emphasizes cloud-assisted analysis, human policy choice, and fine-grained tuning to cut false positive volume while keeping visibility where it matters.

talks.title: FortiEDR's Incident Workflow and Role-Based Administration | Endpoint Security
talks.teaser: Shows a SOC team triaging and escalating an endpoint event in FortiEDR, from a level 1 analyst to a level 3 engineer.
talks.summary:
The demo opens in the administration area of the FortiEDR console, where a hoster account manages users for a customer tenant. It shows how a new level 1 SOC analyst is created, with assigned roles, optional two-factor authentication, and sign-in options through local accounts, LDAP for Active Directory, or SAML single sign-on with an identity provider.

The walkthrough then follows the new analyst through an alert. The analyst's view lists only events not yet marked as handled. The first event involves a legitimate Microsoft process that could be abused to load a malicious DLL through search order hijacking, and since the classification is uncertain, the analyst adds a comment and escalates it to a level 3 engineer.

The senior engineer reviews the cloud-based automatic analysis, which flags an in-memory payload and a DLL named windbio.dll masquerading as a legitimate library. Using the forensic view, the engineer confirms the activity is malicious, records a note for the analyst, and marks the event handled so it drops out of the unhandled queue. The demo is based on a real zero-day attack by the FIN7 group that aims to steal credentials, which the vendor's research team has published about. The takeaway is how role separation and comment-based escalation let a SOC move an alert from triage to resolution in one console.

talks.title: FortiEDR's Automated Remediation of Complex Threats | Endpoint Security
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how an EDR playbook in protection mode automatically responds to malware and Metasploit detections.
talks.summary:
This short demo picks up from an earlier segment on manual remediation and shows how the FortiEDR platform can respond to threats automatically through playbooks. Playbooks set which actions run for each event classification, and different playbook policies can apply to different collector groups. The presenter reviews the notification options, which can send email, forward messages to a SIEM or open tickets in a system such as ServiceNow.

The investigation actions include isolating a device, either through the collector's own communication control or through a NAC integration such as FortiNAC. A playbook can also move an infected device into a stricter collector group with tighter policies until it has been analysed and cleaned. Out-of-the-box remediation covers process termination, file deletion, removal of malware persistence and blocking of threat communication at the firewall. Custom actions can be configured on the integration page and then appear in playbooks.

For the demo, the playbook is switched from simulation to protection. A malware sample is run on an endpoint and its file is deleted within seconds. Cloud analysis classifies the event as malicious, which triggers Active Directory actions that reset the user's password and log the user off, along with file deletion and blocking of the attacking IP address on FortiGate. A Metasploit run on a Linux device then produces a similar set of automatic responses in the event viewer. The main takeaway is that response actions can be tuned per classification and per group, and can be checked in simulation before enforcement is turned on.

talks.title: Applying Safety and Social Distancing Guidelines Within FortiCentral AI-enabled VMS | FortiCentral
talks.teaser: Shows how to configure mask detection, occupancy limits and concierge messaging in an AI video management system.
talks.summary:
Pandemic-era offices need to track safety measures without staff stationed at every door. This video walks through FortiCentral features for monitoring mask wearing and building occupancy limits inside an AI-enabled video management system.

For mask detection, the presenter enables the mask algorithm in the analytics settings. A visual overlay frames each face and labels the person as masked or unmasked, with a confidence indicator and an adjustable strictness threshold. An event filter then lets an operator search earlier weeks for maskless face events and open the matching footage. Custom media messages can be set to play when someone without a mask is detected at an entrance, asking them to put one on, and media can also play between notifications on customer-facing kiosk displays.

For occupancy control, person detection is enabled on selected cameras, typically those covering dining or reception areas. The occupancy manager sets a per-camera limit and an averaging filter that controls how quickly counts respond. Historical graphs show the counts, and lines turn red when a limit is exceeded. A concierge application can pair with this to show enter, wait and stop messages on an entrance monitor, based on whether thresholds are exceeded. The takeaway is that entrance guidance can be automated rather than handled by a person at the door.

talks.title: Auto Provisioning for 3rd Party Phones | FortiVoice
talks.teaser: A demo shows FortiVoice licensed auto provisioning for third-party SIP phones via TFTP, DHCP option 66, and CSV bulk loading.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the limits of unlicensed manual SIP provisioning on FortiVoice: every third-party handset must be touched to enter server details and extension credentials, which becomes burdensome at scale. Auto provisioning for third-party phones requires FortiVoice’s third-party phone license, sold in blocks of 10 or 100, and the walkthrough uses a Cisco 8841 from the 7800 or 8800 series with Cisco enterprise standard firmware at version 12.0 or higher.

On the server, administrators enable TFTP under system advanced auto provisioning, confirm the chosen network interface allows TFTP access, and set DHCP option 66 to the TFTP URL or IP address for the phone model. They create an IP extension, attach a FortiPhone device with the phone’s MAC address and the Cisco 8800 series profile, and note that supported Cisco phones can also be loaded from a CSV. The handset is factory reset—either via the keypad sequence after a PoE reboot or through admin settings—then boots, picks up network parameters, and registers; the demo completes with extension 3019 showing a green registered state and an assigned IP in the management UI.

Practitioners should treat enterprise Cisco firmware and TFTP defaults as prerequisites, wire option 66 before rollout, and use licensed auto provisioning when many third-party SIP phones must join FortiVoice without per-device manual entry.

talks.title: Getting Started with a FortiFone IP Phone | Fortinet Unified Communications
talks.teaser: Walks through the buttons, call handling, directory, call history and Do Not Disturb on a FortiFone desk phone.
talks.summary:
This video gives a short overview of the FortiFone 475 desk phone and notes that the other FortiFone models share very similar features. It starts with the physical layout: programmable keys beside the display, a message waiting light, hold, transfer and conference controls, navigation keys, call history, and voicemail, directory, headset and speakerphone buttons below the keypad, along with volume controls.

Call handling comes next. An incoming call can be answered, ignored, forwarded or rejected, and a rejected call follows the extension's busy routing, which defaults to voicemail. The conference button builds a three-way call by adding a second party and then joining everyone on a second press. A blind transfer dials the target and completes on a second press of transfer, while an attended transfer lets the caller speak with the target first, then either complete or cancel the transfer.

The directory combines a personal local list with a remote corporate directory pulled from the phone system, and both can be searched and dialed. Call history logs incoming and outgoing calls and can show missed calls on the display. The Do Not Disturb button routes incoming calls to voicemail and turns a red indicator on, and the video closes by switching it off again.

talks.title: FortiFone Desktop Softclient Setup | Product Demo
talks.teaser: A product demo walks through outgoing and incoming calls, transfers, conferencing, and visual voicemail on the FortiFone soft client.
talks.summary:
The session introduces FortiFone Desktop Softclient as a unified communications application for Windows and macOS, highlighting call history, peer dialing, visual voicemail, and conference features before moving into hands-on use.

The demonstration covers placing outgoing calls from the dial pad, keyboard, call history, favorites, and directory contacts. It shows in-call volume controls, answering or declining incoming calls, muting ringers, forwarding to voicemail, attended and blind transfers, three-way conferences with merge and manage options, and color-coded visual voicemail playback, callback, and deletion.

Practitioners evaluating or rolling out the soft client gain a concise map of everyday calling workflows and where each control lives in the interface, without deployment or admin configuration detail beyond references to FortiVoice call-handling settings for declined calls.

talks.title: MITRE Sightings Report | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Explains MITRE's sightings ecosystem report and how observed attacker techniques help teams prioritize defenses.
talks.summary:
Derek Manke and Douglas Santos of FortiGuard Labs walk through the MITRE Sightings Ecosystem report, which FortiGuard Labs helped lead. The report shows which tactics, techniques and procedures attackers use in the wild, so organizations can decide where to focus. Santos links this to the pyramid of pain: IP addresses, URLs and hashes are easy for attackers to swap, while changing TTPs is costly.

The project gathers observations from multiple vendors and partners to paint a picture of adversary behavior worldwide. Santos said FortiGuard Labs had collected similar data internally for a couple of years. He compared ATT&CK's more than 370 techniques to a chess game: if an opponent is likely to use only about ten of them, defenders can plan around those. FortiGuard used the data to build heat maps of currently hot techniques, which SOC teams can map to mitigations.

Santos argued the work shifts attacker economics, since genuinely new techniques surface roughly once a quarter and require heavy research. Manke added that FortiGuard Labs is a research sponsor of MITRE's Center for Threat-Informed Defense, which now runs roughly 20 to 25 projects. The takeaway is strategic, high-return prioritization over chasing millions of indicators.
