talks.title: FortiGate 3500F Series | NGFW
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning FortiGate 3500F Series | NGFW.
talks.summary:
## Overview
The FortiGate 3500F Series is a high-performance next-generation firewall (NGFW) from Fortinet designed to deliver industry-leading threat protection, intrusion prevention, and SSL inspection. The appliance is housed in a compact 2RU form factor while offering one of the highest port densities available on the market.

## Key Hardware and Design
The 3500F includes two high-availability 25 gigabit SFP28 slots, 30 standard 25 gigabit SFP28 slots, and six 100 gigabit QSFP28 slots. The 3501F variant adds two 2TB onboard SSDs for logging flexibility. Power redundancy is provided through two hot-swappable power supplies to optimize connection performance and reliability.

## Technical Architecture
The firewall leverages Fortinet's breakthrough security processing architecture. Three NP7 network processors work inline with FortiOS to deliver superior performance for multicast traffic, VPN, CGNAT, WAP, and IP tunnel acceleration. Eight CP9 content processors (Fortinet's 9th generation custom security processing units) handle pattern matching acceleration, application identification, pre-scan signature correlation, and real-time IPS signature matching to support the main CPU.

## Performance Specifications
The 3500F Series delivers exceptional throughput capacity: 595 gigabits per second firewall throughput, 165 gigabits per second IPsec VPN throughput, 72 gigabits per second IPS throughput, and 65 gigabits per second next-generation firewall throughput. Threat protection throughput reaches 63 gigabits per second. With the hyperscale license and NP7 processors, the device supports up to 5 million connections per second. The platform also provides elephant flow and VXLAN acceleration for hybrid and hyperscale data center deployments.

## Deployment Capabilities
The 3500F Series supports extensive deployment flexibility for network segmentation, secure web gateways, intrusion prevention systems, and mobile security. CGNAT is optimized for both 4G and 5G mobile security deployments. The appliance is positioned for deployment at the enterprise edge, in hybrid data center cores, or across internal network segments.

## Takeaways
The FortiGate 3500F Series is positioned as an ideal partner for large enterprises and service providers requiring high-performance, multi-layered security in a compact form factor. Its combination of specialized network and security processors, high port density, and substantial throughput capacity makes it suitable for complex network environments demanding both performance and comprehensive threat protection.

talks.title: Pike Corporation Chooses Fortinet | Customer Stories
talks.teaser: A utility engineering network architect describes using Fortinet for cellular WAN sites and single-appliance branch firewalls.
talks.summary:
Walter Schulze, lead network architect at Pike Enterprises, explains why his group relies on Fortinet. Pike Enterprises supports the other Pike divisions with engineering services for utilities and telecommunications. When he arrived about two years earlier, Fortinet firewalls were already deployed in a multi-data center build-out and at branch offices.

The main theme is cellular WAN on 4G and 5G. Small construction trailers that need land services use it, as does a mobile command trailer deployed for emergencies, currently in Louisiana, where staff log their hours through systems reached via a firewall with a cellular SIM. He criticizes competing branch products built as two boxes, such as a virtual machine or merchant silicon running Linux, because they add single points of failure. He prefers a purpose-built branch appliance and says a 40F model with 3G/4G fits small sites well. For 5G locations near high-bandwidth service, an external antenna on a roof works well.

He closes by arguing that eliminating risk should be a priority for a network architect, and that a vendor with deep engineering helps him track a changing threat landscape he could not follow alone. Practitioners can take away his preference for single-appliance branch designs and cellular links for temporary sites. Since this is a customer testimonial, the claims are his own experience rather than independent measurement.

talks.title: Careers in Cybersecurity | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Explores how newcomers can break into threat intelligence, with advice on skills, self-study and learning from the community.
talks.summary:
Host Jonas talks with Glenn Maiden, a member of the intelligence team at FortiGuard Labs, about how people can build careers in cybersecurity. Glenn traces his path from an IT role at the Australian Department of Defense in the 1990s to the Australian Signals Directorate, then the private sector and FortiGuard Labs. He notes that the field has drawn in people from very different backgrounds.

The conversation covers what threat intelligence involves: gathering broad telemetry, normalising it and analysing campaigns early so protections can be in place. Roles range from investigative work on threat actors and their infrastructure to data science. For newcomers, Glenn stresses a hacker-style curiosity about how systems can be undermined and a willingness to learn, noting that non-technical people can be taught basics such as the OSI model and TCP/IP. Jonas adds that free resources such as capture-the-flag videos, the Hack The Box platform and Discord communities let people train on their own and learn from others.

They close by stressing that the field has few hard barriers to entry and that public reports from national CERTs and industry groups help newcomers get up to speed. Glenn recalls building a reasonable understanding of the Log4j vulnerability within about an hour by reading posts on Twitter. The takeaway is that passion, humility and an openness to learning from others matter more than a specific degree.

talks.title: State of Threats in Healthcare & Critical Infrastructure | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding State of Threats in Healthcare & Critical Infrastructure | FortinetLIVE.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this FortinetLIVE session, Rick Peters, Field CISO for Operational Technology (OT) in North America at Fortinet, speaks with Troy Ament, Fortinet's Field CISO for Life Sciences and Healthcare. Together, they examine the intersection of critical infrastructure, operational technology, and healthcare security heading into 2022. The discussion highlights how the rapid digital transformation prompted by the COVID-19 pandemic expanded attack surfaces and attracted targeted adversary activity, creating critical challenges around operational resilience, supply chains, and clinical continuity.

### Key Topics
- **Digital Acceleration and Changing Attack Surfaces:** Over the course of the pandemic, healthcare organizations underwent massive shifts, including remote workforce mobilization (such as moving thousands of employees home in weeks), dramatic expansion of virtual visit platforms from roughly 100 to over 45,000 monthly visits in large systems, data sharing with local and state governments, and automated tracking of PPE and ICU capacities. In life sciences and pharmaceutical manufacturing, rapid vaccine production amplified visibility and made these organizations prime targets.
- **Evolution of Adversary Tactics:** While attackers largely held off targeting providers in the initial months of 2020, they soon exploited the strain on health systems. Spikes in ransomware caused major disruptions, prompting tens of millions of dollars in ransom demands. Attacks have also expanded beyond hospital facilities to upstream third-party cloud service providers offering payroll, staffing, billing, revenue cycle services, and electronic medical records (EMRs).
- **Convergence of Healthcare and Operational Technology:** Both OT and healthcare share critical dependencies on reliability and safety. Both sectors face high consequences from outages and must proactively protect distributed environments that span on-premises equipment, cloud platforms, and software-defined networking.

### Technical Details
- **Zero Trust and Multi-Factor Authentication:** Health systems are increasingly adopting Zero Trust principles to minimize blast radiuses and attack footprints. This adoption is accelerated by cyber insurance requirements, notably driving multi-factor authentication (MFA) adoption beyond previous ~70% levels.
- **Integrated Security Architecture:** The speakers advocate for moving away from fragmented tools toward integrated mesh or fabric-based security architectures that embed governance and protection directly into clinical workflows and business systems.
- **Behavioral Analysis and Telemetry:** Enhancing situational awareness requires utilizing behavioral analysis and data-driven visibility to recognize anomalous adversary activity early across IT, OT, and connected domains.

### Takeaways
- **Operational Downtime Awareness:** Executive leadership and CEOs now recognize that cyber incidents can cause two to three months of severe operational downtime, shutting down critical workflows such as EMR access and electronic prescription routing.
- **Maturing Security Operations:** Healthcare entities that weathered near-misses have demonstrated that investing in mature security operations centers and proactive defenses significantly reduces operational damage.
- **Collaborative Defense:** Cybersecurity in critical infrastructure cannot be tackled in isolation. Healthcare and OT organizations must treat cybersecurity as a team sport, working closely with external partners and peers to build resilience as threats evolve into 2022.

talks.title: State of Threats in 2022 | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: A threat-hunting view of Log4j waves, Patch Tuesday volume, and deception telemetry heading into 2022.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens on the Log4j crisis carrying from late 2021 into 2022, including initial remote code execution, follow-on denial-of-service issues, and reports of wormable botnet abuse. Researchers note easy proof-of-concept exploitation, heavy telemetry from sensors and signatures, and repeating spikes as attackers chain or pivot to related flaws. They highlight a shrinking window from public exploit material to command-and-control use—just over 80 minutes after a December 9 proof of concept—and the strain on patching when fixes land in waves while intelligence still catches up.

Activity is framed as recurring campaigns rather than a single burnout, with peaks into late December and expectations of later waves akin to Exchange-style incidents. Copycat abuse tied miners, ransomware, and remote access tooling to the same theme, and scrutiny of JNDI-style misuse spread to other Java stacks after vendors stripped risky functionality. January’s Patch Tuesday brought on the order of 96 CVEs; one standout, CVE-2022-21907 at CVSS 9.8, combines wormable propagation with remote code execution, though patches exist and in-the-wild exploitation had not been observed at the time of the discussion.

For defenders, the emphasis falls on SOC attentiveness at disclosure, fast mitigation, and sustained monitoring after headlines fade. Deception and honeypot decoys—including deliberately vulnerable services used to study Log4j hits—are presented as both research telemetry and a way to misdirect attackers while gathering intelligence.

talks.title: Log4j Vulnerability | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Examines how Log4j exploitation spread into many campaigns and why fast patching and layered detection matter.
talks.summary:
This FortiGuard Live interview opens with the host and Fortinet's field CTO framing the Log4j flaw as a long-running problem rather than a one-off event. They compare it with earlier incidents such as Conficker, Heartbleed and Shellshock, and note that the vulnerability has become a commodity, with at least ten separate campaigns reusing the exploit code within a few weeks.

The middle of the discussion covers how attacks are likely to change. Early exploitation relied on sending requests to web pages with a crafted host header, but the guest expects attackers to target any input that gets logged, including wireless and SMS-based systems. Fixes for the library moved through several versions in about a week, which the guest credits to a wider community review of small open-source projects that many products depend on, while also noting that attackers move just as fast. Software bills of materials are presented as a way for organisations to find where affected components sit in their networks. The malware seen so far includes ransomware, remote access trojans and crypto miners, many built as Linux ELF binaries aimed at servers and IoT devices.

The closing part makes the case for layered defence. Patching is essential, but the guests also point to IPS and web application firewall signatures, detection of new malware families, and scanners that look for the vulnerability itself. Because payloads are being obfuscated and changed, they recommend repeating checks rather than running a single scan. Fortinet's outbreak alerts are described as a way to look back at past activity and keep monitoring, while SOC services can help filter the very large volume of alerts. Listeners are pointed to Fortinet's threat research blog and threat signals for updates.

talks.title: FON-480 Overview | Fortinet Product Demo
talks.teaser: Walks through the FON-480 IP phone's everyday calling features, from call handling and parking to transfers, LED states and voicemail.
talks.summary:
This six-minute product demo introduces the FON-480, an IP desk phone with calling, conference and voicemail features. It starts with placing outgoing calls from the call history, using the handset, the speakerphone or a connected headset. It then covers answering incoming calls with the handset, speaker or headset keys, ignoring a call so it stops ringing, and declining it so the phone's configured call handling applies. Putting a call on hold and resuming it is shown too, and a held call can be picked up from another extension.

The middle of the demo focuses on call parking and transfers. Dialing star 40 during a call, or pressing an auto park key set up by the administrator, places the caller in the first free park slot, and a prompt announces the slot number. A park slot key can be programmed so its LED flashes yellow when a call is parked there, and pressing it connects to that call. Transfers are covered in two forms: an attended transfer, where the user speaks to the recipient before completing it, and a blind transfer, which sends the caller straight through. Three-way conferencing is added by pressing the conference key and dialing another party.

The demo closes with the meaning of programmable key LEDs, which show solid green for idle, flashing green for an incoming call, solid red for an active call, flashing yellow for a held call and solid yellow when do not disturb is enabled. It then shows voicemail: the message indicator and on-screen notice, retrieving messages with the voicemail button and PIN, moving between folders, playing and deleting messages, and returning a call from a message. The result is a quick reference for the phone's core day-to-day functions.

talks.title: Configuring Devices for FortiVoice Cloud | Fortinet Product Demo
talks.teaser: Shows how to register desk phones, mobile apps and desktop clients with a FortiVoice Cloud phone service.
talks.summary:
This short product demo walks through connecting phones and software clients to the FortiVoice Cloud telephony service. Before starting, the extension must be provisioned by the service administrator, who sends a registration email with the details needed for each device. Keeping that information on hand matters, since every configuration step relies on it.

For the FON-480 desk phone, the menu leads to the cloud section and then the desk phone area, where the cloud ID, user ID and cloud PIN are entered and submitted. The phone shows the progress of configuration and registration, then returns to the home screen when finished. For the mobile client on Android or iOS, the user scans a code from the welcome email on first launch, or adds an account later from the menu. The desktop client for Windows and macOS is installed from a link in the same email, and on first run the user logs in with the credentials from that message before the interface loads.

The demo ends once each device has connected, at which point the endpoints can use the cloud service for calls. The practical takeaway for administrators and end users is to complete provisioning first, then follow the steps for each device type in order.

talks.title: Configuring Active-Passive HA Mode in FortiMail | Fortinet Product Demo
talks.teaser: Shows how to set up an active-passive high availability pair on a FortiMail unit, including sync and failover monitoring.
talks.summary:
This product demo covers configuring active-passive high availability on a FortiMail unit, one of the two HA modes the appliance supports. The other mode is config-only. Before starting, each unit must be registered in the HA group on the vendor support site and physically connected to the cluster. A dedicated interface carries heartbeat and synchronization traffic, linked either directly or through a switch.

The demo walks through the HA settings page. For this example the unit is set as primary, with failover set to wait for recovery and restore the original role. Both units share the same HA password. In the advanced options, mail directories are synchronized unless mail is stored on a NAS, and the MTA queue directory can also be synchronized. The presenter notes that this adds processor and bandwidth load but acts as a safety measure if a failure occurs. The default base port and heartbeat threshold were kept, with a warning that an overly short failure detection time can cause a secondary unit to flag false failures during heavy load. The remote server is enabled as a heartbeat.

Service monitoring is not synchronized between units, so it must be set on each one. The administrator selects the table row, enables monitoring, and enters the peer IP address, the peer SMTP port, a connection test timeout and the test frequency. If the secondary detects a failure, the primary's operating mode switches to off or failed, an alert email is sent, and the secondary takes over the primary role. The demo ends with the unit running in active-passive mode.

talks.title: Configuring Archiving in FortiMail | Fortinet Product Demo
talks.teaser: A step-by-step walkthrough enables archive accounts, policies, exceptions, and inbox review in FortiMail.
talks.summary:
Organizations that outgrow mailbox storage need a controlled way to retain mail without losing searchability. The presentation positions FortiMail email archiving as a configurable answer and assumes the viewer’s admin account already has read and edit rights, with deeper privilege setup deferred to the product guide.

The walkthrough creates an archive account: naming credentials, choosing header indexing to speed searches, enabling the account for reuse elsewhere, turning on IMAP access, setting rotation to overwrite when usage passes 200 megabytes, and picking local versus remote storage with the correct remote address when needed. It then adds an archive policy tied to that account, using default sender matching so messages from a pattern such as all senders at example.com are stored. A separate exempt policy blocks archiving for another pattern, illustrated with messages from test.com senders.

To validate the setup, the demo opens the monitor view for the archive account, browses inbox or bulk archive folders, and runs content search. The intended takeaway is a minimal but complete archival loop—account, selective policy, exceptions, and review—ready for production tuning.

talks.title: Configuring FortiMail Calendar Sharing | Fortinet Product Demo
talks.teaser: A product demo walks through enabling WebDAV and CalDAV on FortiMail and pairing Outlook and Thunderbird for shared calendars.
talks.summary:
The walkthrough opens with FortiMail’s support for calendar sharing and LDAP-based address book sharing across standard mail clients, aimed at scheduling, free-busy coordination, and office organization. Calendar sharing is available only when FortiMail runs in server mode. Enabling it starts in the administrative UI: under domain and user calendar settings, administrators turn on WebDAV and CalDAV, apply the change, then create a new calendar resource with the required details.

Next, service URLs are taken from webmail settings via the service URL control and saved for client setup. For Thunderbird, publishing a calendar uses Events and Tasks with the copied URL and FortiMail credentials; subscribing adds an on-the-network calendar located through CalDAV, with automatic synchronization once connected. Outlook follows a parallel path: publishing online to the WebDAV server and opening a calendar from the internet for subscription, each step using the saved URLs and authentication.

The demo closes after both clients are configured, with subscribed calendars syncing to the FortiMail CalDAV service so shared scheduling works end to end from server settings through everyday mail clients.

talks.title: Gateway Mode Deployment in FortiMail | Fortinet Product Demo
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Gateway Mode Deployment in FortiMail | Fortinet Product Demo.

talks.title: Transparent Mode Deployment in FortiMail | Fortinet Product Demo
talks.teaser: Covers FortiMail transparent mode as inline SMTP filtering without MX changes, plus DNS, domain, and proxy interface setup.
talks.summary:
FortiMail supports transparent, gateway, and server operating modes. The demonstration centers on transparent mode, where the appliance acts as a bump in the wire: it does not require changing existing DNS MX records for the protected domain, proxies inbound SMTP, applies anti-spam and anti-virus processing, and then forwards or relays messages. It can enforce authentication on behalf of the protected domain and optionally deliver mail to external recipients to offload the internal server.

The sample topology places the unit in front of the mail server, with one port internet-facing and the second connected to the internal SMTP server. Before switching modes, only the internet port should be connected. Transparent mode is selected from the dashboard status page or via CLI, followed by the quick start wizard. While protected-domain DNS often stays as-is, public records for the FortiMail host itself—MX, A, and PTR—support spam-report web release links when that hostname is not otherwise configured.

Transparent-only domain settings tie the protected SMTP server to a network interface, optionally hide the appliance from that server while preserving client identity, and allow outbound mail through the protected server. Parallel session profile options mask the unit toward the mail server. SMTP proxy and implicit relay pickup on each interface determine whether connections are inspected or allowed through unmodified when pickup is disabled.

talks.title: Setting Up FortiMail | Fortinet Product Demo
talks.teaser: Walks through the initial setup of a FortiMail unit, from web interface access to the quick start wizard and backup.
talks.summary:
This Fortinet product demo walks through the basic setup of a newly received FortiMail unit. It begins by connecting to the web interface: the management computer is placed on the same subnet as the port 1 interface, and the default address is opened in a browser to log in. The presenter then chooses an operating mode from gateway, transparent and server. Gateway is described as suitable for most environments and is the default, so it is used throughout the demo.

The quick start wizard comes next, covering time settings, port 1 addressing, primary and secondary DNS servers, the default gateway, the local domain, the host name and a stronger admin password. The demo stresses verifying the DNS connections, since faults there can cause many problems. Protected domains are then defined with their primary SMTP server and port, at least one being required, and SMTP recipient verification is enabled. Scan policies determine whether inbound or outbound mail is inspected before the settings are applied.

Topology-specific settings and the other operating modes are left to the admin guide and separate videos. The video closes by advising a configuration backup under the maintenance menu once testing is complete.

talks.title: The Evolution of Threat Partnerships in Cybersecurity | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Covers how threat intelligence sharing between vendors, governments and law enforcement builds trust and speeds up defence.
talks.summary:
Derek Menke hosts this FortiGuard LIVE conversation with Glenn Maiden, who works with FortiGuard Labs across Australia and New Zealand. They argue that threat intelligence has shifted from passing along raw speeds-and-feeds data to a people-driven practice built on trust. Glenn explains that a shortage of trained analysts and a flood of alerts make context and personal contacts essential.

Fortinet's industry work includes co-founding the Cyber Threat Alliance in 2014, sponsoring MITRE's threat-informed defense research, and cooperating with Interpol on disruption efforts. Glenn describes a nation-state campaign called Copy Paste that targeted government and large private organizations. Before it became public, indicators of compromise, web shell hashes and malicious domains and IPs were shared with the Australian Cyber Security Centre, so FortiGate customers were protected before they knew of the threat.

The pair stress that cybercrime ignores borders while defenders face legal and policy barriers. They point to the World Economic Forum's Partnership Against Cybercrime, which brings top analysts together, and its Atlas project, which maps the criminal ecosystem as a business. The takeaway is to combine private sector context with public sector reach and to share actionable intelligence early.

talks.title: Operational Technology Threats in 2022 | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Operational Technology Threats in 2022 | FortinetLIVE.

talks.title: FortiExtender Cellular Gateways: Extend, Ensure & Secure the Enterprise Network--Anywhere
talks.teaser: Shows how 5G and LTE gateways add cellular failover and out-of-band links to keep branch networks online.
talks.summary:
Fortinet presents the FortiExtender, a 5G or LTE cellular gateway meant to extend, ensure and secure enterprise networks at locations where wired links fall short. The speaker argues that branches in healthcare, retail and industrial settings increasingly depend on the internet, and that SD-WAN connections suffer when an internet provider goes down or when cable or DSL is not available at a site. Cellular is framed as a way to reach places where wired service is missing or unreliable.

The talk describes layering cellular on top of cable or DSL, together with out-of-band management, as a way to raise branch reliability by up to 5x. This lets a business keep its digital operations running during a disaster. Fortinet's newer models offer 5G and dual-modem options. One design point is that the cellular modem is separated from the edge platform and connected over a single cable that also carries power, so the modem can sit where the signal is strongest while data travels over higher-quality cabling.

The speaker places the device inside Fortinet's broader security platform, stating that it is integrated with the rest of the Fortinet security-driven networking approach. Devices can be managed through Fortinet's management tools or through its cloud service. The practical takeaway is that cellular can serve as a widely available, resilient path for branch connectivity, with the same security controls applied to it as to other links.

talks.title: Tech Bytes: The Security Fabric Advantage | Packet Pushers Podcast
talks.teaser: Explains why an integrated security fabric can beat stitching together best-of-breed point products, with zero trust as an example.
talks.summary:
This sponsored podcast episode looks at the idea of a security fabric, an integrated set of products that share threat and posture information to help manage risk across the network and endpoints. Fortinet's director of systems engineering, Stephen Watkins, presents the concept as a platform approach rather than a collection of standalone devices.

The main contrast is with buying best-of-breed tools from several vendors. Watkins argues that multi-vendor setups rely on integration points that can break when one product is upgraded, leaving gaps in information sharing, policy enforcement and visibility, and that managing many consoles adds to the burden. He describes a fabric in which firewalls, intrusion prevention and other enforcement points exchange threat data in both directions, so policy can change dynamically when a specific threat is detected.

For zero trust, he explains that FortiOS runs as the firmware across FortiGate appliances, virtual machines and public cloud, combining next-generation firewalling, SD-WAN, routing and access proxy functions under one license. A single management plane extends to switches and wireless controllers, while FortiClient and EMS bring posture data from laptops and phones into the same policy model. The host questions whether tag-based approaches from other vendors work reliably across mixed device fleets. The takeaway is that simpler licensing and unified management, with consistent policy enforcement points, are what customers are asking for.

talks.title: Trending Cyber Attack Techniques | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Trending Cyber Attack Techniques | FortiGuardLIVE.

talks.title: Threat Predictions | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Walks through predicted 2022 threats: aggressive ransomware, deepfake scams, Linux malware, satellite attacks and dark web growth.
talks.summary:
Derek Manky and Aamir Lakhani review the cyber threat predictions for 2022 in this FortiGuard Labs discussion. They start with ransomware, which they expect to become more targeted and destructive, with more wiper variants that overwrite the master boot record. Attackers are also adding zero-day exploits and threatening to release stolen data.

Next they cover AI-driven social engineering, where machine learning is used to mimic people and produce deepfake voice and video that make impersonation scams harder to spot. Linux is highlighted as a growing target across cloud, embedded, vehicle and critical infrastructure systems. Satellite internet is framed as an expanding attack surface, where ground stations carry traffic and denial-of-service and latency attacks are amplified. Blockchain verification, crypto wallets and esports revenue streams are also flagged as likely targets.

The discussion closes with edge devices and living-off-the-land techniques, in which attackers use tools already present on a system to stay under the radar, with dwell times of about 200 days cited. They finish with the dark web, where ransomware-as-a-service and insider recruitment are growing, which they describe as organized, advanced persistent cybercrime. Practitioners are pointed toward mitigation advice and ongoing tracking on the company blog.

talks.title: FortiMonitor VMware Stack Installation to Onsight Collector | FortiMonitor
talks.teaser: Shows how to add an on-premises VMware stack to FortiMonitor through an on-site collector for health and performance monitoring.
talks.summary:
This short vendor tutorial walks through connecting an on-premises VMware environment to FortiMonitor so its health and performance can be tracked. It starts from the add-new menu, where the VMware option is chosen, and then selects an existing on-site collector appliance to act as the path into the private network.

Next, the presenter enters read-only VMware credentials and completes the installation. Discovery can take several minutes depending on how many virtual machines the stack contains. In the example shown, discovery found three VMware hosts and 168 instances. The cluster view then organizes these by instance type, separating hosts, virtual machines, datastores and clusters into their own groups.

To close, the video notes that the grouped instances can be sorted by group type, that alert timelines can be applied for incident management, and that tags can be added to identify particular instances. The practical takeaway is that a collector deployed inside the network, paired with read-only access, gives a single organized view of an entire VMware stack for ongoing monitoring.

talks.title: Deploying a Network Device Using SNMP Polling | FortiMonitor
talks.teaser: A walkthrough shows how to register an on-prem network device in FortiMonitor using SNMP polling through an on-site collector.
talks.summary:
The presentation covers onboarding a network appliance in an on-premises FortiMonitor deployment when monitoring relies on SNMP polls executed by an on-site collector rather than cloud-only agents.

The walkthrough starts from the account UI: add a network device with advanced port health and performance options, choose the on-site location, supply device identity and SNMP credentials, and wait while credentials are verified and interfaces are discovered. The example completes against a FortiGate 2000e and reports sixty-five ports found before finishing installation.

After the device appears in the inventory, the speaker reviews incident and monitoring views, SNMP trap and activity areas, completed port discovery, performance readings such as sessions, CPU, disk, HA sync, memory, and ping, plus per-port bandwidth, discard, and error counters. The intended takeaway is the end-to-end checklist—site, credentials, discovery, and validation of metrics and port detail—before relying on the device in production monitoring.

talks.title: Checkers Drive-In Restaurants | Customer Stories
talks.teaser: A quick-service chain leader recounts centralizing SD-WAN and security after years of fragmented store networking.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes joining a mid-sized drive-in brand with roughly 850 sites in 38 states and finding highly fragmented IT: little standardization, poor reliability, and ad hoc hardware purchases. Rather than locking in a single incumbent vendor, the organization ran a competitive proof of concept and invited Fortinet to participate alongside an existing supplier relationship.

The chosen direction emphasizes cloud-managed networking with centralized administration, templated rollouts, and visibility suited to opening dozens of new restaurants annually. Fortinet SD-WAN now serves on the order of 265 corporate sites, pairing primary broadband with cellular backup for high availability while supporting a shift toward SaaS applications. Day-to-day operations reportedly shrank from a heavy manual burden to something much lighter, with fewer full-time staff dedicated to the same scope.

For practitioners, the arc is operational: distributed retail needs repeatable edge connectivity, consistent security policy, and threat-intelligence-backed controls at scale. The speaker also outlines intent to extend the same platform to hundreds of franchise locations and frames staffing reallocation and multi-year cost avoidance as part of the business case.

talks.title: Global Partnerships and Cybersecurity Skills Gap | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Explores how public and private partnerships, early threat sharing and trust are helping disrupt ransomware and cybercrime groups.
talks.summary:
Derek Menke and Glenn Maiden talk about how cybercrime is fought through cooperation across borders and sectors, timed to cybersecurity awareness month. Glenn explains that local context matters, including regional regulation, skills levels and organisational maturity, and that partnerships let each group combine its strengths.

The discussion covers a ransomware increase described as tenfold in the first half of 2021, alongside measurable progress in disruption. A botnet taken offline in January saw its activity fall by almost 75 percent, while TrickBot returned but was far less active. Glenn also describes a copy-paste campaign aimed at Australian government and industry, where indicators shared early by the Australian Cyber Security Centre were already blocked before the campaign became public. The Cyber Threat Alliance, co-founded in May 2014, has more than 30 members and has completed over 250 early shares. A World Economic Forum partnership against cybercrime, with about 40 members, is working to map the criminal ecosystem into a single source of truth.

The main lesson is that early sharing and trust, built over years, let defenders prepare before a campaign goes public and keep criminals off balance. Linking shared infrastructure and recurring individuals across criminal groups can help disrupt their supply chain. For practitioners, the message is to invest in relationships before an incident, because proactive coordination is what makes the biggest difference.

talks.title: Deploying a FortiMonitor Linux Agent in VMware | Network Performance Monitoring
talks.teaser: Shows how to install the FortiMonitor Linux agent on an Ubuntu machine in an on-prem VMware setup and review the new instance.
talks.summary:
This video is a short walkthrough of adding a FortiMonitor Linux agent to a server in an on-premises VMware environment. The presenter explains that the agent is a local monitoring utility installed directly on a physical server, virtual machine or cloud host. It tracks resources, processes and services, and it supports plugins for applications such as Apache, Cassandra and SQL Server. The agent is compatible with Windows, Linux and Unix.

The setup begins in the FortiMonitor account, where the add option leads to the Linux choice and then Ubuntu. Using the quick install instructions, the commands are copied and pasted into an SSH session on the Ubuntu machine, and the process is left to run for a minute or two. Once the agent reports a successful connection, the installation is finished from the portal. The new instance then appears in the incoming servers folder after it finishes processing.

Opening the instance shows its agent status, FQDN, server key, alert timeline and monitoring location. The Linux core template is applied automatically. The performance section charts bandwidth, CPU, disk, memory and NTP. Because the host was only just added, the graphs contain little data so far, and the video closes by noting that these views help gauge the health of the Linux instance over time.

talks.title: FortiMonitor Windows Agent Installation in VMware | Network Performance Monitoring
talks.teaser: Walks through installing a Windows monitoring agent on an on-prem VMware machine and checking its first metrics.
talks.summary:
This product demo shows how to add a FortiMonitor Windows agent to a Windows machine running in an on-premises VMware environment. The presenter describes the agent as a local monitoring utility that runs directly on a physical server, virtual machine or cloud server, tracking the host's resources, processes and services. Plugins can also extend it to watch applications such as web servers, databases and caches.

The walkthrough starts in the FortiMonitor account, where the Windows agent option is selected and its quick install instructions are copied. The presenter opens a remote desktop session to the Windows machine, runs the install from an elevated PowerShell window, and waits a minute or two for it to finish. Back in the portal, the agent connection is confirmed, the installation is marked complete, and the new instance appears in the incoming servers folder while it is processed.

Once processing finishes, the instance details show its agent status, host name, server key, timeline and monitoring location, along with the Windows core template applied to it. The performance views for bandwidth, CPU, disk and memory are still empty because the device was just added. The takeaway is the basic enrollment workflow: install the agent from an elevated shell, confirm the connection, and verify that the new host appears with its template ready to report health data.

talks.title: Tech Bytes: Why Fortinet Zero Trust Works For You | Packet Pushers Podcast
talks.teaser: Explains how Fortinet's ZTNA approach rechecks device posture and user identity for each application session on FortiGate firewalls.
talks.summary:
This sponsored podcast episode features Peter Newton, senior director of products and services at Fortinet, discussing zero trust network access (ZTNA). The host frames ZTNA as the successor to VPN-based remote access, driven by remote work and applications moving from on-premises data centres into public and private clouds. Newton's main point is that zero trust depends on continuous verification and per-application control, so user identity and device posture are rechecked for each session rather than only at the morning login.

Newton describes Fortinet's client-initiated model, where a FortiClient agent already on the endpoint reports posture details such as operating system version, antivirus presence and recent device events. He argues this is faster for users than a service-initiated model that requires a browser plugin download, and gives administrators more visibility into the device. Access is mapped through existing directory user groups and role-based rules enforced on the FortiGate, so organisations keep their current authentication systems. Single sign-on remains in use, and step-up multi-factor authentication can be triggered for unusual context or sensitive applications.

The discussion then covers licensing and performance. ZTNA is presented as an unlicensed feature on FortiGate devices running FortiOS 7.0.x firmware with FortiClient, and Newton links Fortinet's custom ASIC to keeping throughput high when several security functions are enabled. These are vendor claims. For practitioners, the practical takeaways are to check how ZTNA would plug into existing identity and device management, and to test the feature in a lab before deciding.

talks.title: What's Trending in the Threat Landscape? | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Surveys recent shifts in attacker behavior, from Linux malware to Monero ransom payments and physical-world impact.
talks.summary:
This short FortiGuardLIVE segment has the host and guest Steve McCauley walk through recent shifts in the threat landscape. The first theme is malware moving beyond Windows. Linux is now a mainstream target, helped by IoT devices, data center servers and container platforms. They describe a new Linux rootkit built to go after SSH credentials and bash activity, and Linux ransomware that appears in campaigns. Attackers are less interested in user files and more in the credentials and keys that sit on servers. Windows Subsystem for Linux widens the attack surface further.

The middle section covers Mystery Snail RAT, which used a Windows zero-day that the team confirmed also affects Windows 11. The speakers explain that attackers recycle older malware once a fresh exploit gives them a new way in, which is why old families can seem to return. They then discuss a recent ransomware campaign that asked for payment in Monero rather than Bitcoin. Monero is harder to trace than Bitcoin, and attackers often convert Bitcoin through mixers to reach it, so victims face extra work to obtain it.

The closing part looks at operational technology. Ransomware is increasingly reaching systems tied to everyday life, such as gas pumps, hospitals, pipelines and water treatment plants, so the impact extends to consumers. The takeaways are to patch quickly, expect older malware to resurface, build Linux analysis and defense skills alongside Windows, and treat connected products as possible sources of real-world risk.

talks.title: Establishing an SSL VPN Connection to FortiGate using Azure AD | FortiGate
talks.teaser: Shows how to configure FortiGate SSL VPN sign-in with Azure AD acting as the SAML identity provider.
talks.summary:
This video demonstrates remote SSL VPN access to a FortiGate firewall where sign-in is delegated to Azure AD as the identity provider. A remote user starts authentication from a web browser or the FortiGate client, is redirected to Azure AD, and is sent back to the firewall once sign-in completes. The demonstration shows the user experience in both web mode and the client, ending with the user reaching an internal application through the tunnel.

The administrator walkthrough covers five configuration steps on the FortiGate, with Azure AD setup treated as a prerequisite. The first step creates a CLI-based SAML identity provider and a user group, using the entity ID, sign-on and logout URLs from the Azure AD enterprise application, the imported Azure AD certificate, the user principal name claim as the username attribute, and the group's object ID. The next step creates an SSL VPN portal with tunnel mode, policy-based routing, a source IP pool and web mode enabled, plus a predefined bookmark. The third step enables SSL VPN settings on the chosen interface and port and maps the authentication to that portal.

The final step creates a firewall policy that runs from the SSL VPN tunnel interface to the internal network, uses the Azure AD-backed user group as the source, and allows the destination servers with all services turned on. For practitioners, the main takeaway is that the identifiers and URLs must match exactly between Azure AD and the FortiGate CLI, and the policy must reference the same group for the configuration to work end to end.

talks.title: Threat Landscape and Cyber Skills Gap | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: An interview on entering cyber security covers learning paths, specialty exposure, and core skills for newcomers.
talks.summary:
This interview episode has host Omar talking with guest Jonas about how people enter cyber security and where the skills gaps lie. Jonas explains that his own path started with an interest in offensive security and a wish to learn from experienced specialists, which led him to join a vendor. He stresses that networking fundamentals come first and that real progress comes from practice.

He describes building a home lab with virtualization so he could test and break products, and strengthening his systems administration skills on Windows, Linux and router operating systems. For him, defensive product work came first, and offensive techniques followed so he could defend better. To stay motivated, he points to genuine enjoyment of technology and a sense of duty to help everyday people avoid harms such as ransomware.

On breaking in, he advises newcomers to sample many areas, from the software lifecycle to compliance, legal matters and cybercrime, and to use free vendor training and capture-the-flag events. Asked for essential skills, he names curiosity, the habit of piecing clues together, and a passion for technology, alongside virtualization and operating system administration. He closes by noting that the attack surface has shifted from networks to web, client, and now API and cloud targets, so anticipating the next shift matters.

talks.title: FortiGate SSL VPN Authentication with FortiAuthenticator as IdP Proxy for Azure AD
talks.teaser: Demonstrates SSL VPN logins on FortiGate delegated to Azure AD via FortiAuthenticator, with FortiToken MFA.
talks.summary:
Remote workers need VPN access, and organizations want one place to manage authentication and a second factor across their firewalls. This demo shows a FortiGate SSL VPN login that hands the first factor to Azure AD, with FortiAuthenticator acting as an identity provider proxy in front of it. FortiToken then supplies the second factor. The walkthrough covers both web mode and the FortiClient. In each case the login is redirected from FortiAuthenticator to Azure AD, and a push notification to the FortiToken mobile app completes the second factor. After connecting, the user reaches an internal web page, and the FortiGate shows the client's assigned address and services.

The presenter then checks the FortiAuthenticator and Azure AD logs, which record both the first and second factor for the session. The configuration is covered in order. In Azure AD, an application is created and set up for SAML single sign-on, with claims and the federation metadata exported and imported into FortiAuthenticator. Azure AD also needs a directory reader role for the application, and its client ID and client secret are entered into FortiAuthenticator. On FortiAuthenticator, a SAML service provider is created, its identity details are copied into the FortiGate CLI, and the FortiGate's entity and login URLs are returned to FortiAuthenticator. The FortiGate side then gets a user group mapping, an SSL VPN portal and settings, and a firewall policy for the tunnel interface. Finally, Azure AD users are imported into FortiAuthenticator, and a FortiToken Mobile token is activated by scanning a QR code from an emailed attachment.

The main takeaway is that a central identity proxy lets several FortiGates share one authentication and token management point. Attribute names and user groups must match across FortiGate, FortiAuthenticator and Azure AD, or logins will fail.

talks.title: Creating 3D Maps in FortiCentral | Fortinet
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a 3D site map in FortiCentral with walls, doors, windows, cameras and saved monitoring sectors.
talks.summary:
Gaps in camera coverage can leave a monitored site with blind spots exactly when footage matters most. This walkthrough shows how FortiCentral's 3D maps tool turns a floor plan into a three-dimensional model that displays camera locations, the angle of view in both directions, and the coverage range of each camera. The floor plan can be loaded from a file or captured from a web map, which provides the outside perimeter and a sense of scale.

The demo then builds the model in edit mode. Walls are traced over the floor plan by clicking points, with height and thickness adjusted by sliders, and misplaced points can be dragged, added or removed. Doors and windows are made by selecting a wall segment, enabling an opening on it, and setting the top and bottom edges. Walls can be recolored or given textures. Cameras are dropped in from predefined models or the device panel, then tuned for height, position, horizontal field of view and tilt, and a camera view mode shows what each one actually sees. A guard model is placed in the lobby as an example of a static element.

Finally, sectors are saved as named views of part of the map, such as a cafeteria or lobby, so each area can be monitored in its own pane. The takeaway for operators is that a carefully matched 3D model helps confirm coverage and reach the right camera feed quickly.

talks.title: Ransomware in Life Sciences & Healthcare | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Traces how ransomware crews pick healthcare targets and why takedowns and early threat intelligence can blunt the damage.
talks.summary:
Troy Amet, Fortinet's healthcare field CSO, interviews Derek Manke, chief of security insights, about ransomware across industries, with healthcare long a target. The discussion cites a sharp rise in ransomware activity in the first half of 2021, put at about 10.7-fold. Derek explains that criminal groups now pair the funding and planning of nation-state style attackers with business-like units, doing reconnaissance on applications, services and open ports. They aim at pivotal areas such as laboratories, cardiology, radiology and pharmacy, where a few disabled systems can disrupt the whole health system.

The conversation then turns to defense. Defense in depth, zero trust and multi-factor authentication are the priorities many security leaders focus on, and Derek notes that paying a ransom is often a business decision. On the positive side, cooperation between public and private sectors, including law enforcement and threat intelligence sharing, has disrupted criminal infrastructure. One botnet used to spread ransomware lost about half its activity after a January takedown and had not recovered, while TrickBot stayed offline for six months before returning. Troy adds that many health systems only began taking security seriously about a decade ago.

Troy also describes recent healthcare outages lasting four to six weeks that affected clinical records, admissions, prescriptions and lab results. Organizations with 24/7 monitoring and strong partnerships were able to limit downtime. Derek closes with a new intelligence model in the threat report that tracks attacker methodologies rather than only ransomware families. The practical takeaways are to shrink the external footprint attackers scout, prepare in advance, and use quality threat intelligence and inspection points to spot intrusions early.

talks.title: FortiSIEM for Operational Technology | Security Operations
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiSIEM collectors, Purdue modeling, and dashboards give SOC teams OT visibility and abnormal cross-level traffic.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with FortiSIEM deployment options—a virtual or hardware appliance that can scale by adding worker nodes clustered with a primary supervisor—and stresses collectors as the linchpin for operational technology. Collectors ingest flows, syslog, and API events, discover assets, gather performance metrics, and can sit in separate network segments while filtering noise, compressing payloads, and capping bandwidth for constrained remote sites.

For OT, the speaker maps environments with the Purdue model, from level-one PLCs and RTUs through historians and HMIs, control centers, enterprise systems, and external VPN, cloud, and IoT connectivity. FortiSIEM ships an operational-technology business service with those tiers pre-defined so assets inherit context, criticality, and rules that flag intra- or inter-level traffic that violates expected boundaries. Discovery enriches devices with versions, utilization, and reachability checks; packaged reports and dashboards highlight Modbus activity, unexpected internet egress, and large transfers.

A live walkthrough starts from a risk-ranked engineering workstation on the plant floor, shows Purdue grouping and criticality settings, then pivots through incidents, analytics on level-two sources, anomalous destinations such as Singapore, optional FortiGuard enrichment, and MITRE ATT&CK-oriented views including possible exfiltration. Practitioners should treat Purdue-aligned modeling, collector placement, and correlation rules as the backbone for SOC visibility without flattening OT segmentation.

talks.title: Tech Bytes: Fortinet Secures Work-From-Anywhere With SD-WAN And ZTNA | Packet Pushers Podcast
talks.teaser: Explains how Fortinet combines SD-WAN and zero trust network access into one platform for remote and distributed workers.
talks.summary:
The podcast traces how SD-WAN has grown from branch link balancing into a platform that includes zero trust network access for distributed workers. The guests argue that remote users need checks on every application they reach, not a single check when they connect. Fortinet's approach combines the FortiGate access proxy, the FortiClient device agent and the EMS cloud policy and trust checks, so customers already running SD-WAN add only the agent and cloud policy.

The middle section covers the four ZTNA components and how existing VPN policies can be imported and extended with application-level business rules. The speakers contrast ZTNA with a traditional IPsec VPN, which typically authenticates once and then leaves the session broadly trusted. They also describe treating remote work locations as a separate segment that stays isolated from data center, corporate and internet segments, with the aim of raising the security floor across the whole network.

Near the end, the guests note that SD-WAN now accounts for a large share of Fortinet's revenue and that no separate license is needed for SD-WAN or the access proxy. For practitioners, the takeaway is to check whether an existing SD-WAN deployment can extend to zero trust access on one management platform rather than through another product.

talks.title: Tech Bytes: Protecting Public Schools With Fortinet’s Security Fabric | Packet Pushers Podcast
talks.teaser: Explains how a Nebraska school service unit runs shared Fortinet firewalls, log analysis and VPN for its districts.
talks.summary:
Bill Pulte, chief information officer of an educational service unit in Nebraska, describes how the unit provides shared services to public school districts, including internet access for its 18 districts. He explains that the state's Network Nebraska program steered many districts toward FortiGate firewalls, and that the unit chose Fortinet after an RFP because throughput held up as services such as antivirus, application control, intrusion prevention, web filtering and VPN were switched on.

The unit also runs FortiAnalyzer as a shared log collector. Its multi-tenancy lets each district see only its own logs, with about 1.5 terabytes allocated per district, and the device was sized for roughly 12 districts over a five-year term. Pulte argues that one shared appliance costs far less than separate purchases by each district. He notes that most districts only review logs after an incident, but that a state school insurer's cyber questionnaire may push them toward more proactive log analysis.

Pulte also recalls the pandemic, when staff moved to remote work within a day because the endpoint VPN client was already deployed and only group membership had to change, while student access proved harder. He closes by discussing plans to add endpoint security and Office 365 protections alongside the firewalls, and upcoming access point and phone system decisions that also lean toward Fortinet.

talks.title: SD-Branch Architecture
talks.teaser: A vendor overview explains how converged firewalls, switches, and access points secure distributed branch WAN and LAN edges.
talks.summary:
Distributed branch sites strain IT when remote users, local staff, and internet-of-things gear all reach the cloud and software-as-a-service apps directly. The presentation positions Fortinet’s secure SD-Branch model as security-driven networking that folds WAN and LAN edge controls into one stack.

Core pieces include FortiGate next-generation firewalls on FortiOS, with SD-WAN features such as application identification on encrypted traffic, multi-path steering, segmentation, and WAN resiliency. FortiExtender adds cellular backup. FortiLink lets the FortiGate act as a controller for FortiAP and FortiSwitch so switching and Wi-Fi share the firewall’s policy model, including SSIDs presented as firewall interfaces and switch ports treated like firewall ports. FortiOS network access control supports device discovery and zero-trust onboarding at the device edge.

Deployments can be run from the FortiGate UI for simpler sites, while Fabric Management Center supports scaled zero-touch rollout across branches. The closing emphasis is lower operational overhead, unified management, and total cost of ownership versus piecing together separate LAN, wireless, and security tools.

talks.title: Don't Let Your Guard Down | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Cyber hygiene guidance covers password reuse, MFA options, mobile app permissions, phishing, and safe return-to-office device practices.
talks.summary:
Breaches across phishing, OT, and critical infrastructure still often start with credential habits the speakers see daily. The conversation frames password reuse as a major enabler: leaked databases fuel tools that apply common substitutions and keyboard patterns, then automate login attempts across many sites. Unique usernames and passwords, ideally via managers such as 1Password or LastPass, limit blast radius when one site leaks, though master vault passwords still need strong protection.

Multifactor authentication is urged, with SMS called out as weak against SIM abuse and apps that harvest messages. Stronger options include authenticator apps, spare backup phones, and hardware tokens such as FortiToken or YubiKey. On mobile, excessive app permissions, toll-fraud SMS abuse, and oversharing contacts or notes can undermine privacy. Phishing via believable email and SMS themes remains a core attack path; mitigations include awareness training, digital signatures, separate internal and external inboxes, and avoiding “enable macros” unless IT confirms a real need.

Closing guidance addresses hybrid return-to-office: home networks and BYOD may already be compromised, so bringing those machines inside corporate boundaries needs care. The through-line is layered hygiene—credentials, MFA choice, device behavior, and user judgment—to keep clean environments from becoming entry points.

talks.title: Tech Bytes: Batteries Plus Powers Its Branches With Fortinet SD-WAN | Packet Pushers Podcast
talks.teaser: Batteries Plus shows how Fortinet SD-WAN and SD-Branch keep its retail stores online with LTE failover and central policy.
talks.summary:
This sponsored Packet Pushers Tech Bytes episode looks at how Batteries Plus, a retailer of batteries, chargers and lighting with more than 700 stores, uses Fortinet SD-WAN and SD-Branch. Jason Thielen explains that the company's older firewalls offered no automated failover, so when a store's primary connection dropped, staff had to attach an LTE backup device and call the help desk, and sales were lost in the meantime. Today each store runs a terrestrial primary circuit with an LTE backup, and failover is usually seamless enough that staff rarely notice it.

Courtney Radke, a retail product manager at Fortinet, argues that connectivity has moved from a nice-to-have to a requirement for retailers, and that SD-WAN lets them open or close stores quickly without waiting weeks for circuit provisioning. On security, both guests say SD-WAN should have security built in rather than bolted on. Thielen describes separate wireless networks on separate VLANs for different in-store services, and central policies that push uniform URL rules and segmentation to every site so payment systems stay isolated.

The closing segment covers SD-Branch, which brings switching, wireless and WAN under one management platform so policy is set once and applied everywhere. Radke frames the value as integration, orchestration and automation, and both speakers tie this to a zero trust approach. The takeaway for multi-site retailers is that resilient backup links, consistent central policy and unified branch management reduce coverage gaps and operational blind spots.

talks.title: Cloud Security & Edge Computing Trends | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Discusses how multi-cloud and hybrid deployments strain security visibility, and one unified approach offered as a response.
talks.summary:
Vincent Wang joins the host to discuss the security problems organizations face as they run mixed environments of on-premises systems and several public clouds. They describe a common pattern: legacy applications stay on-premises while newer workloads move to one or more providers, and skills and staff shortages make the job harder. Adding clouds often brings more management consoles and security tools, so teams can end up with less visibility and control than they expected.

The conversation then turns to survey findings they cite. Faster time to market, better customer experience and cost savings are named as the main drivers for moving to cloud, and they argue that under pressure teams sometimes accept visibility gaps and imperfect configurations to protect customer experience. They also look ahead to edge computing, where workloads are spread across regional deployment points, and note that networking, application performance and security are often managed separately, creating bottlenecks.

As a response, Wang presents a unified security fabric approach, with hardware, virtual and integrated deployment options across cloud providers, consistent policies and a single point of management. He stresses that choices made now need not be throwaway, since components can be added or changed later. The session closes on a key takeaway for anyone weighing a multi-cloud or hybrid model: find the common layer that gives persistent visibility and control across data centers, clouds and edges, supported by integrations with AWS, Azure and GCP.

talks.title: Securing the 5G Future | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Explains how 5G's low latency and machine traffic shift security toward zero trust and edge devices.
talks.summary:
The two presenters open by framing 5G as a major step for businesses, offering higher bandwidth, very low latency and precise geolocation. Designed for machine-to-machine traffic rather than voice alone, it is expected to spread across IT, operational technology and industrial settings. They argue that organisations should plan for its security early and fit it into their wider security posture.

The discussion then turns to edge computing. Plants such as refineries and factories run time-critical processes locally, so the computers and connected valves or actuators there become attack surfaces that need protection. With every device effectively its own edge, the traditional perimeter no longer applies, and zero trust is presented as the answer: verify who is connecting, not just where. Behaviour analytics learn how each device acts under maintenance and under production, so unusual activity can be flagged or isolated without halting operations unless necessary. Multi-factor authentication and per-application access rules limit what a compromised device or user can reach. A Formula 1 analogy illustrates how a stolen credential can be exposed by abnormal driving behaviour.

The closing point is that protection must be broad, integrated and automated, forming one security fabric rather than a single control at one edge. CISOs should extend their existing posture to cover 5G, and the approach should stay open through APIs and connectors rather than locked to a single vendor.

talks.title: Securing Global Access with Fortinet and GCP's Network Connectivity Center | Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Demonstrates FortiGate firewalls linking AWS and Azure sites through Google Cloud's Network Connectivity Center hub.
talks.summary:
The demo presents a joint setup of Fortinet FortiGate and Google Cloud's Network Connectivity Center, aimed at organizations running applications across several clouds. The scenario places two remote sites, one in an AWS VPC and one in an Azure VNet, that need to reach each other, with Google's hub carrying the traffic between them.

An automation script, launched from a Linux machine, provisions the Google Cloud pieces: VPCs, subnets, FortiGate instances and NCC spokes. The presenter then builds an IPsec tunnel from the AWS side to Google Cloud and runs a ping between applications on the two clouds, which succeeds. Running the script again with different parameters adds a second spoke with a FortiGate in an eastern US region, so that an Azure workload can enter the network at a point closer to it and reach the California application over Google's network.

The presenter then shows dynamic route exchange between the FortiGates and Cloud Router in the VPC routes, and the AWS-side FortiGate learns the protected Azure subnet 10.1.2.0/24 over BGP. A final ping from the AWS application to the Azure application succeeds. The takeaway is that Network Connectivity Center can serve as a central hub for network visibility, and that this approach supports resilience and avoids dependence on a single cloud vendor while delivering services from any platform.

talks.title: Securing the Connected Building | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Explores securing IoT and OT systems in connected buildings, with advice on planning security into building architecture.
talks.summary:
This conversation looks at the security of digitally connected buildings, campuses and cities. The guest describes a network-as-a-service business that serves high-rise and multi-family residential buildings. As occupants return to offices after remote work, touchless access, elevators, HVAC, lighting and fire alarm sensors add IoT and OT devices that widen the attack surface. He describes attackers disrupting elevators, triggering fire alarm systems and shutting down heating and cooling, which causes costly outages for property owners.

The discussion then moves to segmentation and centralised control. The guest explains that a single security fabric lets his team set a policy once and push it to every site, which cut the staff time spent patching many separate systems. He stresses that building data needs protection wherever it sits, and that edge locations inside buildings need malware detection, intrusion prevention and next-generation firewall services.

For peers, he advises treating building complexity as a given, bringing a security architect into infrastructure planning from the start, and designing for both current and future needs. The overall message is that building systems must keep operating safely, and that security should be planned as part of the design rather than added later.

talks.title: State of Threats | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Researchers survey COVID phishing persistence, spear-phishing shifts, ransomware payouts, and leaks from public sample sharing.
talks.summary:
The discussion frames today’s threat climate as exhausting but not stagnant, highlighting continued investment in machine learning, intelligence sharing, and cross-industry collaboration while walking through concrete trends visible in telemetry and field work.

COVID-19 social-engineering campaigns remain a steady weekly drumbeat more than a year into the pandemic, with only the narrative changing—from lockdowns and reopenings to vaccines and related news hooks. Speakers warn that constant headlines breed numbness just as criminals refine impersonation, including emails that pose as corporate IT or security teams offering anti-phishing guidance while delivering malicious links. They tie this to ransomware-as-a-service “support” that mimics defender thinking, forum chatter about infiltrating security jobs, and a shift from profitable mass mail toward spear phishing, expanded business-email-compromise plays, and multi-million-dollar extortion against organizations attackers believe will pay discreetly.

Research and hunting practices receive equal attention: uploading suspect messages or files to open analysis platforms can leak sensitive corporate details that other gangs harvest for targeted attacks, so teams must scrutinize what cloud and sharing services do with submitted data. The exchange ends with a balanced view of industry wins—disruptions, takedowns, and a reported U.S. Department of Justice recovery of over two million dollars in Bitcoin linked to the DarkSide ransomware case—while stressing that enterprises still bear the burden of prevention and timely detection on the left side of the attack chain.
