talks.title: A Conversation on the Kill Chain | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Examines ransomware's shift to organized RaaS models and defensive strategies mapped across the cyber kill chain.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a discussion of how ransomware moved from high-volume, opportunistic encryption with modest ransom demands toward targeted "big game" campaigns backed by ransomware-as-a-service economics. Affiliates, commissions, and deep funding have stretched attack timelines so intrusions can resemble APT operations, with attackers dwelling on networks for long periods before striking IT systems that maximize financial pain.

The middle of the conversation covers how mature gangs behave like businesses: repeat negotiators, tiered pricing, optional "consulting," and leak or sale of stolen data when victims refuse to pay. Cryptocurrency and dark-web marketplaces supply capabilities across the attack chain, while defender visibility often remains fragmented across endpoints, WAN, data center, and cloud. The speakers tie this to defense in depth along the cyber kill chain—hygiene still matters but is insufficient alone—and stress integrated inspection, current threat intelligence, EDR/XDR, and machine learning to detect persistence and anomalies earlier.

Closing guidance for security leadership emphasizes shifting left before execution, baking actionable intelligence into security controls, planning incident response around dependencies between IT and OT, and pursuing integrated architectures rather than siloed stacks. A final precaution is proactive monitoring of underground forums to learn whether the organization, brand, or executives are already being discussed as targets.

talks.title: Tactics and Techniques of Cyber Adversaries | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Shows how to map adversary techniques to MITRE ATT&CK and test whether your defenses and detections actually catch them.
talks.summary:
Tony G, practice director of FortiGuard responder services, and red team expert Amar Lakhani discuss why organizations should measure their defenses against adversary behavior, not just high-level security frameworks. They argue that a penetration test run once or twice a year is a snapshot that goes stale quickly, and that attackers usually avoid obvious malware, relying instead on built-in tools such as PowerShell and system administration utilities that blend into normal activity.

The pair describe deception as a detection layer: honey accounts, honey files with embedded web bugs, and similar tripwires that act as early warning. When one of these is triggered, automation can isolate a workstation or user account before the intrusion spreads. For operationalizing MITRE ATT&CK, Lakhani recommends starting with a single threat actor and working through its full lifecycle, from initial access and persistence to credential theft. For each stage, teams should ask whether suspicious processes can be spotted, and how the security team would respond if an attack got through. He points to MITRE's open-source Caldera tool as a way to prepare a Windows test system for specific techniques, then check whether controls block the attack and whether the team detects it when they do not.

They note that threat actors reuse techniques and that the same methods appear across groups, so work on one actor carries over to others. They close by saying vendor assurances should be backed by your own testing, mapping each threat to ATT&CK and showing which defenses cover it. The framework, they argue, gives the industry a common language for discussing threats.

talks.title: Cloud and SD-WAN | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Explains how multi-cloud SD-WAN and cloud on-ramp link branches to cloud workloads under consistent security policies.
talks.summary:
This interview segment features Vince from Fortinet talking with host Rob about multi-cloud SD-WAN and cloud on-ramp. The conversation opens with the pressures of heavy cloud use: most organizations now run hybrid or multi-cloud environments, and teams struggle to keep policies consistent while absorbing extra overhead for network, security and cloud operations.

Vince describes three things customers ask for: a simple way to connect from a branch or campus to the cloud, optimized performance for the workloads they reach there, and automation that makes the setup easier for users to manage. He argues that applications spread across clouds, regions and data centers should be interconnected so users stay unaware of where they run. He also warns that unmanaged clouds create visibility gaps that attackers can exploit, and recommends centralized control and visibility through a security fabric with consistent policies.

The pair then turn to Fortinet's announced integration with Google Cloud's Network Connectivity Center, which makes it easier to deploy FortiGate and SD-WAN into Google Cloud. Fortinet already supports Azure Virtual WAN and AWS, and offers middle-mile connectivity through Megaport. The main takeaway is that multi-cloud adds complexity that organizations have to accept, and the goal is to keep security, network and cloud operations simple and seamless on one platform.

talks.title: FortiGate Video Filtering Security | FortiOS 7.0
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiOS 7.0 video filtering blocks or allows YouTube videos by FortiGuard category and by channel ID.
talks.summary:
This short demo walks through the video filtering security service added in FortiOS 7.0. The service lets an administrator filter YouTube by FortiGuard categories, or by individual channel ID for finer control over one channel, user or video. The setup is a typical branch network in the Security Fabric, with a FortiAP connected to a FortiGate that acts as the wireless controller and a client attached to the access point. The video filter profile combines category filters with channel overrides, and the firewall policy is switched from flow mode to proxy mode, with the profile attached and SSL inspection set to deep inspection.

Before the filter applies, an unsigned YouTube session plays a music video without issue, and the FortiGate web filter logs show no video entry yet. The demo then covers three cases. A channel override blocks videos once the viewer signs in to the listed account, showing a replacement message and a blocked entry in the web filter logs with detail in the raw log view. A FortiGuard sports category block stops a sports video after a refresh, logged under that category. A knowledge category set to allow lets a video from a listed Fortinet channel keep playing.

The practical takeaway is that category rules and per-channel overrides can sit together in one profile, and that the logs confirm which action was applied to each video. The demo does not cover how the filter behaves on other platforms or with other SSL configurations.

talks.title: SOAR On-ramp with FortiSOAR Management Extension Application | SOAR
talks.teaser: A demo delivers Fortinet's SOC maturity model and FortiSOAR management extension setup in FortiAnalyzer for growing teams.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with Fortinet's SOC maturity model for organizations that start small without a dedicated security operations team. Early priorities favor quick deployment, easy maintenance, and visibility through FortiAnalyzer for fabric analytics, central logging, and infrastructure-wide insight. As requirements increase, FortiAnalyzer's built-in SOAR handles basic workflows such as automatic incident creation when a compromised host is detected and quarantining malware-affected endpoints.

At larger scale, with multiple vendors and heavier data volumes, FortiSOAR is positioned to complement FortiAnalyzer for aggregation, processing, and multi-vendor visibility, often alongside a dedicated SOC team and streamlined processes. Teams may adopt SOAR through providers or self-guided content packs. Customers already on FortiAnalyzer can add the FortiSOAR management extension without a full node, gaining the same capabilities as a dedicated installation until they need a separate node for performance.

The demo covers installation from FortiAnalyzer or FortiManager: select the ADOM, open Management Extension, enable FortiSOAR if it is grayed out, and use an interface matching a dedicated FortiSOAR node for threat intelligence, automation, orchestration, and incident response. The closing point is a seamless upgrade path to a dedicated node without operational interruption as the security program matures.

talks.title: Tech Bytes: Auto Dealer Takes Network Control With Fortinet | Packet Pushers Podcast
talks.teaser: A dealership group explains taking its 19-site network in-house with Fortinet SD-WAN and PCI segmentation.
talks.summary:
A car dealership group with 19 locations across the United States explains why it moved network operations away from an outside managed service provider. The IT director and a system administrator describe slow support and difficulty getting answers as the main problems, which led them to run the network themselves and standardize on Fortinet equipment.

They began with firewalls, then added switches and wireless access points, managing all of it from a central console so one security policy can be pushed to every site. SD-WAN was adopted so both internet connections could carry traffic at the same time, instead of leaving a secondary link idle. For compliance, card terminals sit on an isolated VLAN, and the central console gives auditors quick evidence of segmentation in place of paper configurations. Guest Wi-Fi runs on the same hardware but in a separate segment from business traffic, with no URL filtering applied.

The guests say that visibility into policies, devices and bandwidth has cut the time they spend waiting on support, and that an integration can quarantine a compromised host. They say the arrangement has not added late nights, though one admits some lingering unease about the setup.
